institutional perspective of Academy of Managed Care Pharmacy on AMCP Dossier

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000178
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept AMCP Dossier
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Academy of Managed Care Pharmacy
has page URL https://www.amcp.org/resource/amcp-format-formulary-submissions-guidance
has perspective summary AMCP describes its Format for Formulary Submissions as advisory and not mandatory. It sets out the clinical and economic evidence that manufacturers present to health care decision-makers in a standard, living product dossier that runs from the pre-approval phase through the post-approval period. The Format recommends economic analyses and models that project budget and cost impact on the decision-maker's organisation and members and assess cost-effectiveness, with assessments of economic value applying only to approved product dossiers. Format 5.0 of April 2024 remains the current version; public comment on version 6.0 closed on 22 April 2026.
has perspective title Advisory Dossier Format, With Economic Value for Approved Products Only
has primary source label Academy of Managed Care Pharmacy, AMCP Format for Formulary Submissions web page (accessed 4 October 2026), covering Format 5.0 (April 2024) and the Format 6.0 public comment period (17 March to 22 April 2026)
has wiki record identifier amcp-dossier

institutional perspective of Actuarial Standards Board on Actuarial Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000058
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Actuarial Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Actuarial Standards Board
has page URL https://www.actuarialstandardsboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/asop005_186.pdf
has perspective summary The Actuarial Standards Board defines the unpaid claims liability as the unpaid portion of incurred claims, including unreported claims and claims reported but not yet paid. Its standard describes the development, or lag, method, which groups past claims by the periods in which they were incurred and paid to build a payment pattern, as appropriate and widely used for short-term benefits. Projection methods may supplement it for the most recent months, and the actuary should consider plan provisions, economic influences, claimant behaviour, seasonality and credibility.
has perspective title ASOP No. 5 on Estimating Incurred Health Claims and Unpaid Claims
has primary source label Actuarial Standards Board, Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 5: Incurred Health and Disability Claims, revised edition, Doc. No. 186, March 2017, effective 1 September 2017, sections 2.5, 2.17, 3.2, 3.4.1 and 3.4.2
has wiki record identifier actuarial-analysis
is perspective of body Actuarial Standards Board
isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

institutional perspective of Actuarial Standards Board on Actuarial Value

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000065
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Actuarial Value
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Actuarial Standards Board
has page URL https://www.actuarialstandardsboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/asop050_182.pdf
has perspective summary The Actuarial Standards Board defines actuarial value as the proportion of total allowed medical costs for a specified population that a health insurance plan is contractually obliged to pay. Its standard tells actuaries to use the HHS calculator when placing plans in metal levels and, for plan designs the calculator cannot accommodate, to keep data, methods and assumptions consistent with those underlying it. Unreasonable calculator results that regulators still require should be documented. Actuarial values calculated for premium setting fall outside the standard.
has perspective title ASOP No. 50 on Determining Actuarial Value Under the ACA
has primary source label Actuarial Standards Board, Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 50: Determining Minimum Value and Actuarial Value under the Affordable Care Act, September 2015, effective 31 January 2016, sections 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 to 3.6

institutional perspective of Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality on Outcomes Research

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000762
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Outcomes Research
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
has page URL https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1320b-12
has perspective summary US federal law directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the AHRQ Director, to conduct and support research on the outcomes, effectiveness and appropriateness of health care services and procedures. Priorities include conditions where many people could benefit, where services or outcomes vary widely among physicians and where spending is substantial, and the law also calls for research using claims data and patients' clinical and functional status. AHRQ's fact sheet describes outcomes research as seeking to understand the end results of care, including quality of life as well as mortality.
has perspective title Statutory Research on Outcomes, Effectiveness and Appropriateness of Care
has primary source label United States Code, Title 42, section 1320b-12 (Social Security Act section 1142, as added by Public Law 101-239, 19 December 1989), subsections (a) to (c); AHRQ, Outcomes Research Fact Sheet, AHRQ Publication No. 00-P011, March 2000
has wiki record identifier outcomes-research
is perspective of body Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality

institutional perspective of Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality on Random Sampling

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000817
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Random Sampling
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
has page URL https://meps.ahrq.gov/data_files/publications/mr38/mr38.shtml
has perspective summary AHRQ states that because the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey is a complex probability sample with stratification, clustering and unequal selection probabilities, methods that assume a simple random sample are generally not appropriate and can give biased estimates and inaccurate significance levels. Valid estimates and standard errors must use the survey weights and the design's strata and clusters. Standard software that assumes simple random sampling will usually underestimate the variance, so AHRQ supplies strata and cluster variables for Taylor series linearisation.
has perspective title MEPS Analyses Must Reflect Its Complex Probability Sample Design
has primary source label AHRQ, Methodology Report #38: Estimation Procedures for the 2023 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey Household Component, AHRQ Publication No. 26-0018, August 2026, sections 1 and 6 (Variance Estimation)
has wiki record identifier random-sampling
is perspective of body Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

institutional perspective of American Heart Association, American College of Cardiology and Heart Failure Society of America on NYHA Functional Classification

has display order 2

has page URL https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001063
has perspective summary The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline describes the NYHA functional class as a subjective assessment by a clinician that can change over time. It states that reproducibility and validity can be limited and that the class can be inconsistently assessed from one clinician to another, resulting in poor reproducibility. The guideline also states that the NYHA functional classification is an independent predictor of mortality and that it is widely used to determine eligibility for treatment.
has perspective title NYHA Class Is a Subjective Clinician Assessment That Predicts Mortality

institutional perspective of Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing on Affordability Threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000132
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Affordability Threshold
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
has page URL https://www.pbs.gov.au/industry/listing/procedure-guidance/8-procedures-positive-recommendation-list/8-5-finalisation-of-the-budget-impact
has perspective summary Australian Government procedure guidance for the PBS states that the financial impact of every listing is considered across government, with the finalised cost considered by the Department of Finance and included in the recommendation to the Minister. The Minister for Health, Disability and Ageing can approve PBAC-recommended listings with a financial impact of AUD 20 million or less. Where the net cost to the Australian Government exceeds AUD 20 million in any of the forward years, the Minister refers the listing to Cabinet.

institutional perspective of Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing on Appeal Process

has display order 1
has institution label as shown Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
has page URL https://www.pbs.gov.au/general/independent-review/independent-review-pbs-info-for-applicants
has perspective summary Australia's Independent Review (PBS), set up under the Australia-United States Free Trade Agreement, is open to any applicant whose PBAC submission did not lead to a recommendation to list, or whose requested extension of an existing listing was declined. The review rests only on information already before the PBAC; where new evidence is relevant, a resubmission must be made instead. A convenor appoints a reviewer free of conflicts of interest, and the PBAC reconsiders the submission with the review findings and the sponsor's comments.
has perspective title Independent Review of PBAC Rejections, Limited to Evidence Already Considered

institutional perspective of Australian Government on Activity-Based Funding

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000056
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Activity-Based Funding
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Australian Government
has page URL https://federalfinancialrelations.gov.au/sites/federalfinancialrelations.gov.au/files/2026-04/nhra-2026-31-addendum-consolidated.pdf
has perspective summary The 2026 to 2031 Addendum to Australia's National Health Reform Agreement defines activity based funding as funding public hospital and health services for individual patients through national classifications, cost weights and national efficient prices developed by the Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority (IHACPA). For each ABF service category, the Commonwealth pays the volume of weighted services in National Weighted Activity Units multiplied by the national efficient price and an input contribution rate whose minimum rises from 40.5% in 2026-27 to 42.5% in 2030-31. The national efficient price also gives States a price signal for access, efficiency and quality.
has perspective title Activity Based Funding in the National Health Reform Agreement 2026 to 2031
has primary source label Addendum to the National Health Reform Agreement 2026-2031 (compilation, Federal Financial Relations), clause 15, Schedule A clauses A8, A20 to A22, A36 and A58, and Appendix A (Definitions)

institutional perspective of Australian Treasury on Aging-Driven Cost Growth

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000145
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Aging-Driven Cost Growth
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Australian Treasury
has page URL https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-09/p2026-797917.pdf
has perspective summary The 2026 Intergenerational Report projects Commonwealth health spending rising from 4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 6.2 per cent by 2065-66, and attributes around 33 per cent of that increase to population ageing. Treasury estimates the ageing effect against a counterfactual that holds the age and gender mix at June 2026 shares, finding the largest effect in aged care, followed by health and pensions. Other drivers include higher-quality services and decisions to subsidise new health technologies, and public hospitals account for over 60 per cent of the rise.
has perspective title Ageing Drives About a Third of Projected Health Spending Growth
has primary source label Australian Treasury, 2026 Intergenerational Report (21 September 2026), Part III, chapter 12, Box 12.2 and section 12.2 'Health'
has wiki record identifier aging-driven-cost-growth
is perspective of body Australian Treasury
isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Adherence

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000081
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Adherence
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary KCE's Belgian guidelines ask analysts to consider whether adherence, compliance or persistence matter for the technology and differ between trials and the real world, since this can substantially change effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. The impact of poor adherence should be quantified from appropriate evidence and explored in sensitivity analyses, and the cost of medicine wastage, including wastage from non-compliance, belongs in the reference case. Adjusting only incremental costs for compliance is incorrect: the reference case uses trial evidence, with the effect of non-compliance on both incremental costs and effects shown in a scenario analysis.
has perspective title Real-World Adherence and Medicine Wastage in Economic Evaluations
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (first edition 8 May 2025, second edition 18 June 2025), sections 4.2.4 and 5.9.3.3
has wiki record identifier adherence

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Administrative Data

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000094
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Administrative Data
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary KCE's Belgian guidelines describe administrative databases as a potentially useful source for measuring and valuing resource use, since they can provide cost information reflecting real-world conditions in Belgium, but analysts should check that the data are reliable and fit for purpose. Real-world data from registries or administrative databases are, under usual circumstances, unsuitable for showing added therapeutic benefit because there is no randomised comparison group. Such data remain useful for valuing specific variables that an economic evaluation needs in the Belgian context.
has perspective title Administrative Databases for Belgian Costs, Not for Added Benefit
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (first edition 8 May 2025, second edition 18 June 2025), sections 4.2.4 and 5.9 (Guideline 9)

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Cost-Effectiveness Plane

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000404
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness Plane
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary The Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre requires every economic evaluation to present a cost-effectiveness plane and a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, with uncertainty around incremental costs, incremental effects and ICERs shown by confidence intervals. When simulations are spread over different quadrants of the plane, the percentage of simulations in each quadrant should be reported. On the plane, incremental life years or QALYs sit on the horizontal axis and incremental costs on the vertical axis, with the comparator at the centre, giving four quadrants for the intervention.
has perspective title Plane and Acceptability Curve Required, With Quadrant Shares Reported
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (published 8 May 2025), Guideline 16 (sections 5.16 and 5.16.2) and Appendix 6.1
has wiki record identifier cost-effectiveness-plane

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Demand Forecasting

concerns wiki concept Demand Forecasting
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary For budget impact analyses, the Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre requires the anticipated size of the target population to be specified and the estimation method justified, preferably with Belgian epidemiological data, and its evolution over time with and without the new technology considered, including shifts in incidence and prevalence. Market share and the degree of implementation must be justified, with evidence-based estimates preferred. Where future patient numbers or market share rest on expert assumptions, comprehensive deterministic sensitivity analyses, including best and worst cases, are recommended.

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Differential Discounting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000484
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Differential Discounting
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary The Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre requires future costs to be discounted at 3% and future outcomes at 1.5%, a lower outcome rate intended to avoid penalising too strongly interventions that generate most of their outcomes in the future, such as screening and vaccination. Both rates are kept from earlier guidelines for consistency, since the change in the value of health over time is highly uncertain. Mandatory scenarios apply equal rates of 0%, 3% and 5% to costs and outcomes, the 3% scenario reflecting the base case in many other countries' guidelines.
has perspective title Lower Outcome Rate to Avoid Penalising Future Benefits
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (published 8 May 2025), Guideline 12 (section 5.12)
has wiki record identifier differential-discounting
is perspective of body Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Disutility

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000532
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Disutility
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary The Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre defines a disutility as the decrement in utility due to a particular symptom or complication. It states that combining utilities and disutilities for multiple adverse events or multimorbidity should be treated with caution, and names the additive approach, which applies a marginal disutility for each additional state, the multiplicative approach and the minimum approach. Because none of these methods is free of bias, the chosen approach must be justified and alternative plausible assumptions tested in scenario analyses.
has perspective title Rules for Combining Disutilities Must Be Justified and Tested
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (published 8 May 2025), Guideline 10 (section 5.10.2.2) and Glossary

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Equity-Efficiency Trade-off

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000565
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Equity-Efficiency Trade-off
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary The Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre requires all outcomes, such as QALYs, to be weighted equally in the reference case, whoever receives or is affected by the intervention. It notes that no societal equity weights have been set in Belgium and that such weights could shift with changing governments and health policy priorities. So that decision makers can discuss equity during appraisal, reports should show the QALYs gained in each target population in disaggregated form, for example highlighting unmet needs of disadvantaged groups.
has perspective title No Equity Weights in the Reference Case, QALYs Shown by Group
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (published 8 May 2025), Guideline 13 (section 5.13)
has wiki record identifier equity-efficiency-trade-off

has display order 4
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary KCE's Belgian guidelines state that no equity weights should be applied to outcomes in the reference case, so all outcomes such as QALYs are weighted equally regardless of who receives them. The guidelines note that Belgium has no standardised way to weight outcomes for equity, since no societal equity weights have been determined, and that such weights might change with governments and policy priorities. To support appraisal, reports should show QALY gains disaggregated by target population, highlighting unmet needs of disadvantaged groups.
has perspective title No Equity Weights in the Belgian Reference Case
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (first edition 8 May 2025, second edition 18 June 2025), Guideline 13 (section 5.13)

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Evidence Adaptation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000067
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Evidence Adaptation
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary KCE's Belgian guidelines state that resource use should be valued at Belgian prices rather than foreign prices converted to euros, and simple currency conversion of foreign values is not recommended except where the item is minor or no reliable Belgian data exist. Foreign costs should be inflated with the source country's consumer price index and then converted using purchasing power parity indices. Studies may not be excluded from the literature review merely for not being Belgian, and context-specific studies are preferred to transferring results from other countries.
has perspective title Belgian Prices Preferred Over Converted Foreign Costs
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (first edition 8 May 2025, second edition 18 June 2025), sections 5.2, 5.9.3.1 and 5.15, and appendix 8.2

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Markov Model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000693
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Markov Model
has display order 3
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary The Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre names decision trees and Markov models as the major categories of model and asks that a model be kept as simple as possible. For each health state in a Markov model the nature of the state, temporary or absorbing, should be specified and the choice of states justified. Transition probabilities should be presented, for example as a matrix, stating whether each is constant or variable, and the cycle length should be justified. The glossary notes that Markov models have a limited ability to remember earlier cycles.
has perspective title Markov Models With Specified States and Justified Cycle Length
has primary source label Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE), Belgian guidelines for economic evaluations and budget impact analyses: third edition, KCE Reports 400C (published 8 May 2025), Guideline 14 (section 5.14.2) and Glossary

institutional perspective of Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE) on Opportunity Cost

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Opportunity Cost
has display order 4
has institution label as shown Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre (KCE)
has page URL https://kce.fgov.be/sites/default/files/2025-05/KCE400_Method_guidelines_economic_evaluations.pdf
has perspective summary The Belgian Health Care Knowledge Centre states that costs in an economic evaluation are valued at opportunity costs. In practice these are approximated by market prices or reimbursement mechanisms, such as the Belgian per diem hospitalisation price, which are used in the reference case for consistency across analyses even though they do not always reflect real opportunity costs. Alternative cost estimates, for example from micro-costing, can be presented in scenario analyses with arguments for why they are more appropriate.
has perspective title Costs Valued at Opportunity Cost, With Prices as Proxies

Transition probabilities should be presented, for example in matrix form, with an indication of whether each probability is constant or variable, and the choice of cycle length should be justified. has perspective summary CIHI describes population ageing as a modest but steady driver of health spending in Canada. From 2014 to 2019, total health care spending grew by an average of 3.9% a year, of which population growth contributed 1.2 percentage points, public-sector inflation 1.5, ageing 0.6 and other factors 0.6. CIHI uses the 2014 to 2019 ageing effect as a proxy for 2023 to 2025 and treats other factors, such as technology, service use and system efficiency, as a residual.

The conditions are epileptic convulsions, chronic lower respiratory disease, asthma, diabetes, heart failure and pulmonary oedema, hypertension and angina, with discharges by death excluded and cardiac procedure cases excluded from some groups. institutional perspective of Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Attack Rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000222
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Attack Rate
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
has page URL https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/section2.html
has perspective summary CDC's epidemiology training text lists attack rate, risk and cumulative incidence as synonyms for incidence proportion: new cases during a specified period divided by the population at the start, a proportion because every case is also in the denominator. In outbreaks the term means the risk over a period such as the outbreak's duration. An overall attack rate divides all new cases by the whole population, a food-specific rate uses people who ate a given food, and a secondary attack rate counts cases among contacts, often with household members minus primary cases as the denominator.
has perspective title Attack Rate as Incidence Proportion in Outbreak Settings
has primary source label Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, third edition (SS1978), Lesson 3: Measures of Risk, Section 2: Morbidity Frequency Measures, page last reviewed 18 May 2012 (CDC archive)

institutional perspective of Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Case Fatality Rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000311
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Case Fatality Rate
has display order 1
has institution label as shown Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
has page URL https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/section3.html
has perspective summary CDC defines the case fatality rate as the proportion of persons with a particular condition who die from that condition, and treats it as a measure of the severity of the condition. Because it is a proportion, its numerator is restricted to deaths among the cases in its denominator, although the two time periods need not be the same, and some epidemiologists prefer the term case fatality ratio. It differs from the death-to-case ratio, whose deaths in a period need not come from the new cases counted in that period.
has perspective title A Proportion of Cases Who Die, Measuring Severity
has primary source label Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, third edition, Lesson 3 (Measures of Risk), Section 3 (Mortality Frequency Measures), archived page last reviewed 18 May 2012

institutional perspective of Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Cost-Benefit Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000388
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Benefit Analysis
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
has page URL https://www.cdc.gov/polaris/php/economics/cost-benefit.html
has perspective summary CDC's POLARIS economics guidance describes cost-benefit analysis as comparing the costs and benefits of an intervention with both expressed in monetary units. Unlike cost-effectiveness analysis, it places a monetary value on health outcomes, counting benefits such as medical costs averted, productivity gains and the monetary value of health improvements. The output is net benefit, benefits minus costs, which indicates the economic value an intervention provides to society and allows health and non-health interventions to be compared.
has perspective title Public Health Cost-Benefit Analysis and Net Benefits

has perspective summary In the Medicare Shared Savings Program, an accountable care organisation agrees to be held accountable for the quality, cost and experience of care of an assigned fee-for-service population, and must have at least 5,000 assigned beneficiaries. has perspective summary CMS regulations for the Medicaid Community First Choice option define activities of daily living as basic personal everyday activities such as eating, toileting, grooming, dressing, bathing and transferring, and separately define instrumental activities of daily living, such as meal preparation, managing finances and shopping. Eligibility requires an annual determination that, without these services, the person would otherwise need an institutional level of care, such as a nursing facility.

has perspective summary The CMS Office of the Actuary produces annual projections of US national health expenditure by source of funds, type of service and sponsor, with the latest running from 2025 to 2034. Its methodology rests on accepted econometric and actuarial projection techniques within a current-law framework that assumes no legislative change, with demographic inputs by age and sex taken from the Social Security Trustees' projections. CMS projects average spending growth of 5.4% a year against GDP growth of 4.1%, raising health's share of GDP from 18.0% in 2024 to 20.6% in 2034, and states that uncertainty increases with the projection horizon.

has perspective summary CMS's interim final rule on the Medicaid community engagement requirement makes states first try to verify compliance ex parte from reliable electronic data, and notes that screening questions can reduce administrative barriers. Its impact analysis assumes that 7% of applicable people who meet the requirement would still lose coverage for administrative or procedural reasons, such as unanswered verification requests. Under its 2024 prior authorisation rule, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP payers must decide expedited requests within 72 hours and standard requests within seven calendar days, generally from January 2026, and give a specific reason for each denial.

Its 2024 interoperability and prior authorisation rule requires Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP and federally facilitated exchange plans to run a FHIR-based Prior Authorization API from January 2027 to reduce the burden of prior authorisation. HHS will not take HIPAA enforcement action against covered entities that use an all-FHIR API instead of the X12 278 standard.

has perspective summary CMS pays for advance care planning, a voluntary face-to-face discussion of a patient's wishes should they become unable to make their own medical decisions, under CPT code 99497 for the first 30 minutes and 99498 for each additional 30 minutes. Discussions of 15 minutes or less are not billed as advance care planning. Medicare pays for it as an optional element of the annual wellness visit or as a separate Part B service, waives the deductible and coinsurance when it is billed with that visit under set conditions, and sets no limit on how often it is reported.

has perspective summary The CMS Office of the Actuary projects US national health spending growing 5.4% a year over 2025 to 2034, faster than GDP at 4.1%, raising health spending from 18.0% to 20.6% of GDP. Medicare grows fastest among major payers, at 7.7% a year on average. For 2029 to 2034, when Medicare growth is projected at 7.3% a year, the actuaries note that the baby boomer generation will enrol through 2029 and its oldest members will reach ages at which health care use typically increases.

has perspective summary CMS covers annual alcohol screening for Medicare beneficiaries, including pregnant women, and up to four brief face-to-face behavioural counselling interventions a year for those who screen positive for alcohol misuse without meeting criteria for dependence. Counselling must be furnished by qualified primary care practitioners in a primary care setting, which excludes emergency departments, inpatient hospital settings and skilled nursing facilities, and should follow the 5A's approach. CMS does not prescribe a screening tool, and based coverage on a grade B recommendation from the US Preventive Services Task Force.

Type institutional perspective record

has page URL https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/02/2025-21767/medicare-and-medicaid-programs-calendar-year-2026-home-health-prospective-payment-system-hh-pps-rate
has perspective summary Medicare's DMEPOS competitive bidding ranks suppliers' composite bids from lowest and sets the cut-off at the bid where cumulative supplier capacity meets or exceeds projected demand; bidders at or below it become contract suppliers. CMS's 2025 final rule replaces the maximum winning bid for the lead item, used since Round 2021, with the 75th percentile of winning bids, after median pricing before 2021, and limits the number of contracts awarded, because awarding too many weakens the incentive to bid competitively. Lead item pricing itself was adopted to stop unbalanced bidding across items.

has perspective summary Federal regulations allow premiums in the individual and small group markets to vary only by whether the plan covers an individual or a family, by rating area, by age and by tobacco use. Age variation may not exceed 3 to 1 for adults aged 21 and over, and tobacco variation may not exceed 1.5 to 1. The rate must not vary by any other factor, so health status and claims experience cannot be used. Family premiums are built by adding the premium for each member, counting no more than the three oldest children under 21.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
has page URL https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/out-of-pocket-maximum-limit/
has perspective summary Federal rules cap the cost sharing that an insured person pays in a plan year. Deductibles, copayments and coinsurance for covered in-network care count towards the limit, after which the plan pays 100% of covered benefits; premiums, uncovered services, out-of-network care and charges above the allowed amount do not count. For Marketplace plans the limit is 10,600foranindividualand10,600 for an individual and 10,600foranindividualand21,200 for a family in 2026, rising to 12,000and12,000 and 12,000and24,000 in 2027. The self-only limit is uprated each year by the premium adjustment percentage, and the family limit is twice the self-only limit.

has perspective summary CMS states that, without an adjustment for health status, Medicare Advantage plans would have a strong incentive to target the enrolment of beneficiaries who are healthier than average, and that selection can arise from plan practices such as high copayments for specialist visits. It counters this with risk adjustment and benefit-related policies. For the individual and small group markets, CMS describes risk adjustment payments to issuers whose plans attract higher-risk members, such as people with chronic conditions, as reducing the incentive to design benefits or marketing to avoid them.

has perspective summary In its FY 2027 inpatient prospective payment final rule, CMS distinguishes real case-mix change, meaning actual changes in the mix and resource needs of Medicare patients, from changes in documentation and coding that assign cases to higher-weighted DRGs without higher resource requirements. Federal law lets CMS adjust payments to remove the effect of coding or classification changes that do not reflect real case mix. With real case-mix growth projected at 0.5% a year, CMS sought public input on a default maximum threshold above which growth could prompt a prospective payment reduction.

has perspective summary CMS requires network-based Medicare Advantage plans to meet maximum time and distance standards, which measure the relationship between the approximate locations of beneficiaries and of network providers and facilities, and which vary by county type. For primary care the base standard is 10 minutes and 5 miles in large metro counties, rising to 70 minutes and 60 miles in counties with extreme access considerations. At least 90% of beneficiaries in large metro and metro counties, and 85% elsewhere, must have at least one provider of each specialty type within the standards.

has perspective summary Under Medicare, a provider or supplier accredited through a CMS-approved accrediting organisation's programme is deemed to meet the Medicare conditions, and for some provider types seeking this deemed status is voluntary. has display order 1

has perspective summary CMS's Part D Star Ratings measure adherence to diabetes medications, RAS antagonists and statins as the share of beneficiaries with a proportion of days covered of 80% or more. PDC is the share of days in the treatment period covered by claims for the same drug or another in its class, from the first fill, with at least two fills and a treatment period of at least 91 days. Overlapping fills of the same drug are shifted, and inpatient and skilled nursing stays are removed. Each adherence measure carries a weight of 3.

has perspective summary CMS's HealthCare.gov glossary defines urgent care as care for an illness, injury or condition "serious enough that a reasonable person would seek care right away, but not so severe it requires emergency room care". For Medicare Advantage, federal regulation defines urgently needed services as non-emergency covered services immediately required for an unforeseen illness, injury or condition while the member is outside the plan's service area or its network is unavailable, and using the plan is not reasonable. Plans must pay for them inside or outside the network, regardless of prior authorisation, with cost sharing capped at the professional services limit.

has perspective summary CMS describes the AHEAD Model as a voluntary state total cost of care model aimed at multi-payer alignment. The participating states, Maryland in Cohort 1, Connecticut and Hawaii in Cohort 2, and Rhode Island and New York in Cohort 3, are held accountable for statewide or sub-state cost targets for Medicare fee-for-service and across all payers, and for statewide quality targets, with state Medicaid agencies aligning with CMS on hospital global budgets. The model also selects Geo AHEAD entities by competitive bidding to take total cost of care accountability, and runs to 31 December 2035 for all cohorts.

has perspective summary Under Medicare Part A, CMS treats an inpatient admission as generally appropriate when the admitting physician expects hospital care to cross two midnights, with shorter inpatient stays allowed on documented clinical judgement and inpatient-only procedures exempt from the benchmark. Former exclusions, such as extensive blood loss or major invasion of body cavities, became safety factors for physicians to weigh.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
has page URL https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/prospective-payment-systems/acute-inpatient-pps
has perspective summary Under the Medicare inpatient prospective payment system, each case is assigned to a diagnosis-related group, and each group has a payment weight based on the average resources used to treat Medicare patients in it. The base payment rate, with its labour-related share adjusted by the area wage index, is multiplied by the DRG relative weight. Percentage add-on payments follow for hospitals serving a high share of low-income patients and for approved teaching hospitals, and unusually costly outlier cases receive an additional payment.

has perspective summary Under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, national relative values for work, practice expense and malpractice, adjusted for geographic cost differences, are multiplied by a conversion factor to give payment rates. institutional perspective of Cochrane on Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Cochrane
has page URL https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-10
has perspective summary The Cochrane Handbook states that a generic inverse-variance meta-analysis needs an effect estimate and its standard error from each study, and that a fixed-effect analysis assumes all estimates target the same underlying effect. It warns that the chi-squared test for heterogeneity has low power when studies are few or small and that thresholds for interpreting I-squared can be misleading. Simulation studies favour other between-study variance estimators, such as Paule and Mandel or REML, over DerSimonian and Laird, and random-effects pooling gives relatively more weight to smaller studies.
has perspective title Inverse-Variance Pooling, Heterogeneity and Random Effects

has perspective summary The Community Preventive Services Task Force recommends increasing the unit price of alcohol by raising taxes, on strong evidence from a review of 73 studies, and expects public health effects to be proportional to the size of the increase. Reported price elasticities were -0.50 for beer, -0.64 for wine, -0.79 for spirits and -0.77 for total alcohol, and higher prices were consistently linked to fewer motor vehicle crashes and less cirrhosis mortality. Taxes levied on volume erode with inflation unless adjusted regularly.

has perspective summary The CIOMS international ethical guidelines require, before research with children or adolescents, both permission from a parent or legally authorised representative and the child's assent, obtained in keeping with capacity after information suited to the child's maturity. Assent is a process, not merely the absence of dissent, and is preferably written for literate children. A child's refusal or deliberate objection must be respected even if parents consent, unless the research offers treatment unavailable elsewhere with a clear prospect of clinical benefit and is judged the best available medical option.

has perspective summary CIOMS defines conflicts of interest as conflicts between the primary goal of health-related research and secondary interests such as scientific recognition or financial gain. Research institutions should develop policies to mitigate them, researchers should disclose relevant interests to research ethics committees, and committees should evaluate each study in light of those interests. Measures should be proportional, from disclosure for a minor conflict to excluding a researcher, and a committee may decide not to approve a study when a serious conflict cannot be adequately mitigated.

institutional perspective of Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences on Equipoise

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences
has page URL https://cioms.ch/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/WEB-CIOMS-EthicalGuidelines.pdf
has perspective summary The CIOMS ethical guidelines, prepared with the World Health Organization, hold that participants in a control group should, as a general rule, receive an established effective intervention. When there is credible uncertainty about whether that intervention is superior to an investigational agent, which the guidelines call clinical equipoise, the two may be compared directly, because participants are not deprived of care believed to be effective. Withholding an established intervention instead requires compelling scientific reasons and no more than a minor increase above minimal risk.
has perspective title Credible Uncertainty Permits Comparison Against an Established Intervention
has primary source label Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences, International Ethical Guidelines for Health-related Research Involving Humans (Geneva 2016, prepared in collaboration with WHO), Guideline 5, Choice of control in clinical trials, and commentary

has perspective summary The Dutch general guidance treats social cost-benefit analysis as an information tool for the ex ante assessment of policy options. It sets out the effects, risks and uncertainties of a measure and values the resulting costs and benefits to society as a whole in euros, including effects without a market price such as nature and community safety, to give a balance of benefits minus costs. The analysis does not value how different groups experience these effects but can reveal them, and it is not considered appropriate where human dignity or moral values are the main consideration.
has perspective title Social Cost-Benefit Analysis as an Ex Ante Policy Information Tool

institutional perspective of CPB and PBL (Netherlands) on Willingness to Pay

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000920
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Willingness to Pay
has display order 4
has institution label as shown CPB and PBL (Netherlands)
has page URL https://www.pbl.nl/uploads/default/downloads/pbl-cpb-2015-general-guidance-for-cost-benefit-analysis_01512.pdf
has perspective summary The Dutch general guidance for social cost-benefit analysis states that welfare changes caused by policy measures are expressed through people's willingness to pay for their positive effects. Market prices are used as far as possible, and the valuation of non-priced effects must be based on willingness to pay, so valuations based on expert judgement are not acceptable. Revealed preference methods rest on observed behaviour but may value an effect only partially, while stated preference methods suit existence values but can be biased. The same willingness to pay approach is required for health and social care markets.
has perspective title Non-Priced Effects in Dutch Cost-Benefit Analysis Valued by Willingness to Pay
has primary source label CPB Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis and PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency, General Guidance for Cost-Benefit Analysis (2015), sections 3.1 and 7.1, footnotes 12 and 59, and Chapter 8 box on willingness to pay and health and social care markets

has perspective summary The NHS Constitution for England gives patients a right to start consultant-led treatment within a maximum of 18 weeks from referral for non-urgent conditions. Where this is not possible, the commissioning integrated care board or NHS England must take all reasonable steps to offer suitable alternative providers able to treat the patient sooner. The right ceases to apply where the patient chooses to wait longer, delay is in the patient's best clinical interests, active monitoring is clinically appropriate or treatment is no longer necessary. Maternity services and services that are not consultant-led are outside the right.

has perspective summary EMA states that a generic applicant is not required to provide the results of pre-clinical tests and clinical trials if it can show that the product is a generic of a reference medicinal product authorised in the EU for at least 8 years. has perspective summary The CHMP may grant a conditional marketing authorisation on less comprehensive clinical data than normally required for medicines for seriously debilitating or life-threatening diseases, including orphan medicines, or for a public health emergency. All criteria must be met: a positive benefit-risk balance, the likelihood that comprehensive data will follow, an unmet medical need, and a benefit of immediate availability that outweighs the risk of data still being required. has perspective summary EMA's guideline on anticancer medicines asks development programmes to study secondary resistance to treatment alongside primary resistance. has perspective summary ICH E10, adopted by EMA, describes an active control trial as one in which subjects are randomly assigned to the test treatment or to an active control treatment. A non-inferiority or equivalence trial needs assay sensitivity, deduced from historical evidence that similarly designed trials regularly distinguished effective treatments from less effective or ineffective ones, and from appropriate trial conduct. Without that historical evidence, showing efficacy through non-inferiority should not be attempted, and the margin cannot exceed the smallest effect the active drug would reliably be expected to have against placebo.

has perspective summary EMA's reflection paper, still its current effective version, says design modifications in a phase III trial contradict its confirmatory nature and will rarely be acceptable without further justification. The interim analysis and the anticipated type of modification must be described and justified in the protocol, and adaptations introduced without proper planning make the trial exploratory. An adaptive design must control the pre-specified type I error, give correct estimates and confidence intervals for the treatment effect, and pre-plan methods to assess homogeneity across stages. ICH E20 on adaptive designs remains a Step 2b draft at EMA.
has perspective title Adaptations to Confirmatory Trials Must Be Planned and Justified
has primary source label European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, Reflection paper on methodological issues in confirmatory clinical trials planned with an adaptive design (CHMP/EWP/2459/02, adopted 18 October 2007), executive summary

institutional perspective of EMA on Additive Interaction Scale

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Additive Interaction Scale
has display order 2
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/scientific-guidelines/investigation-subgroups-confirmatory-clinical-trials
has perspective summary EMA's guideline on subgroups in confirmatory trials states that statistical interactions are scale and model dependent: interactions in linear models are departures from additivity, meaning differences in treatment effects on an absolute scale, while those in logistic or Cox models are departures from a multiplicative model. A similar relative effect across subgroups can still give a larger absolute effect in severe disease that offsets the risks and a smaller one in mild disease that does not. Interactions should be explored first on the usual scale for the endpoint, with supplementary analyses on the complementary scale where inconsistency appears.
has perspective title Statistical Interactions Are Scale and Model Dependent

has perspective summary In the EU, ICH M12 on drug interaction studies came into effect on 30 November 2024, superseding most of EMA's own interaction guideline. M12 calls a well-performed clinical mass balance study the keystone for identifying a drug's principal elimination routes, recommends that its results be available before phase 3, and uses ADME properties to decide whether transporter data are needed. EMA keeps the mass balance appendix of its earlier guideline in force, which asks that recovery of radioactivity preferably exceed 90% of the dose and that metabolites above 10% of drug-related exposure be characterised.

has perspective summary The EMA states that commonly used methods for comparing survival times are valid only if censoring is uninformative, and that this assumption generally holds for administrative censoring of patients with complete follow-up and no event at the data cut-off. The extent of informative censoring should be discussed in the clinical trial report.

has perspective summary EMA states that all advanced therapy medicinal products are authorised centrally through a single evaluation. Its Committee for Advanced Therapies prepares a draft opinion on quality, safety and efficacy, on which the CHMP bases its recommendation to the European Commission. Developers unsure whether a product is an ATMP can use an optional classification procedure, set up to settle borderline questions early, for example with medical devices. The committee issues a scientific recommendation within 60 days of receiving the request, after consulting the Commission, and summaries of outcomes are published.

has perspective summary EMA describes medication errors as the most common preventable cause of undesired adverse events in medication practice. Under EU pharmacovigilance law, adverse reactions resulting from medication errors are reported to EudraVigilance like other suspected adverse reactions, while errors without harm, intercepted errors and potential errors should be recorded but are not valid individual case safety reports. Marketing authorisation holders summarise medication errors in periodic safety update reports whether or not harm occurred, and reflect the risk of errors in risk management plans.

has perspective summary EMA's pharmacovigilance guidance applies the EU definition of an adverse reaction as a noxious and unintended response to a medicinal product, covering use within or outside the marketing authorisation, including off-label use, overdose, misuse, abuse and medication errors, as well as occupational exposure. Spontaneous reports from healthcare professionals or consumers count as suspected adverse reactions unless the reporter excludes a causal link. Serious valid reports must be submitted to EudraVigilance within 15 days of receipt and non-serious ones within 90 days.

has perspective summary The ICH E9 guideline on statistical principles for clinical trials, adopted by the EMA, states that the treatment for the next subject should be allocated only once that subject's entry to the randomised part of the trial has been confirmed. Details that make the sequence predictable, such as block length, should be kept out of the protocol, investigators should generally be blind to block length, and the randomisation schedule should be filed securely by the sponsor or an independent party. In multicentre trials randomisation should be organised centrally, and deterministic dynamic allocation should be avoided.
has perspective title Next Allocation Released Only After Trial Entry Is Confirmed

has perspective summary The EMA's reflection paper on adaptive designs notes that interim analysis plans adjust the nominal significance level to maintain the overall level, and that statistical theory permits a flexible spending of the type I error over a trial. Interim data should generally pass from an independent statistician to an independent committee, and sponsor involvement is discouraged.

has perspective summary The EMA guideline on diagnostic agents treats ROC curves mainly as a way to select cut-off points for prospective use in confirmatory trials. In comparative trials with an active comparator, the area under the ROC curve can illustrate diagnostic performance by turning sensitivity and specificity into a single variable, although observed differences may be hard to interpret clinically. The guideline also asks for sensitivity and specificity with confidence intervals, cut-off values fixed in the protocol before the data are evaluated, and discussion of the effect of disease prevalence on predictive values.

has perspective summary EMA's reflection paper on AI in the medicinal product lifecycle makes the trial sponsor, applicant or marketing authorisation holder responsible for ensuring that all algorithms, models, datasets and data pipelines are fit for purpose, with scrutiny scaled to patient risk and regulatory impact. In late-stage confirmatory trials, models used for high-impact purposes such as the primary endpoint should be tested on prospectively generated data, incremental learning is not accepted, and the data pipeline and models should be frozen and documented in the statistical analysis plan before unblinding. AI applications affecting indication or posology count as high risk.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-missing-data-confirmatory-clinical-trials_en.pdf
has perspective summary EMA's guideline on missing data in confirmatory trials states that trials should aim to capture all data from all patients, including those who discontinue treatment, and that simply ignoring missing data is not an acceptable option. There is no rule on the maximum acceptable amount, but a substantial proportion can leave efficacy unestablished. Because every handling method rests on assumptions that cannot be verified, methods must be pre-specified in the protocol or analysis plan, and robustness should almost always be checked with sensitivity analyses making different assumptions.
has perspective title No Maximum for Missing Data, but Ignoring It Is Not Acceptable
has primary source label European Medicines Agency, Guideline on missing data in confirmatory clinical trials (EMA/CPMP/EWP/1776/99 Rev. 1, adopted 2010, legal effective date 1 January 2011), executive summary and sections 5.1 and 7

has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-evaluation-anticancer-medicinal-products-revision-6_en.pdf
has perspective summary EMA describes basket designs as studying one drug or combination in a population made up of different diseases, usually defined in oncology by a presumed response-predictive biomarker; without an internal control, each basket resembles a separate single-arm trial. When baskets are pooled, a homogeneous treatment effect must be supported upfront by mechanistic, pre-clinical and pharmacodynamic data, and sponsors must make it convincingly plausible that interaction with tumour site or histology is negligible. Scientific advice is strongly recommended before master protocols are used to generate the main evidence for marketing authorisation.
has perspective title Pooling Baskets Needs a Strong Upfront Case for Homogeneity

has perspective summary The joint HMA and EMA Big Data Taskforce found no commonly accepted definition and defined big data as extremely large datasets, possibly complex, multi-dimensional, unstructured and heterogeneous, which accumulate rapidly and can be analysed computationally to reveal patterns, trends and associations. A single clinical trial dataset does not strictly qualify, but pooled or linked datasets can. The taskforce held that data quality largely determines the validity of derived evidence, and recommended minimum data quality standards and distributed data networks for sharing sensitive healthcare data.

A planned reflection paper is to discuss whether their use can be reasonable, and the concept paper remains the current EMA document on platform trials.

has perspective summary EMA's policy states that having interests is not the same as having a competing interest, which exists when an interest may affect, or be reasonably perceived to affect, impartiality. has perspective summary Under ICH E9, as adopted by the EMA, blinding is intended to limit conscious and unconscious bias arising from knowledge of treatment, including in the assessment of end points, and the double-blind trial is the optimal approach. Where only a single-blind or open-label trial is possible, clinical assessments should be made by medical staff who are not involved in treating the participants and who remain blind to treatment. Primary variables in such trials should be as objective as possible.

has perspective summary The ICH E4 guideline, in operation at the EMA since November 1994, states that knowledge of the relationships among dose, blood concentration and clinical response, both effectiveness and undesirable effects, is important for safe and effective use, and that dose-response assessment should be an integral part of drug development. It notes that drugs have often been marketed first at excessive doses on the plateau of the dose-response curve, and that no single dose is necessarily optimal for all patients. The randomised parallel dose-response study is described as simple in concept and widely used with considerable success.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Hazard Ratio
has display order 5

has perspective summary In confirmatory oncology trials using progression-free or disease-free survival, the EMA expects the size of effect to be quantified by plotting estimated survivor functions, estimating the hazard ratio, estimating the median and other percentiles, and estimating the percentage of patients event free at particular time points. It cautions against over-reliance on differences in medians. Sensitivity analyses should be planned for important assumptions, including proportional hazards.
has perspective title Hazard Ratio as One Measure of Effect Size in PFS and DFS Trials

institutional perspective of EMA on Historical Control

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000623
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Historical Control
has display order 1
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-e-10-choice-control-group-clinical-trials-step-5_en.pdf
has perspective summary EMA applies ICH E10 as its scientific guideline on choosing a control group. It treats a historical control, a well-documented group of patients observed at an earlier time, as one form of external control, and warns that the lack of randomisation and blinding makes substantial bias inherent and impossible to quantify. An externally controlled trial should generally be considered only when belief in the superiority of the test therapy is very strong and the disease has a well-documented, highly predictable course. The control group, and any matching or adjustment, should be chosen before comparative analyses.
has perspective title External and Historical Controls Only for Highly Predictable Diseases
has primary source label ICH E10 Choice of control group in clinical trials, Note for guidance CPMP/ICH/364/96, Step 5, effective January 2001, sections 1.3.5, 2.5.1, 2.5.2 and 2.5.4
has wiki record identifier historical-control

institutional perspective of EMA on Last Observation Carried Forward

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000670
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Last Observation Carried Forward
has display order 1
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-missing-data-confirmatory-clinical-trials_en.pdf
has perspective summary The EMA guideline on missing data in confirmatory clinical trials describes last observation carried forward as a widely used single imputation method that gives an unbiased estimate of the treatment effect only under certain restrictive assumptions. In a condition that deteriorates over time, such as Alzheimer's disease, it is very likely to be overly optimistic in both arms and is not considered appropriate when active-arm withdrawals come earlier. Where a condition improves spontaneously, as in depression, it might be conservative. Any primary analysis is accepted only if an important bias favouring the experimental treatment can reasonably be excluded.
has perspective title LOCF Gives an Unbiased Estimate Only Under Restrictive Assumptions
has primary source label European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, Guideline on missing data in confirmatory clinical trials, EMA/CPMP/EWP/1776/99 Rev. 1 (adopted 24 June 2010, in effect 1 January 2011), sections 6.3 and 6.3.1
has wiki record identifier last-observation-carried-forward

isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

institutional perspective of EMA on Loss to Follow-Up

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000675
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Loss to Follow-Up
has display order 2
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-missing-data-confirmatory-clinical-trials_en.pdf
has perspective summary EMA's guideline says trials should aim to capture all data from all patients, including those who stop treatment, and that ignoring missing data is not an acceptable option. It sets no maximum acceptable amount of missing data but strongly encourages collecting outcome data after treatment stops. Complete case analysis is not recommended as the primary analysis of a confirmatory trial, methods must be pre-specified, and sensitivity analyses under different assumptions will almost always be needed. Whether censoring in a survival analysis can be assumed non-informative should be discussed in the protocol or study report.
has perspective title Missing Data Cannot Be Ignored in Confirmatory Trials
has primary source label European Medicines Agency, Guideline on missing data in confirmatory clinical trials (EMA/CPMP/EWP/1776/99 Rev. 1, adopted 2010, legal effective date 1 January 2011), Executive summary and sections 5.1, 6.2 and 6.5

institutional perspective of EMA on Minimisation (Trial Allocation)

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000706
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Minimisation (Trial Allocation)
has display order 1
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-adjustment-baseline-covariates-clinical-trials_en.pdf
has perspective summary The EMA accepts dynamic allocation, which measures imbalance on each prognostic factor separately and minimises a weighted sum of those imbalances, as a way to balance several factors at once when stratification is impractical, especially in small trials. It does not guarantee balance within combinations of factors, deterministic schemes should be avoided and each allocation should include an element of randomisation. Because conventional methods do not always control the type I error under dynamic allocation, re-randomisation methods should be considered in the analysis.
has perspective title Dynamic Allocation Accepted Only With a Random Element
has primary source label EMA Guideline on adjustment for baseline covariates in clinical trials (EMA/CHMP/295050/2013, adopted by CHMP 26 February 2015), section 4.2; and ICH Topic E9, Statistical principles for clinical trials, Step 5 (CPMP/ICH/363/96, September 1998), section 2.3.2

institutional perspective of EMA on Multiple Regression

has display order 1
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-adjustment-baseline-covariates-clinical-trials_en.pdf
has perspective summary The EMA guideline on adjustment for baseline covariates states that adjusting for a covariate strongly or moderately associated with the primary outcome generally improves efficiency and avoids conditional bias from chance imbalance. Covariates must be pre-specified in the protocol, only a few should be included, and the baseline value of a continuous outcome should usually be one of them. Variables measured after randomisation, or chosen because of imbalance observed post hoc, should not enter the primary analysis.
has perspective title Pre-Specified Baseline Covariates in the Primary Analysis
has primary source label EMA, Guideline on adjustment for baseline covariates in clinical trials (EMA/CHMP/295050/2013), adopted 26 February 2015, in effect from 1 September 2015, Executive summary and sections 5.4 to 5.6, 6.1 and 6.2

has display order 3
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/points-consider-switching-between-superiority-and-non-inferiority_en.pdf
has perspective summary EMA guidance states that when a superiority trial fails to detect a significant difference, interest may turn to the lesser objective of non-inferiority, which raises fewer problems if the protocol contains an acceptable, prospectively defined margin. Without one, the margin must be justified after the results are seen, which in many situations will not be possible. The comparator also needs consistent evidence of efficacy, and the confidence interval gives the precision actually achieved, superseding any power calculation made before the trial.
has perspective title Failed Superiority Trial Needs a Prespecified Non-Inferiority Margin
has primary source label EMA CPMP, Points to consider on switching between superiority and non-inferiority, CPMP/EWP/482/99, 27 July 2000, sections IV.2, IV.2.1 and IV.2.2

has display order 3
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-e-9-statistical-principles-clinical-trials-step-5_en.pdf
has perspective summary The ICH E9 guideline, adopted by EMA as a scientific guideline, states that blinding and randomisation are the most important design techniques for avoiding bias in clinical trials. Blinding aims to limit conscious and unconscious bias arising from knowledge of treatment, including its influence on subjects' subsequent care and their attitudes to the treatments. The double-blind trial is described as the optimal approach, and where only single-blind or open-label designs are feasible the protocol should explain the degree of blinding and other steps taken to minimise bias.
has perspective title ICH E9 Treats Blinding as a Main Safeguard Against Trial Bias
has primary source label ICH Topic E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials, Step 5, CPMP/ICH/363/96, EMA scientific guideline, legal effective date 1 September 1998, sections 2.3 and 2.3.1

has display order 3
has institution label as shown EMA
has page URL https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-evaluation-diagnostic-agents-revision-1_en.pdf
has perspective summary EMA's guideline on diagnostic agents uses the term standard of truth for the reference against which diagnostic performance is judged, and treats one as required in general. Its choice must be justified, and in confirmatory trials it should be established independently of the investigational agent and comparator results, without including information from the agent under test. Where no standard of truth is available, a surrogate standard, such as a combination of tests, clinical data and follow-up, may be used if fully described and justified.
has perspective title Standard of Truth Required for Confirmatory Diagnostic Agent Trials
has primary source label EMA CHMP Guideline on clinical evaluation of diagnostic agents (CPMP/EWP/1119/98/Rev. 1), adopted 23 July 2009, in effect from 1 February 2010 and currently under revision, sections 5.4.1 to 5.4.3

has perspective summary EU law defines an unmet medical need as a condition with no satisfactory authorised method of diagnosis, prevention or treatment, or one where the new medicine would be of major therapeutic advantage. EMA's CHMP grants a conditional marketing authorisation only if, among other criteria, the medicine fulfils such a need, and applicants must review available methods, quantify the need with medical or epidemiological data and justify how far the product addresses it. PRIME gives enhanced support to medicines with the potential to address an unmet medical need to a significant extent.

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's scoping guidance for EU joint clinical assessments defines a comparator as the treatment or treatments against which the technology under assessment should be compared, with each Member State defining comparators for the patient populations it requests. Comparators may be licensed or, depending on national context, unlicensed, and can include any intervention, best supportive care or watchful waiting. Naming standard of care alone is not sufficient: its components must be specified, and Member States should clarify whether background therapy applies in both groups.

institutional perspective of EU HTA Coordination Group on Added Therapeutic Value

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000073
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Added Therapeutic Value
has display order 4
has institution label as shown EU HTA Coordination Group
has page URL https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/7be11d76-9a78-426c-8e32-79d30a115a64_en?filename=hta_jca_scoping-process_en.pdf
has perspective summary Under the EU HTA Regulation, joint clinical assessment reports must not contain any value judgement or conclusions on the overall clinical added value of a technology. They are limited to the relative effects on the health outcomes in the assessment scope and the certainty of those effects. Member States must give due consideration to the reports but keep the competence to draw their own conclusions on overall clinical added value for their healthcare system. The HTA Coordination Group's scoping guidance adds that the listing of outcomes should be free of value judgement or ranking.
has perspective title Joint Clinical Assessments Leave the Added Value Verdict to Member States
has primary source label Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 of 15 December 2021 on health technology assessment, recital 28 and Articles 9(1) and 13(1)(a); HTA Coordination Group, Guidance on the scoping process, V1.0 of 13 November 2024 (adopted 28 November 2024), section 3.1.4

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Additive Interaction Scale
has display order 1
has institution label as shown EU HTA Coordination Group

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's guidelines for EU joint clinical assessments state that whether a variable is an effect modifier, and the size and direction of its effect, is specific to the scale on which the treatment effect is measured. In its example, a vaccine cuts risk from 10% to 5% in women and from 6% to 3% in men, so sex modifies the effect on the risk difference scale but not on the relative risk scale. Syntheses must pool relative treatment effects from each trial, and any analysis across levels of an effect modifier must be described and justified.
has perspective title Effect Modification Depends on the Scale of the Treatment Effect
has primary source label HTA Coordination Group, Practical Guideline for Quantitative Evidence Synthesis: Direct and Indirect Comparisons, adopted 8 March 2024 under Regulation (EU) 2021/2282, sections 3, 3.2.1 and 4.1; Methodological Guideline for Quantitative Evidence Synthesis: Direct and Indirect Comparisons, adopted 8 March 2024, section 6.1

institutional perspective of EU HTA Coordination Group on Adverse Event

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group requires joint clinical assessments of medicinal products to use the term adverse event, not adverse reaction or side effect, and to report adverse events irrespective of any causality assessment. The main report gives numbers and percentages per arm for all adverse events, serious adverse events, severe events such as CTCAE grade 3 or above, deaths related to adverse events, and treatment discontinuation and interruption due to adverse events. An appendix gives relative effects, including events by system organ class and preferred term with an incidence of at least 5% in any arm.

institutional perspective of EU HTA Coordination Group on Allocation Concealment
