has display order 3
has institution label as shown EU HTA Coordination Group
has page URL https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/guidance-validity-clinical-studies-joint-clinical-assessments_en
has perspective summary Guidance adopted by the HTA Coordination Group requires risk of bias in randomised trials used in EU joint clinical assessments to be assessed with the Cochrane RoB 1 tool, whose domains include biased allocation to interventions, which the guidance calls confounding bias rather than selection bias. Although RoB 2 was intended to replace RoB 1, the group judges RoB 1 currently preferable because it is well established and less time-consuming. A low overall rating requires low risk in all key domains, and assessors should describe the relevant trial characteristic, ideally verbatim, to make each judgement transparent.
has perspective title Cochrane RoB 1 Required for Trials in Joint Clinical Assessments
has primary source label Member State Coordination Group on Health Technology Assessment, Guidance on validity of clinical studies, V1.0 (adopted 19 September 2024 under Article 3(7)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2021/2282), section 4.1

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Average Treatment Effect
has display order 2
has institution label as shown EU HTA Coordination Group

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's guideline for joint clinical assessments names the average treatment effect and the average treatment effect among the treated as the most common estimands for propensity score methods. Assessors should evaluate whether the chosen estimand matches the inferential goal, and whether the propensity score method suits that estimand, noting that matching primarily estimates the effect among the treated. The assumptions of positivity, overlap and covariate balance must be checked and reported, and a violation of balance stated if any absolute standardised difference is 0.25 or more.
has perspective title Chosen Estimand, ATE or ATT, Must Match the Inferential Goal
has primary source label HTA Coordination Group, Practical Guideline for Quantitative Evidence Synthesis: Direct and Indirect Comparisons, adopted 8 March 2024 under Regulation (EU) 2021/2282, section 6.2.1

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Bayesian Information Criterion
has display order 2
has institution label as shown EU HTA Coordination Group

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's guideline for joint clinical assessments states that fractional polynomial network meta-analysis of time-to-event data requires selection of the most appropriate model for the hazard rates. This can be assessed using measures of statistical fit such as AIC, BIC or, in a Bayesian framework, DIC, together with visual fit to the observed hazards and survival functions and clinical plausibility. Because different fractional polynomial models can lead to different conclusions on relative treatment effects, sensitivity analysis is important.

has primary source label HTA Coordination Group, Practical Guideline for Quantitative Evidence Synthesis: Direct and Indirect Comparisons, adopted 8 March 2024 under Regulation (EU) 2021/2282, section 4.3.3

institutional perspective of EU HTA Coordination Group on Bayesian Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000277

concerns wiki concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis
has display order 4

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's guideline for joint clinical assessments accepts a Bayesian approach as a general alternative to frequentist meta-analysis, provided the required prior distributions are available and can be justified, and notes that it is especially useful with very few studies. In that setting a random-effects Bayesian meta-analysis with a weakly informative prior for the heterogeneity parameter may help, but the choice of prior needs a clear rationale and its impact should be explored in sensitivity analyses.

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's practical guideline names the Mantel-Haenszel method as the standard fixed-effect approach for meta-analysis of binary data. With rare events the Peto method can be applied, but not when treatment effects are large and trial arms are unbalanced, and with many double-zero studies a beta-binomial model can be used. The choice of method must be justified, with account taken of the number of events and of the effect scale, such as the odds ratio, risk ratio or risk difference.
has perspective title Mantel-Haenszel, Peto and Beta-Binomial Methods for Binary Data
has primary source label HTA Coordination Group, Practical Guideline for Quantitative Evidence Synthesis: Direct and Indirect Comparisons, adopted 8 March 2024 under Regulation (EU) 2021/2282, section 4.1.1

has perspective summary For joint clinical assessments, Member States define the comparators for each patient population they request, and more than one comparator can be relevant. Comparator treatments need not be licensed in the EU, can be drug classes, and should not specify dosage or regimen. has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's outcomes guidance requires uncategorised data always to be presented, with outcomes conceived as continuous, such as health-related quality of life, assessed by measures and methods consistent with that property, for example change in scores over time. Responder definitions can aid interpretation, but because they discretise continuously measured variables they should complement continuous scores rather than replace them. One measure of treatment effect should be pre-specified as the primary analysis to avoid data dredging and an inflated type 1 error rate.

has perspective summary For outcomes drawn from randomised trials, the HTA Coordination Group requires risk of bias in a joint clinical assessment to be judged with the Cochrane RoB 1 tool, whose domains include detection bias, both for each domain and overall. Judgements are made separately for outcomes where bias from lack of blinding differs, although outcomes sharing data collection, blinding and evaluation may be grouped. Reports should state who was blinded, such as participants, care providers or outcome assessors, instead of using the terms single blind or double blind.

has perspective summary The EU HTA Coordination Group's guidance on outcomes for joint clinical assessments regards anchor-based methods, which link a change in score to the patient's own global rating of change, as the most appropriate way to estimate a minimal important difference. Distribution-based methods use only the overall variability in scores and are criticised for not referring to what a change means to patients, although they are still used as secondary approaches to triangulate a plausible range. The guidance names Cohen's d values of 0.2 and 0.5 and one standard error of measurement as the commonest yardsticks.

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group states that a meta-analysis or network meta-analysis of hazard ratios requires the proportional hazards assumption to hold for all pairwise comparisons, assessed for every included study, preferably using individual or reconstructed patient data. If the assumption is implausible for any comparison, hazard ratios should not be meta-analysed, and restricted mean survival time or flexible survival models are the preferred alternatives. Submissions should report log-cumulative hazard plots, Schoenfeld residual plots and any statistical tests of the assumption.

has perspective summary The Coordination Group's guideline on direct and indirect comparisons notes that single-arm evidence is sometimes compared with historical controls or an unrelated contemporaneous study. The comparison then depends on every other aspect that differs between the groups and studies, so exchangeability probably does not hold, and no gold-standard method exists. Use of such evidence in joint clinical assessment is described as highly problematic, with a high risk of not providing valid and reliable relative effect estimates, and naive comparisons between arms of different studies should not be performed.

has page URL https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4ec8288e-6d15-49c5-a490-d8ad7748578f_en?filename=hta_methodological-guideline_direct-indirect-comparisons_en.pdf
has perspective summary The EU HTA Coordination Group guideline uses indirect comparison as the broadest term, covering network meta-analysis, population-adjusted methods and comparisons in disconnected networks. Where no direct trial evidence exists or several treatments must be compared, only anchored indirect comparisons through a shared comparator are appropriate, since they respect randomisation, while naive comparisons break it. These rely on exchangeability, assessed through similarity, homogeneity and consistency, and if any fails the result is unlikely to be meaningful. The Bucher method suits simple networks and should be avoided when random-effects pooling feeds it.
has perspective title Only Anchored Indirect Comparisons, Resting on Exchangeability
has primary source label Methodological Guideline for Quantitative Evidence Synthesis: Direct and Indirect Comparisons, adopted by the HTA CG on 8 March 2024 under Regulation (EU) 2021/2282, sections 1, 5 and 5.1 (Key Points 3)

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group names the inverse variance method as the standard fixed-effect approach for continuous data, although a random-effects model is usually the standard model. For frequentist random-effects meta-analyses with five or more studies it recommends the Knapp-Hartung method with the Paule-Mandel heterogeneity estimator. The choice of method must be justified with regard to the effect scale, including the mean difference, and random-effects results should report prediction intervals alongside confidence intervals.

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group states that where between-trial heterogeneity is too large for an overall synthesis but can be explained, syntheses should be run in groups of trials, in patient subgroups or by meta-regression, followed by a new assessment of heterogeneity. In joint clinical assessments, subgroup analyses are often more useful than meta-regression because they help target the right intervention to the right subgroup. Meta-regression needs enough studies to estimate every model parameter, and any such analysis must be described and justified.

has perspective summary The Coordination Group's methodological guideline treats network meta-analysis as a generalisation of meta-analysis that combines direct and indirect evidence and rests on exchangeability, judged through similarity, homogeneity and consistency. Only anchored indirect comparisons that respect randomisation in a connected network are generally appropriate, and a random-effects model is the appropriate choice in most practical situations. Frequentist and Bayesian approaches may both be used, with clear justification of any priors, and comparators beyond those needed to connect the network should generally be avoided.

has perspective summary The Coordination Group's validity guidance defines non-randomised controlled trials as trials that allocate participants by methods that are not random, such as investigator's choice, participant's choice or calendar dates. They allow direct estimation of relative effects, but non-random allocation breaks exchangeability and is likely to cause confounding bias, and any adjustment rests on the unverifiable assumption that all relevant confounders and effect modifiers are known and measured. Risk of bias should be assessed with ROBINS-I for each outcome, with domain and overall judgements.

has perspective summary The EU HTA Coordination Group guideline treats direct comparisons as standard pairwise meta-analyses of trials comparing the treatment of interest with the same comparator, after checking similarity and homogeneity. For fixed-effect pooling the standard methods are inverse variance for continuous data and Mantel-Haenszel for binary data. DerSimonian-Laird is no longer recommended, and Knapp-Hartung with the Paule-Mandel estimator is the standard random-effects method with five or more studies, alongside prediction intervals. With fewer studies or rare events, alternatives include a qualitative summary, Bayesian methods or the beta-binomial model.
has perspective title Knapp-Hartung as the Standard Random-Effects Method From Five Studies

has perspective summary The HTA Coordination Group's guidance for joint clinical assessments warns that the term cross-over is sometimes used incorrectly for treatment switching, which in a broad sense covers any move from the randomised intervention to another. Such switching is common in oncology trials and can influence estimated effects on survival, and statistical adjustment can reduce this bias although the methods have limitations.

has perspective summary ECDC's surveillance report on 2024 data finds the estimated EU incidence of MRSA bloodstream infections 20.4% below the 2019 baseline, already past its 2030 target of a 15% reduction. has perspective summary Recommendations of the expert group on clinical trials, published by the European Commission for the EU Clinical Trials Regulation, note that the Regulation lets national law require a capable minor's assent in addition to the legal representative's consent, and that the investigator must respect the explicit wish of a capable minor to refuse or withdraw. has perspective summary The European Commission states that the European Health Data Space Regulation, published on 5 March 2025 and in force from 26 March 2025, establishes a harmonised legal and technical framework for electronic health record systems. Manufacturers must certify that their systems meet security and interoperability criteria. Exchange of patient summaries and ePrescriptions is due in all Member States from March 2029, with medical images, laboratory results and hospital discharge reports following by March 2031.

For user testing, a satisfactory outcome is that 90% of participants can find the requested information and 90% of those can show they understand it, which means 16 out of 20 participants for each question. has page URL https://eurohealthobservatory.who.int/publications/i/health-system-efficiency-how-to-make-measurement-matter-for-policy-and-management-study
has perspective summary The European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies describes the core idea of efficiency as maximising valued outputs relative to inputs, while noting that it is often hard to make operational, particularly at health system level. It distinguishes allocative inefficiency, where the wrong mix of services or inputs is used given societal preferences, from technical inefficiency, which arises mainly at provider and practitioner level. It argues that efficiency measures must take account of external factors the health sector cannot control, such as the social determinants of health.

has perspective summary Under the EU health technology assessment regulation, joint clinical assessments carried out through the Member State Coordination Group cover only clinical domains: the health problem and current technologies, technical characteristics, relative clinical effectiveness and relative safety. EuroQol defines value sets as country-specific lists of utilities for every EQ-5D health state, anchored at 1 for full health and 0 for dead. has perspective summary FDA states that generic applications are termed abbreviated because they are generally not required to include preclinical or clinical data to establish safety and effectiveness. The applicant must instead show that its product performs in the same manner as the brand-name drug it references, the reference listed drug, delivering the same amount of active ingredient into the bloodstream in the same amount of time. FDA notes that the Hatch-Waxman Amendments of 1984 established bioequivalence as the basis for approving generic copies and created 180-day generic drug exclusivity.

has perspective summary FDA guidance for industry recommends that direct-to-consumer promotion present efficacy and risk probabilities as absolute frequencies, such as 57 out of 100, or as percentages. Where a study has a control group, the corresponding figure for that group should also be given. If a relative figure such as a 50% reduction in risk is used, the absolute probabilities should appear prominently alongside it, because consumers understand relative figures less easily and may misjudge a drug's benefit or risk.

has perspective summary Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the FDA may approve a product for a serious or life-threatening condition on an effect on a surrogate endpoint that is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. It may require postapproval studies to verify the predicted clinical benefit. Since the December 2022 amendments, the FDA may require these studies to be underway before approval and must set their conditions, such as enrolment targets and milestones, by the approval date. It may withdraw approval through expedited procedures if a sponsor lacks due diligence or a study fails to verify benefit.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/non-inferiority-clinical-trials
has perspective summary The FDA's guidance notes that the effect of the active control cannot be measured in a non-inferiority trial, because there is no concurrent placebo group, so its entire effect (M1) must be estimated from past performance, preferably in placebo-controlled trials. Ruling out a loss of M1 shows only that the test drug has some effect, so the margin is usually a smaller M2, the largest clinically acceptable degree of inferiority, set by clinical judgement. A larger M2 may be justified if the test drug has an important advantage, such as on safety.
has perspective title Non-Inferiority Margins M1 and M2 Based on the Active Control Effect
has primary source label FDA, Non-Inferiority Clinical Trials to Establish Effectiveness: Guidance for Industry (final, November 2016), sections III.A and III.C

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Adaptive Trial Design
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/adaptive-design-clinical-trials-drugs-and-biologics-guidance-industry
has perspective summary FDA's final guidance defines an adaptive design as a clinical trial design allowing prospectively planned modifications to one or more aspects of the design based on accumulating data from trial subjects. Trials intended to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness should adequately control the chance of erroneous conclusions, estimate treatment effects reliably, prespecify the design completely and maintain trial integrity. Adequately prespecified adaptations based on non-comparative data have no or limited effect on the Type I error probability, while conventional end-of-trial estimates that ignore the adaptations tend to overestimate the treatment effect.
has perspective title Prospectively Planned Adaptations With Controlled Error Rates
has primary source label U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics: Guidance for Industry (final, November 2019; docket FDA-2018-D-3124), sections II.A, III, III.A, III.B and IV

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/158178/download
has perspective summary FDA guidance calls a human radiolabelled mass balance study the most direct way to obtain quantitative information on a drug's absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, and says one should generally be conducted for all new molecular entities, with justification when it is not. Exceptions include biologics with known elimination pathways and drugs with 90% or more of the dose recovered unchanged in urine. The study should be run early, at the latest before late-phase trials. Total recovery should preferably exceed 90% of the dose, and metabolites above 10% of drug-related exposure should be structurally characterised.
has perspective title Mass Balance Study Expected for Every New Molecular Entity

has perspective summary FDA guidance on electronic health records and medical claims data notes that claims data, sometimes called administrative healthcare claims data, are information submitted to insurers to receive payment. Because a record exists only when a patient interacts with the health care system, sponsors should address continuity of insurance coverage and recognise that such data may miss non-prescription drugs and drugs not reimbursed by health plans. Operational definitions of study variables should be validated with measures such as sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value.

Requests are made with an IND or later, ideally by the end-of-phase 2 meeting, and FDA responds within 60 calendar days. has perspective summary FDA's postmarketing reporting rule uses the term adverse drug experience, meaning any adverse event associated with the use of a drug in humans, whether or not considered drug related, including events from overdose, abuse or withdrawal and any failure of expected pharmacological action. Applicants must report each serious and unexpected adverse drug experience within 15 calendar days of first receiving the information, and report all others periodically: quarterly for three years after approval, then annually. An unexpected experience is one not listed in the current labelling.

has perspective summary FDA's IND safety reporting rule defines an adverse event as any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of a drug in humans, whether or not considered drug related, and a suspected adverse reaction as one where there is a reasonable possibility that the drug caused it. Sponsors must report serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions within 15 calendar days and unexpected fatal or life-threatening ones within 7 calendar days. Any clinically important increase in the rate of a serious suspected adverse reaction over that listed in the protocol or investigator brochure must also be reported.

has institution label as shown FDA

has perspective summary FDA's draft guidance on overall survival in oncology trials defines it as the time from randomisation until death from any cause, and describes it as both an efficacy and a safety endpoint that drug toxicity can lower. All randomised oncology trials should be designed to assess overall survival so that potential harm can be evaluated, with a pre-specified safety analysis even when overall survival is not an alpha-controlled efficacy endpoint. Interim analyses for futility or harm should be event driven, and crossover should generally be limited because it can confound treatment effect estimates.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Alpha Spending
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/78495/download
has perspective summary FDA guidance states that testing every look of a group sequential trial at the conventional one-sided 0.025 level would inflate the Type I error probability. The Lan-DeMets alpha-spending approach specifies how that probability is spent while allowing flexibility in the number and timing of interim analyses, but timing chosen in response to accumulating results can inflate error, so sponsors should set a targeted number of analyses, an approximate schedule and a decision framework independent of the treatment effect. Conventional estimates tend to be biased towards greater effects, and adjusted methods exist.
has perspective title Lan-DeMets Spending With Safeguards on Analysis Timing
has primary source label U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics: Guidance for Industry, November 2019, section V.A (Group Sequential Designs)

has perspective summary FDA's guidance on manufacturer communications with payers states that health care economic information relates to an approved indication if it concerns the disease, its manifestations or its symptoms in the labelled population, even when it draws on information absent from the labelling. Its examples include modelling economic consequences beyond the duration of the labelled studies where labelling sets no limit on use, extrapolating trial results to other settings, such as from hospital to ambulatory care, and using burden of illness studies. has perspective summary FDA's draft guidance on non-interventional studies lists cohort, case-control and self-controlled designs as options for evidence on drug effectiveness or safety, and warns that inferences may be incorrect if estimates are affected by confounding or by other biases, such as patient selection, misspecified follow-up or differential outcome measurement. has perspective summary FDA's draft guidance on clinical outcome assessment endpoints lets sponsors use anchor-based methods to identify a meaningful score difference, mapping known meaningful differences on an external anchor, such as a patient's rating of change in symptom severity, onto the outcome measure. has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA

has perspective summary FDA guidance describes a basket trial as a master protocol testing a single investigational drug or drug combination in different populations defined by cancer type, disease stage, histology, number of prior therapies, genetic or other biomarkers, or demographic characteristics. Substudies are usually single-arm, activity-estimating trials with overall response rate as the primary endpoint, and a strong response signal may allow a substudy to expand to generate data that could support a marketing application. Each substudy needs specific objectives, a rationale for each population and a statistical analysis plan with sample size justification and stopping rules.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/78495/download
has perspective summary FDA guidance describes Bayesian adaptive designs as those using features such as predictive modelling to govern the timing and decision rules of interim analyses, assumed dose-response relationships, explicit borrowing of external information through informative prior distributions, or posterior probabilities as success criteria. The same principles apply as for adaptive designs without Bayesian features. For trials using Bayesian inference with informative priors, Bayesian statistical properties are more informative than the type I error probability, and simulations of operating characteristics can be particularly resource intensive because many Bayesian methods rely on Markov chain Monte Carlo.
has perspective title Same Principles as Other Adaptive Designs, With Simulated Performance
has primary source label US Food and Drug Administration, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics: Guidance for Industry, November 2019, section VI.B (Bayesian Adaptive Designs)

has perspective summary FDA's final guidance on voluntary patient preference information for medical devices lists best-worst scaling case 3 among the methods commonly used to quantify the trade-offs patients are willing to make between attributes, alongside discrete choice experiments, the threshold technique, swing weighting and multi-dimensional thresholding. Where the main research question is to prioritise endpoints, best-worst scaling case 1 may be sufficient, because it asks which item is most or least important and yields an ordinal ranking. Sponsors planning a best-worst scaling study are encouraged to describe its experimental design in the study protocol.

has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-314/subpart-B/section-314.80
has perspective summary FDA regulations require applicants with an approved drug application to review adverse drug experience information from every source, including reports in the scientific literature. Each adverse drug experience that is both serious and unexpected must be reported no later than 15 calendar days after initial receipt. For the literature, this requirement applies only to reports found in scientific and medical journals as case reports or as the result of a formal clinical trial, and each such report must be accompanied by a copy of the published article.

has perspective summary The FDA's statistical guidance on diagnostic test studies defines diagnostic accuracy as the extent of agreement between a new test and a reference standard, and recommends describing it with paired measures, such as sensitivity and specificity or positive and negative likelihood ratios, or with ROC analysis, together with confidence intervals. It discourages the stand-alone use of overall agreement, the share of all subjects classified alike, because overall agreement can look good when positive or negative agreement is very low. Its worked examples show that agreement changes with condition prevalence.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 2

has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/174976/download
has perspective summary FDA draft guidance on master protocols recommends that the control group for the primary comparison of each drug include only concurrently eligible participants, meaning those who could have been randomised to that drug but were concurrently randomised to control. Nonconcurrent controls risk bias from shifts over time in participants, trial conduct or standard of care. Other control data may be justified in rare circumstances, such as early-phase exploratory trials or rare diseases, and that choice should be agreed with FDA before the trial starts.
has perspective title Primary Comparisons Use Only Concurrently Eligible Controls

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 3
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/77832/download
has perspective summary FDA's 2009 guidance on patient-reported outcome measures defines construct validity as evidence that relationships among items, domains and concepts conform to a priori hypotheses about logical relationships with other measures or patient groups, and reviews convergent, discriminant and known-groups evidence. Its October 2025 guidance on fit-for-purpose clinical outcome assessments treats validity as a unitary concept, describing sources of evidence instead of types of validity, and asks sponsors to show that correlations with other measures and differences between known groups match relationships hypothesised a priori.
has perspective title Construct Validity as Evidence Against Prior Hypotheses

has perspective summary FDA guidance on diagnostic test studies recommends reporting the 2x2 table of results comparing the candidate test with the reference standard or comparative method, together with sensitivity and specificity pairs or agreement measures and their confidence intervals. Results should also be reported by site and by relevant clinical and demographic subgroups. FDA advises against revising the original 2x2 table through discrepant resolution, because the revised table rests on untested assumptions and its sensitivity and specificity are not valid estimates of performance.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Convergent Validity
has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/159500/download
has perspective summary FDA's final guidance on fit-for-purpose clinical outcome assessments uses the term convergent evidence, noting that it was previously called convergent validity, in line with testing standards that treat validity as a unitary concept. When a measure reflects the meaningful aspect of health only indirectly, sponsors may relate its scores to other variables more directly tied to the patient's experience, such as performance tests, and predict the expected correlation in advance. Correlation cutoffs should reflect the hypothesised relationship, and interpretation should allow for restriction of range and unreliability.
has perspective title Convergent Evidence for Clinical Outcome Assessments
has primary source label U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Patient-Focused Drug Development: Selecting, Developing, or Modifying Fit-for-Purpose Clinical Outcome Assessments, final guidance (Guidance 3, October 2025), section IV.H and footnotes 33, 42 and 43

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Criterion Validity
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/77832/download
has perspective summary FDA defines criterion validity as the extent to which the scores of a patient-reported outcome instrument are related to a known gold standard measure of the same concept. It reviews this property only in rare cases, such as a new sleep scale compared with polysomnography, because for most patient-reported outcomes no criterion measure can exist, as with any symptom known only to the patient. Where a criterion is used, sponsors should give a rationale for it, and FDA reviews the correlation with the instrument and the sensitivity, specificity and predictive value of the criterion measure.
has perspective title Criterion Validity Reviewed Only When a Gold Standard Exists
has primary source label U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Guidance for Industry. Patient-Reported Outcome Measures: Use in Medical Product Development to Support Labeling Claims, final guidance (December 2009), section III.E.2 and Glossary

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 4
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/71147/download
has perspective summary FDA defines the diagnostic accuracy of a new qualitative test as the extent of agreement between its outcome and the reference standard, the best available method for establishing whether the target condition is present. It recommends using a reference standard to estimate sensitivity and specificity, adjusted for verification bias when it is applied to only some subjects. Where only a non-reference comparator exists, results should be reported as positive and negative percent agreement rather than sensitivity and specificity, and FDA advises against discrepant resolution and the elimination of equivocal results.
has perspective title Accuracy Needs a Reference Standard, Otherwise Report Agreement

has perspective summary FDA classifies computerised behavioural therapy devices for psychiatric disorders as prescription-only Class II devices, used as an adjunct to clinician-supervised outpatient treatment. Special controls require clinical data validating the therapy model as the device implements it, and labelling that warns the device is not a standalone therapy or a substitute for medication. A 2024 classification for ADHD digital therapy devices adds clinical performance testing with a validated measure of effectiveness and capture of all adverse events.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/71195/download
has perspective summary The FDA generally defines disease-free survival (DFS) as the time from randomisation until disease recurrence or death from any cause. The most frequent use of the endpoint is in the adjuvant setting after definitive surgery or radiotherapy, and DFS can be an important endpoint in situations where survival may be prolonged, making a survival endpoint impractical. A treatment effect measured by DFS or event-free survival can be a surrogate endpoint to support accelerated approval, a surrogate endpoint to support traditional approval, or it can represent direct clinical benefit.
has perspective title Disease-Free Survival Can Support Approval as a Surrogate or as Direct Clinical Benefit
has primary source label US Food and Drug Administration, Clinical Trial Endpoints for the Approval of Cancer Drugs and Biologics, Guidance for Industry, December 2018, section on disease-free survival and event-free survival

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Distribution-Based MID
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/77832/download
has perspective summary FDA's guidance on patient-reported outcome measures states that the empirical evidence for any responder definition is derived using anchor-based methods. Distribution-based methods, using for example the between-person standard deviation or the standard error of measurement, can classify changes as small, moderate or large and can be combined with anchor-based estimates, but they are supportive only and not appropriate as the sole basis for a responder definition. FDA's April 2023 draft guidance on endpoints, not yet final, likewise finds them insufficient as the sole basis for a meaningful score difference.
has perspective title Distribution-Based Methods Only Support Anchor-Based Responder Definitions
has primary source label U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Guidance for Industry. has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/164555/download
has perspective summary FDA's 2024 guidance on oncology dosages states that the maximum tolerated dose paradigm suited cytotoxic chemotherapy with steep dose-response relationships, whereas targeted therapies often show different dose-response relationships, so doses below the maximum may give similar activity with fewer toxicities. Dose- and exposure-response relationships should be evaluated early and used, with safety, tolerability and activity data, to select dosages for each trial. Multiple dosages should be compared before approval, and a randomised, parallel dose-response trial is one recommended design.

has institution label as shown FDA

has perspective summary FDA's patient-focused drug development guidance describes a focus group as a conversation with a group of participants led by a moderator, generally using a semi-structured discussion guide, that elicits a range of experiences and allows participant interaction. The number of groups depends on the complexity and sensitivity of the topic, sample diversity and planned subgroups, and groups of 5 to 10 participants are common. Focus groups can explore a broad topic before one-on-one interviews, which suit sensitive topics and detailed individual experiences.
has perspective title Focus Groups for Eliciting Patient Experience in Drug Development

has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/164960/download
has perspective summary FDA's draft guidance on externally controlled trials describes a historical control as a group of people, treated or untreated, from an earlier time, and treats it as a subset of external controls. Suitability needs case by case assessment, and historical information can potentially serve as the control when the natural history of a disease is well defined and the disease is known not to improve without intervention. Sponsors should finalise the protocol, including the choice of external control arm and analytic approach, before the trial begins. The guidance remains a draft and is not for implementation.

concerns wiki concept Interviewer Bias
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/131230/download
has perspective summary FDA guidance on patient-focused drug development states that, compared with interviewer-administered surveys, self-administration is typically less costly and removes the potential for interviewer bias. Interviewer administration may still suit some groups, such as patients with visual impairment. For qualitative one-on-one interviews, the guidance recommends selecting and training interviewers, pilot testing the interview guide, and phrasing probing questions so that they do not appear to cast judgement on a participant's beliefs or choices.

has perspective summary The FDA states that an investigational device exemption allows an investigational device to be used in a clinical study to collect safety and effectiveness data, and that such studies are most often conducted to support a PMA. Unless exempt, every clinical evaluation of an investigational device needs an approved IDE before the study starts. Requirements include an investigational plan approved by an institutional review board, informed consent from all patients, investigational-use labelling, monitoring and required records and reports, with FDA approval of the IDE as well when the study involves a significant risk device.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Kappa Statistic
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/71147/download
has perspective summary FDA's statistical guidance on diagnostic test studies says that measures of overall agreement, including overall percent agreement and Cohen's kappa, can be misleading when a new test is compared with a non-reference standard, because overall agreement can be good even when positive or negative percent agreement is very low. It therefore discourages their stand-alone use to characterise diagnostic performance. It adds that all agreement measures, kappa included, change with prevalence and that agreement does not mean a test is correct.

has perspective summary The FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research qualified the KCCQ-23 on 9 April 2020 as DDT COA #000084, for patients with heart failure, with heart failure symptoms and their impact on physical limitations as the concept of interest. Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Large Simple Trial
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/181871/download
has perspective summary FDA's draft guidance supports randomised trials with streamlined protocols and procedures that integrate research into routine clinical practice, noting that such trials have sometimes been called point of care trials or large simple trials. Trials fit best when the data needed are collected routinely with minimal extra procedures or visits, and outcomes such as strokes, fractures and myocardial infarctions are more readily captured from practice records. For drugs with well-established safety profiles, selective collection of serious adverse events and adverse events of special interest may be appropriate.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Mantel-Haenszel Method
has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/148910/download
has perspective summary FDA guidance on covariate adjustment in randomised trials states that Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel methods are acceptable for analysing binary endpoints when the interest is in a conditional treatment effect. That effect is assumed to be constant across subgroups defined by a covariate with a discrete number of levels. FDA adds that nonlinear regression models, such as logistic regression, extend these methods by allowing adjustment for continuous covariates such as age, and that sponsors should prespecify any covariate-adjusted analysis before unblinding comparative data.
has perspective title Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel Methods Acceptable for Binary Endpoints
has primary source label FDA, Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products, Guidance for Industry, May 2023, sections III.A and III.C

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference
has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/77832/download
has perspective summary FDA's guidance on patient-reported outcome measures interprets meaningful individual change through an a priori responder definition, the individual score change over a set period that should be interpreted as a treatment benefit. The definition is determined empirically, may vary by population and trial design, and is evaluated in the context of each trial. Its evidence is derived from anchor-based methods, such as patient ratings of change, while distribution-based methods are supportive only. Cumulative distribution displays of change in each arm may be preferable to a single categorical definition.
has perspective title Anchor-Based Evidence Required for Responder Definitions
has primary source label U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Guidance for Industry. Patient-Reported Outcome Measures: Use in Medical Product Development to Support Labeling Claims, final guidance (December 2009), section IV.E

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Minimisation (Trial Allocation)
has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/71336/download
has perspective summary FDA guidance adopting ICH E9 says deterministic dynamic allocation procedures should be avoided and an appropriate element of randomisation should be incorporated for each treatment allocation, with every effort made to keep the trial double blind. The complexity of the logistics and the potential impact on the analysis should be weighed before dynamic allocation is chosen. The FDA's 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment adds that sponsors should discuss proposals for complex covariate-adaptive randomisation with the relevant review division.
has perspective title Deterministic Dynamic Allocation Avoided, Complex Schemes Discussed First
has primary source label FDA, Guidance for Industry E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (September 1998), section II.C.2 (ICH E9 2.3.2); and Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products, Guidance for Industry (May 2023), section III.A

institutional perspective of FDA on Misclassification

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000709
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Misclassification
has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/152503/download
has perspective summary FDA notes that operational definitions in electronic health records and claims data are usually imperfect, so misclassification of exposures, outcomes or covariates can produce false positives and false negatives and bias associations. Sponsors should consider the degree of misclassification, whether it is differential, whether errors are dependent, and the likely direction of bias. FDA expects outcome validation, and states that differential misclassification may bias associations in either direction, whereas non-differential misclassification tends to bias towards the null.
has perspective title Validate Record and Claims Variables Against Misclassification
has primary source label FDA, Real-World Data: Assessing Electronic Health Records and Medical Claims Data To Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products, Guidance for Industry, final, July 2024, sections IV.D.2, IV.D.3 and V.D.3

institutional perspective of FDA on Multiple Regression

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000723
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Multiple Regression
has display order 2
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/148910/download
has perspective summary FDA accepts covariate adjustment through a linear model to estimate the average treatment effect in randomised trials. The outcome is regressed on an intercept, a treatment indicator and baseline covariates by ordinary least squares, and the treatment coefficient is the estimate. FDA states that this remains valid even when the model is misspecified, recommends adjusting for the covariates expected to be most strongly associated with the outcome, and asks sponsors to consider robust standard errors such as the Huber-White sandwich when the model has no treatment by covariate interactions.
has perspective title Linear Regression Adjustment for the Average Treatment Effect
has primary source label FDA, Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products, Guidance for Industry, May 2023, sections III.A and III.B

has perspective summary Under FDA regulations, a Medication Guide is required for prescription products that FDA judges to pose a serious and significant public health concern, mainly those used as outpatients without direct professional supervision. Grounds include patient labelling that could help prevent serious adverse effects, serious risks that could affect a decision to use the product, and products important to health whose effectiveness depends on adherence to directions. The guide must be in nontechnical, understandable English, based on and not in conflict with the approved professional labelling, in type no smaller than 10 points.

has perspective summary The FDA defines patient preference information as qualitative or quantitative assessments of the relative desirability or acceptability to patients of specified alternatives or choices among outcomes or other attributes of health interventions. Its final guidance of March 2026 supersedes the 2016 guidance on voluntary submission in premarket approval, humanitarian device exemption and De Novo reviews, and extends the use of such information to investigational device exemptions, Breakthrough Device requests and 510(k) submissions. Methods may be qualitative, quantitative or mixed, and the FDA separates such information from patient-reported outcomes measured in clinical trials.

has perspective summary The FDA guidance for industry on the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire supports its use as a patient-reported outcome assessment tool in COPD drug development. It states that the minimum clinically important difference for the total score, both between patients and within a patient, is at least 4 units and that no evidence supports other values. Sponsors should use the total score only, not the Symptoms, Activity or Impacts component scores, and responder analysis is the preferred primary method for reporting results. The guidance lists 1-year, 3-month and 4-week recall versions of the 50-item SGRQ, of which only the 3-month and 4-week versions were available as of March 2016.

has perspective summary At the Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee meeting of 13 September 2023 on a supplemental application for patisiran in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, the FDA clinical reviewer presented the APOLLO-B trial, whose primary endpoint was the change in six-minute walk test distance from baseline at month 12. The reviewer reported a median difference of 14.7 metres (95% confidence interval 0.7 to 28.7) against a median baseline of 364 metres and described the effect as statistically significant but small. The committee was asked whether patisiran has clinically meaningful benefits, so statistical significance on walk distance was not treated as settling clinical benefit.

has display order 3

has perspective summary FDA defines an unmet medical need as a condition whose treatment or diagnosis is not addressed adequately by available therapy, covering an immediate need for a defined population and a longer-term need for society, such as antibacterial resistance. Where no therapy exists the need is clear; where therapy exists, a new drug generally qualifies if it affects a serious outcome that current therapy does not, improves on it, helps patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to it, or avoids serious toxicity. The concept underlies fast track, breakthrough therapy, accelerated approval and priority review.
has perspective title Unmet Medical Need as the Gateway to Expedited Programmes

has display order 1
has institution label as shown FDA
has page URL https://www.fda.gov/media/71147/download
has perspective summary FDA recommends comparing a new qualitative diagnostic test with a reference standard where one is available. If applying the reference standard to all subjects is impractical, it can be applied to a subset, such as a random sample, and sensitivity and specificity should then be adjusted to correct for verification bias. FDA states that the simple formulas are not correct for these partial verification designs and give biased estimates, an example of verification or work-up bias.

has perspective summary Under German law and BfArM's guide, a digital health application is listed for statutory reimbursement only if it meets requirements on safety, functionality, quality, interoperability and data protection and shows a positive healthcare effect, either a medical benefit or a patient-relevant improvement of structure and processes in care. has perspective summary The G-BA states that under AMNOG, in force since 1 January 2011, companies launching a new medicine must submit a dossier on its additional benefit over the appropriate comparator, and the G-BA resolution forms the basis for pricing. The GKV-Spitzenverband and the company then have six months to negotiate a reimbursement price, set as a rebate on the company's original price. Without agreement, an arbitration board sets the price using European price levels. A medicine without additional benefit joins the reference price system or, if that is not possible, cannot exceed the comparator's annual treatment costs.

has perspective summary GOLD treats SGRQ scores of 25 or more as very uncommon in healthy persons and gives 10 as the equivalent cut-point for the COPD Assessment Test, which separates less symptomatic from more symptomatic patients in the ABE assessment tool. GOLD states that no equivalent cut-point can be calculated for the mMRC breathlessness scale and recommends a comprehensive symptom assessment. The 2026 report adjusted the criteria for groups A, B and E, with one moderate exacerbation now the threshold for considering treatment escalation, and states that the CAT and the Chronic Airways Assessment Test (CAAT) are equivalent with interchangeable scores.

has display order 1

has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2021-03/doctrine_ct.pdf
has perspective summary The HAS Transparency Committee doctrine, adopted in February 2023, defines the improvement in actual clinical benefit (ASMR) as the medical value a medicine adds to existing care, rated major (I), important (II), moderate (III), minor (IV) or none (V). As a relative judgement, it needs a comparison with a clinically relevant comparator at the same point in the treatment pathway, and a double-blind randomised head-to-head trial is expected where possible. ASMR V covers progress not shown, such as a non-inferiority design, and uncertain added value. The ASMR frames the price negotiation.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS requires that, when the reference case is a cost-effectiveness analysis, the health outcome criterion is life-years and the mortality indicator is the all-cause mortality rate. If all interventions are equivalent on length of life, the reference case should be a cost-minimisation analysis. A surrogate that predicts survival is acceptable only with strong, established evidence of its predictive value; without that demonstration, the reference case should assume no difference in survival between the intervention and its comparators, with any assumed survival gain shown in a scenario analysis.

institutional perspective of HAS on Allocative Efficiency

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Allocative Efficiency
has display order 1
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS states that, within its mandate, the prime objective of economic evaluation is to guide public decisions on allocating collective resources. That requires identifying the options on the cost-effectiveness frontier, which it calls technical cost-effectiveness, and the options that allow optimal allocation of available resources, which it calls allocative cost-effectiveness and defines as maximising individual health benefits in a constrained budget. For analyses whose outcome is not based on survival, HAS cautions that a frontier shows technical cost-effectiveness but that the size of an ICER or incremental net benefit is difficult to interpret in allocative terms.
has perspective title Technical and Allocative Cost-Effectiveness as Separate Evaluation Aims

has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/jcms/p_3284524/en/real-world-studies-for-the-assessment-of-medicinal-products-and-medical-devices
has perspective summary HAS's guide to real-world studies of medicinal products and medical devices favours descriptive, non-comparative observational studies for documenting use in routine practice, and comparative designs, whether real-world comparative studies, pragmatic trials or conventional trials, for comparing efficacy, safety or efficiency with other products. Without randomisation, HAS recommends measures to minimise indication bias, in particular causal inference methods such as adjustment, matching or weighting where their conditions are met. It also recommends a protocol drafted with a multidisciplinary scientific committee and the use of existing data, especially the national health data system.

has perspective summary In France, a company seeking reimbursement of a medicine submits a dossier to HAS after marketing authorisation, and the Transparency Committee, HAS's dedicated appraisal committee, issues an opinion. Its rating of clinical benefit bears on the yes or no reimbursement decision and the reimbursement rate set by the national health insurance union, while its rating of clinical added value is used in price negotiations. The final listing decision rests with the ministers for health and social security and is published in the Official Journal.
has perspective title Transparency Committee Rates Clinical Benefit and Added Value; Ministers Decide

has display order 2

has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/jcms/c_1729421/en/transparency-committee
has perspective summary HAS's Transparency Committee has 29 voting members, 22 full members and 7 substitutes chosen for scientific expertise, including a chair drawn from the HAS Board and two vice-chairs. They include expert doctors and pharmacists, specialists in methodology and epidemiology, and two representatives of patient and user associations. Seven further members take part in an advisory role, representing bodies including the Social Security Directorate, the national health insurance fund and the medicines agency ANSM. Members serve three-year terms, renewable twice.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 2
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS's guidance on economic evaluation asks that model type and structure represent patients' clinical progression and care without needless complexity, with the states, events and links chosen to capture differences in costs and outcomes and with attention to how intercurrent events such as adverse events and treatment stoppages are handled. When extrapolation is used, every assumption, especially on treatment duration and effect size, should be detailed and justified. Sensitivity analyses should quantify the impact of modelling assumptions, and the effect of extrapolation assumptions should be explored systematically.
has perspective title Explain Structural Choices and Test Extrapolation Assumptions Systematically
has primary source label Haute Autorité de Santé, Choices in methods for economic evaluation, methodological guidance (2020 version, adopted 2 July 2020), sections 4.2, 4.3 and 4.5 and Guidelines 22, 23 and 25

institutional perspective of HAS on Average Cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000237
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Average Cost
has display order 1
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS requires resources to be valued at unit production costs, with hospital stays valued at the average cost per homogeneous patient group from the National Cost Study, corrected to exclude structural costs and products funded on top of the stay tariff. HAS notes that these averages can conceal sharp variation between institutions and does not recommend them when the survey rate is below 20%, the sampling error exceeds 30%, or the estimate rests on fewer than 30 stays or a single institution; stays are then valued at the applicable tariffs. Any modification to the average must be explained and justified.
has perspective title Hospital Stays Valued at National Cost Study Averages, Within Reliability Limits

institutional perspective of HAS on Base Case

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Base Case
has display order 5
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS keeps the two terms apart: its reference case analysis, which follows the methodological choices of the HAS frame of reference, comprises a base-case analysis, non-exploratory subgroup analyses and a thorough exploration of uncertainty through sensitivity analyses. The base-case analysis is defined as the analysis of the study population based on the middle values of the model parameters and the adopted assumptions and modelling choices. Sensitivity analyses then explore the uncertainty around the base-case result.
has perspective title Base-Case Analysis Within the Reference Case Analysis
has primary source label HAS, Choices in methods for economic evaluation: methodological guidance, validated by the CEESP on 6 April 2020, HAS frame of reference summary and glossary (reference case analysis, base-case analysis, sensitivity analysis)

has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/jcms/c_1729421/en/transparency-committee
has perspective summary HAS’s Transparency Committee gives each drug two clinical ratings rather than an ICER: the actual clinical benefit (Service Médical Rendu, SMR), which determines whether and at what rate the drug is reimbursed (15%, 30%, 65% or 100%; insufficient SMR = not reimbursed); and the improvement in clinical benefit versus existing treatments (Amélioration du Service Médical Rendu, ASMR, on a I–V scale from major therapeutic progress to no improvement), which guides the price negotiation with the CEPS. Formal cost-effectiveness (by the CEESP) enters only for high-impact products.

has perspective summary HAS asks for the type of model to be justified, with the choice resting partly on whether the most appropriate statistical unit is a group of individuals with homogeneous characteristics, handled by a cohort model, or individuals with heterogeneous characteristics, handled by an individual-centred model. Its model-choice annex states that an individual simulation is probably necessary when too many dimensions, such as numerous risk factors or subdivided states, rule out a cohort approach. Its sample quality grid checks that the sensitivity analysis of a cohort simulation rests on parameter probability distributions.

has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary The reference case analysis should identify all clinically relevant interventions in the population analysed, including options such as therapeutic abstention or non-medicinal therapy, and any exclusion must be justified. The choice should first rest on good practice guidelines published by scientific institutions free of conflicts of interest. Low use alone does not justify excluding a medically relevant intervention, medicines widely used without a marketing authorisation may be included, and the impact of excluding a comparator is tested in a sensitivity analysis.

has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS requires the choice of model type to be justified, mainly by how the model integrates time, including the duration of the simulation, the possibility of recurrence and whether progression over time is discrete or continuous. Its model-choice annex sets discrete-time forms beside continuous-time ones, such as continuous-time Markov chain models, system dynamics based on ordinary differential equations and continuous-time discrete event simulation. Where numerous events are likely to occur in one time unit, it advises a model with short time intervals or a continuous-time model.
has perspective title Discrete or Continuous Handling of Time Must Justify the Model Choice

institutional perspective of HAS on Cost

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 6
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary Only direct costs enter the reference case, identified, measured and valued for the resources linked to the intervention over the time horizon. Resources are valued at their unit production cost in France, with French tariffs used where production costs are unavailable or unsuitable, and hospital stays are valued through the National Cost Study when its precision allows. Each resource is expressed in euros for a reference year using INSEE consumer price indices for health products and services. Indirect costs, mainly productivity losses, may be presented only in a supplemental analysis.
has perspective title Unit Production Costs in France, With Tariffs as the Fallback
has primary source label Haute Autorité de Santé, Choices in methods for economic evaluation (April 2020), Guidelines 18 to 20, sections 3.1 to 3.3

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 3
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary The HAS methods guide limits the reference case to cost-utility and cost-effectiveness analysis, but states that other economic approaches may aid decisions when the question is broader than efficiency. It describes cost-consequence analysis as comparing interventions across several dimensions without an aggregate measure, with costs and other criteria presented separately. HAS considers it appropriate for detailing the diverse impacts of a complex intervention, such as a public health evaluation, but not suitable for estimating cost-effectiveness because it cannot assess opportunity cost.
has perspective title CCA for Complex Interventions but Not Efficiency Estimates

institutional perspective of HAS on Cost-Effectiveness

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000397
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness
has display order 3
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS requires the evaluation of cost-effectiveness to identify the interventions on the cost-effectiveness frontier, meaning those for which no other intervention gives a better or identical health outcome at lower cost. A position on the frontier shows an economically rational choice but says nothing about acceptability in terms of what the community is willing to pay for an extra unit of health. Results are presented as the ICER or as net benefit, and because France has no predefined reference value, net benefit is shown graphically across willingness-to-pay values.
has perspective title Cost-Effectiveness Judged on the Efficiency Frontier
has primary source label Haute Autorité de santé, Choices in methods for economic evaluation, methodological guidance (2020, English version), Guideline 26 and sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2

has perspective summary HAS bases its reference case on cost-utility or cost-effectiveness analysis, using cost-effectiveness analysis with life-years as the outcome when health-related quality of life is not a major consequence. If all interventions are shown to be equivalent on length of life, the reference case analysis should be based on cost minimisation. An analysis using another health outcome criterion may then be presented for information as a supplemental analysis, with the choice of criterion duly justified.

has display order 6
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS uses a cost-utility analysis for the reference case when health-related quality of life is a major consequence of the intervention, with the health outcome expressed in QALYs; otherwise a cost-effectiveness analysis based on length of life is used. A cost-utility analysis should always be accompanied by a cost-effectiveness analysis. Utility scores should come from a generic questionnaire completed by patients and valued using general population preferences, with the EQ-5D-5L and the prevailing French value set recommended.

has perspective summary The HAS Transparency Committee advises ministers on the reimbursement and pricing of medicines using two ratings. Clinical benefit (SMR) is assessed on five factors: efficacy and adverse effects, place in the therapeutic strategy, seriousness of the disease, whether the product is preventive, curative or symptomatic, and public health benefit, and it bears on whether and how much a medicine is reimbursed. Clinical added value (ASMR) is rated from level I (major) to level V (no improvement) and frames price negotiations, with the final decision resting with the ministers.

institutional perspective of HAS on Differential Discounting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000486
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Differential Discounting
has display order 5
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS requires future costs and health outcomes to be discounted whenever the time horizon exceeds 12 months, using the public discount rate that applies to all public investment decisions, which was 2.5% when the guidance was published and falls gradually to a floor of 1.5% beyond 30 years. Costs and health outcomes are discounted at the same rate in the reference case, because the relative price of the health outcome is taken not to vary over time. Sensitivity analysis applies at least a 4.5% rate and a zero rate to costs and outcomes together.
has perspective title One Public Discount Rate for Costs and Health Outcomes
has primary source label Haute Autorité de santé, Choices in methods for economic evaluation, methodological guidance (2020, English version), Guideline 7 (section 1.7)

has perspective summary HAS explains that a decree of 30 March 2023 allows early reimbursement of digital medical devices presumed to be innovative, including therapeutic devices intended for the LPPR list. Coverage lasts one year and cannot be renewed. Its device committee, CNEDiMTS, gives an opinion within 60 days on CE marking in the claimed indication and on presumed innovation in clinical benefit or organisation of care, judged on early data and relevant comparators. The manufacturer must then file an LPPR application within six months.

has perspective summary HAS requires the selected model type to be justified through an analysis of the possible options, based mainly on how the model handles time, whether individuals interact, whether a cohort or an individual-centred unit suits the heterogeneity of the population, and whether parameter randomness must be captured. institutional perspective of HAS on Disutility

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000533
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Disutility
has display order 4
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS notes that trials are generally ill-suited to estimating utility scores for rare events such as adverse effects or acute events. Where such events have a major impact, a pragmatic data collection approach should be planned before the trial; otherwise a systematic literature review should identify the utility score for each event, with extreme values tested in multivariate sensitivity analysis. A mean utility difference between people who did and did not experience the event may be used when trial data or published disutilities are not reliable enough, with its limitations discussed.
has perspective title Utility Loss From Rare Adverse Events Needs a Planned Approach
has primary source label Haute Autorité de santé, Choices in methods for economic evaluation, methodological guidance (2020, English version), section 2.3.3 (rare events)

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 3
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS holds that evaluating cost-effectiveness requires identifying the interventions on the cost-effectiveness frontier, which comprises all non-dominated interventions under strict or extended dominance. Its guidance defines strict dominance as an intervention being less costly for identical or higher effectiveness, or more effective for identical or lower cost. A place on the frontier indicates an economically rational choice but gives no indication of acceptability against willingness to pay, and where the frontier cannot be built a side-by-side comparison of costs and outcomes is presented instead.
has perspective title Cost-Effectiveness Frontier Built From Non-Dominated Interventions
has primary source label Haute Autorité de Santé, Choices in methods for economic evaluation (April 2020), Guideline 26, section 5.1.1 and Glossary

has perspective summary HAS describes its certification of hospitals as the regulatory accreditation process that all French public and private hospitals must undergo, in place since 1996 under the Public Health Code. institutional perspective of HAS on Net Benefit Approach

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000729
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Net Benefit Approach
has display order 1
has institution label as shown HAS
has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS's guidance on economic evaluation adopts net benefit as an alternative to the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for relating additional cost to health gain, citing the ratio's limitations in analysing uncertainty and net benefit's simpler reading of probabilistic analysis with several comparators. The evaluator chooses whether to express it in monetary or health units. With no predefined French reference value, results should be plotted as net benefit against willingness to pay over an interval wide enough to show every intervention that maximises net benefit, with a table of values at each intersection.
has perspective title Net Benefit Adopted as an Alternative Metric to the ICER

has perspective summary For economic evaluations submitted to HAS, a network meta-analysis is recommended when interventions have not been compared directly, subject to validating its feasibility assumptions, including consistency of populations, protocols and risk of bias and verification of transitivity. Bayesian and frequentist approaches are both acceptable, results should appear in tables and forest plots, and the level of evidence of each relative effect should be stated. Matching-adjusted indirect comparisons require justification that a network meta-analysis is impossible, and naive indirect comparisons are not acceptable in the reference case.

has perspective summary HAS states that univariate deterministic sensitivity analyses, or multivariate ones if necessary, should be conducted systematically to identify the parameters with the greatest impact on the results, as a complement to probabilistic sensitivity analysis. The choice of parameters and of the values tested, such as a 95% confidence interval or an arbitrary percentage variation, should be justified. Where a CEESP opinion is required, at least three prices below the base-case price should be tested, and a threshold analysis should be added where appropriate.

has page URL https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2020-11/methodological_guidance_2020_-choices_in_methods_for_economic_evaluation.pdf
has perspective summary HAS regards randomised trials comparing the evaluated intervention directly with relevant comparators, together with pairwise meta-analyses, as the best source of evidence on comparative effectiveness in economic evaluations. Where several studies compare two interventions on the same criteria with comparable protocols, their estimates should be summarised by a pairwise meta-analysis conducted according to existing guidelines. A study that cannot be pooled should still be presented and used to discuss uncertainty, and when several sources inform one model parameter a pairwise meta-analysis should be preferred.
has perspective title Pairwise Meta-Analysis Where Several Comparable Trials Exist

has perspective summary The HAS sample grid for judging the quality of a cost-effectiveness model, adapted from Weinstein et al., asks whether the model includes memory when transition probabilities depend on prior events. It also asks whether the cycle duration has been justified by the pace of disease progression, symptoms, treatment decisions or costs. The HAS glossary defines a transitional event as one occurring during a cycle that moves a patient from one model status to another, unlike an intercurrent event, which generally affects only costs and utility.

has perspective summary HAS measures health-related quality of life in cost-utility analysis through utility scores reflecting preferences for health states, used to weight time in each state when calculating QALYs.
