Direct standard gamble or time trade-off values belong only in sensitivity analysis, and vignettes or visual analogue scales are not acceptable.

has perspective summary HIQA's guidelines prefer routine care as the reference-case comparator, meaning the technology or technologies most widely used in clinical practice in Ireland for the target population, and in practice limit comparators to the recommended standard of care and those in routine use. Comparators must be identified and justified, because the choice critically determines relative cost effectiveness. Unlicensed technologies may be considered if they are part of established clinical practice, and in the absence of an active comparator a comparator of no intervention is appropriate.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA)
has page URL https://www.hiqa.ie/sites/default/files/2025-03/Economic-Evaluation-Guidelines.pdf
has perspective summary HIQA's national guidelines explain that the option with the highest probability of being cost effective at a given threshold will not necessarily have the highest expected net benefit. The cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier therefore plots the option with the highest expected net benefit across values of the cost-effectiveness threshold. The guidelines caution that the frontier ignores the consequences of failing to select the truly preferred option, so it does not adequately reflect the importance of uncertainty, which the expected value of perfect information does capture.
has perspective title The Frontier Follows the Option With the Highest Expected Net Benefit
has primary source label Health Information and Quality Authority, National Guidelines for the Economic Evaluation of Health Technologies in Ireland (published 26 March 2025), section 2.16.2

has perspective summary HIQA's national guidelines require additional QALYs to be treated as of equal value in the reference case, regardless of the characteristics of the population, so equity weights should not be applied to outcomes. The guidelines acknowledge proposals to build equity weights into QALY calculations to reflect societal concerns about severity and the ability to benefit, but cite significant methodological issues in deriving and applying them. Reports should instead highlight equity considerations, such as unmet needs of disadvantaged groups, and describe the technology's potential impact on them.

has perspective summary HIQA's 2025 guidelines require any use of data not derived from the Irish population to be documented and its relevance to the Irish healthcare system established, with assumptions stated and uncertainty explored in sensitivity analysis. Transferring clinical data between countries is usually accepted as reasonable if population criteria are clearly described and key parameters tested, but economic data are generally not considered transferable because prices and resource use differ. Where costs from other countries are used, the transfer assumptions must be reported and costs converted to Irish euro equivalents using purchasing power parity indices.

Because Ireland has no stated threshold, results presented as net monetary benefit should describe clearly the threshold values used.

has perspective summary Ireland's Health Insurance Authority explains that Lifetime Community Rating adds a loading of 2% of the gross cost of an inpatient health insurance policy for each year a person spent aged 35 or over without cover before first buying it. Loadings apply to people first buying cover after 30 April 2015, last for at most 10 years and are capped at 70% for first-time buyers aged 69 or over. People who already hold cover pay no more because of their age, and the rule aims to encourage people to join the market younger.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Community Rating
has display order 2
has institution label as shown Health Insurance Authority
has page URL https://www.hia.ie/information/lifetime-community-rating-lcr
has perspective summary The Health Insurance Authority treats community rating as one of four principles of Irish private health insurance, alongside open enrolment, lifetime cover and minimum benefits. Insurers may not set premiums on the basis of an individual's claims risk, so older or less healthy people pay the same as the young and healthy, with limited discounts for children, young adults and groups. People who first buy cover aged 35 or over pay a loading of 2% of the gross premium for each year spent aged 35 or over without cover, up to 70%, for a maximum of 10 years.
has perspective title Community Rating with Lifetime Community Rating Loadings

has perspective summary The Department of Health and the Health Insurance Authority state that, because community rating stops insurers varying prices with risk, insurers would otherwise be incentivised to avoid older and sicker people. The Risk Equalisation Scheme pays insurers credits, funded by a stamp duty on all health insurance contracts, that subsidise the higher claims costs of these members. One stated aim of the scheme is to reduce the incentives for risk selection, so that insurers are indifferent, or at least less incentivised, to target less risky and more profitable people.

has perspective summary Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the HPRA establishes and maintains the List of Interchangeable Medicines, and pharmacists may substitute a lower-cost medicine only within a group on that list. Interchangeable medicines share the same active substance and strength, pharmaceutical form and route of administration, contain no more than two active substances and, for generics, have shown bioequivalence. Biological medicines are excluded, as are products that cannot be safely substituted, such as some narrow therapeutic range medicines. A prescriber can prevent substitution by writing 'do not substitute' on the prescription.
has perspective title Pharmacists May Substitute Only Medicines on the HPRA Interchangeable List

has perspective summary The Green Book defines the benefit-cost ratio as the present value of monetisable social benefits divided by the present value of monetisable social costs, and asks for it with net present social value and the return on public sector cost for each shortlisted option. These metrics give only an initial ranking. Practitioners should not judge value for money with ratio thresholds, such as rejecting proposals below two, and a ratio below one may still represent value for money if unmonetisable benefits are significant.

has institution label as shown HM Treasury

has perspective summary HM Treasury's Green Book sets the social time preference rate at 3.50% in real terms for years 1 to 30 of an appraisal, 3.00% for years 31 to 75 and 2.50% from year 76 onwards. Effects on the health or life of individuals are discounted at a lower 1.5% in every year, because the wealth effect component of the rate is excluded. The rate is real, so values are converted to real terms before discounting, and inflation and discount rates should not be added together.

has perspective summary The Green Book lists externalities among the market failures that economists often treat as an important rationale for government intervention, defining them as positive or negative impacts of market transactions on parties other than the buyer and seller. It gives pollution as a typical negative externality and education as a typical positive one. For valuation, it states that a good with negative externalities is priced too low from a social value perspective, leading to over-consumption compared with the optimal economic outcome.
has perspective title Externalities as a Market Failure Rationale for Intervention

has perspective summary HM Treasury's Green Book defines a market failure as a situation where the free market, left to its own devices, cannot achieve optimal economic efficiency, and treats it as an important rationale for intervention when an appraisal sets out its case for change. It lists failure to provide public goods, externalities, market power, imperfect information and co-ordination failure, and names equity as a separate rationale. When social costs and benefits are valued, market prices may fail to reflect social value where markets do not function efficiently.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown HM Treasury

has perspective summary HM Treasury's Green Book discounts costs and benefits at a social time preference rate of 3.5% for years 1 to 30, made up of time preference and a wealth effect. Time preference of 1.5% combines pure time preference, described as society's impatience and set at 0.5%, with 1.0% for catastrophic risk, while the wealth effect adds 2.0%. Health and life effects are discounted at 1.5% because the wealth effect is excluded. For appraisals beyond 50 years, a sensitivity analysis without pure time preference shows the wealth transfer it implies.

has perspective summary The Green Book allows analysts to weight costs and benefits by the groups in society that bear them, because additional income is worth more to a low-income household than to a high-income one. A group's welfare weight is the median equivalised income of the national population divided by that of the group, raised to the power 1.3, the estimated elasticity of marginal utility of income. Household incomes should be equivalised first, and weighted estimates must be presented alongside unweighted estimates.
has perspective title Distributional Weights Value Gains to Low-Income Households More

has perspective summary The Green Book states that appraisal estimates the social value of options and that this concept of social value is based on the principles of welfare economics, covering all effects on the wellbeing of UK residents rather than financial returns alone. Because the marginal utility of income diminishes, analysts may weight costs and benefits by who bears them: a group's welfare weight is national median equivalised household income divided by the group's median, raised to the power 1.3, an estimate of the elasticity of marginal utility of income. Weighted estimates must be presented alongside unweighted ones.
has perspective title Social Value Grounded in Welfare Economics, With Income Welfare Weights

has perspective summary HM Treasury's supplementary Green Book guidance on wellbeing explains where, when and how wellbeing evidence may contribute to the appraisal of social or public value, and it is used within the Green Book's five-case model. has perspective summary The Green Book asks appraisers to value social costs and benefits from market prices first, turning to non-market valuation where prices are missing or distorted, and ranks valuation methods in a hierarchy of reliability. Stated preference valuation, which asks people what they would be willing to pay or willing to accept, sits below market prices, generic prices and revealed preference. has perspective summary ICER's reference case sets intervention acquisition costs by three factors: whether the product is generic, biosimilar or branded, whether a provider must administer it, and whether its price is known. Self-administered generics are costed at the median wholesale acquisition cost (WAC), with RED BOOK the primary source, and provider-administered drugs at the average sales price, with the mark-up held as a separate input. has perspective summary To address concerns that the QALY undervalues gains for the elderly, disabled, or terminally ill, ICER reports an equal value of life years gained (evLYG) alongside the conventional cost-per-QALY. The evLYG values every life-year gained at the full value of a healthy year (a fixed utility, ~0.851) regardless of a person’s age or baseline health, while still crediting quality-of-life improvements, so that life extension is valued equally across patient groups.

has perspective summary ICER's Reference Case sets out the methods for its conventional base-case cost-effectiveness analysis, which takes a health care system perspective and is run deterministically where appropriate for the model type. has perspective summary ICER calculates threshold prices, the prices at which a new intervention would reach given cost-effectiveness thresholds, and reports results at USD 50,000, 100,000, 150,000 and 200,000 per QALY and per evLY gained in all assessments. Its Health Benefit Price Benchmark is the range of prices, net of rebates and other concessions, needed to reach USD 100,000 to 150,000 per QALY and per evLY gained. When no non-negative price would make a treatment cost-effective, ICER presents a scenario that excludes health care costs not tied to the intervention or its comparators.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Budget Impact Analysis
has display order 3
has institution label as shown ICER
has page URL https://icer.org/our-approach/methods-process/value-assessment-framework/
has perspective summary ICER estimates the potential budget impact of a new treatment across all US health care spending over five years, assuming 20% of eligible patients start treatment each year, at net and threshold prices. For new drugs, results are compared with an annual threshold, which ICER lowered in October 2025 from 880millionto880 million to 880millionto821 million. When clinical experts expect uptake to exceed that threshold, the final report issues an Access and Affordability Alert. ICER states that the analysis is not intended to suggest a cap on spending.

has perspective summary ICER takes a health care system perspective by default and expects each analysis to add a modified societal perspective. For most analyses that perspective should at least include productivity for the patient and caregiver and disutility for the caregiver. When direct data are lacking, ICER assumes caregiver time equals 75% of the patient's formal labour time lost, valued at a wage plus fringe benefits of $48.05 per hour. A societal co-base case may sit alongside the health system perspective when relevant direct data exist and societal effects, such as caregiver quality of life, are substantial.

has perspective summary The base case includes all relevant health system costs paid by third-party payers, including future related and unrelated health care costs, and any excluded cost must be justified. Branded drug acquisition costs use an estimated net price, with the wholesale acquisition cost kept for calculating the discount needed to reach each price benchmark, and publicly available sources such as Medicare fee schedules are preferred for other costs. All costs are converted to current-year United States dollars with the Personal Consumption Expenditures health care services price index. Patient and caregiver productivity is counted in the modified societal perspective.

has display order 3

has perspective summary ICER's reference case derives expected costs and outcomes for each intervention through probabilistic sensitivity analysis, using sufficient sampling to reflect distributional uncertainty. The output should include a table of the percentage of simulations that achieve 50,000,50,000, 50,000,100,000, 150,000and150,000 and 150,000and200,000 per evLY gained, together with graphs using scatter plots or cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. The CEAC is therefore one of two accepted graphical formats for probabilistic results rather than a mandatory display.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown ICER
has page URL https://icer.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/ICER_2023_2026_VAF_070126.pdf
has perspective summary ICER's 2023 value assessment framework notes that data to apply methods measuring effects on inequality across racial or socio-economic groups are lacking in the US, and that no other HTA agency has adopted such methods, including the equity weights used in distributional cost-effectiveness analysis, as a standard. Its reports instead include the Health Improvement Distribution Index, the prevalence of a condition in a subpopulation divided by its prevalence overall, as one input to deliberation. Severity and other modifiers are handled through deliberation rather than quantified weights, although ICER has said it will explore severity weighting methods used elsewhere.
has perspective title No Formal Equity Weights, With a Distribution Index for Deliberation

has display order 2
has institution label as shown ICER

has perspective summary ICER favours cost-effectiveness thresholds based on an opportunity cost paradigm for conceptual and ethical reasons, and its Health Benefit Price Benchmark uses USD 100,000 to USD 150,000 per QALY and per evLY gained. Prices at or below this range are meant to ensure that patients' health gains are not outweighed by health losses from cost pressures that lead people to delay or abandon care or lose insurance. ICER cites an estimate of about USD 104,000 per QALY within this paradigm and handles other value elements through deliberation, as opportunity cost thresholds reflect trade-offs in health gain alone.

has display order 4
has institution label as shown ICER

has perspective summary ICER's reference case reports incremental cost per QALY gained and cost per equal value life year (evLY) gained as the primary cost-utility outcomes. The evLY applies the same quality-of-life value to every period of life extension, so a year of life added for people with a disability or serious illness counts the same as a year added for healthier people. Citing concerns about how the QALY values life extension, ICER gives the evLY the main role in its health benefit price benchmark while keeping QALY results for comparison with academic and international work.

has perspective summary ICER sets the range for its Health Benefit Price Benchmark at 100,000to100,000 to 100,000to150,000 per QALY and per evLY gained, judging that recent research under both the opportunity cost and willingness to pay paradigms puts an operational threshold at about $100,000 per QALY. It sees a confluence of results between the two approaches in the United States but, for conceptual and ethical reasons, favours thresholds based on opportunity cost. It accepts a case for willingness to pay thresholds that differ by payer type, yet frames one range intended to apply broadly across American health insurance systems.

has perspective summary For the US premium tax credit, the Internal Revenue Service treats an employer plan as affordable for an employee if the employee's required contribution for self-only coverage does not exceed the required contribution percentage of household income; for related family members, the contribution for family coverage is tested. has perspective summary ICH E9 requires interim analyses to be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol, with group sequential designs using statistical monitoring schemes as guidelines for stopping. The protocol should describe the schedule of interim analyses, or at least the considerations governing it, for example where flexible alpha spending function approaches are to be used. The procedures selected should always ensure that the overall probability of type I error is controlled, and the potential effects of early stopping on other important variables should be considered.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown International Council for Harmonisation
has page URL https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E10_Guideline.pdf
has perspective summary ICH E10 defines a concurrent control group as one chosen from the same population as the test group, treated in a defined way within the same trial and over the same period. A similar group studied earlier may serve as a historical control only in unusual cases where the course of illness is predictable; in most situations a concurrent control is needed. Four of the five control types it describes are concurrent, while external controls are set apart because of serious concerns about comparability and bias.
has perspective title Concurrent Control Needed in Most Trials

has display order 2
has institution label as shown International Council for Harmonisation
has page URL https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf
has perspective summary ICH E9 states that concluding equivalence or non-inferiority from a non-significant test of the null hypothesis of no difference between an investigational product and an active comparator is inappropriate. A trial meant to show equivalence or non-inferiority must state this intention in its protocol and specify a clinically justified margin. The guideline warns that such trials are not conservative, since many flaws in design or conduct tend to bias results towards a conclusion of equivalence.
has perspective title Non-Significant Test of No Difference Cannot Show Equivalence

has perspective summary The iDSI reference case, commissioned by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, guides economic evaluations that inform health spending decisions in low- and middle-income countries. institutional perspective of IQWiG on Absenteeism

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Absenteeism
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG treats productivity losses from incapacity to work, occupational invalidity and premature death as indirect costs and considers them primarily on the cost side. When the societal perspective is taken, losses from paid labour should as a rule be valued with the friction cost approach, using average labour costs per working day, with friction costs assumed to be 80% of wage costs. The friction period follows the average time needed to fill a position in Germany, and the human capital approach can be examined in sensitivity analyses.

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Added Therapeutic Value

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Added Therapeutic Value
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary In assessing a company dossier under section 35a of the German Social Code Book V, IQWiG first classifies the probability of an effect on each patient-relevant outcome as proof, indication or hint, then grades the extent of each effect as major, considerable, minor or non-quantifiable. The overall conclusion uses six categories: major, considerable, minor or non-quantifiable added benefit, no added benefit proven, or less benefit than the appropriate comparator therapy. Confidence interval thresholds for extent depend on the outcome, so smaller effects qualify when the outcome is more serious, such as all-cause mortality.
has perspective title Added Benefit Graded by Certainty and Extent in Six Categories

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Adverse Event
has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods note that the term adverse events leaves causality open, whereas adverse effects assume a causal link, and treat harm as an equal component of benefit assessment. As a matter of principle, IQWiG uses the overall rates of serious adverse events, severe adverse events where applicable, such as CTCAE grade 3 or above, and discontinuations due to adverse events. Specific adverse effects are then selected for their relevance to patients and differences between treatment arms, using the most suitable operationalisation, such as a Standardised MedDRA Query instead of a single preferred term.
has perspective title Serious and Severe Adverse Events and Discontinuations in Benefit Assessment

has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods name adequate concealment, meaning that allocation to groups cannot be foreseen and is concealed, as a key aspect of its risk of bias assessment of randomised trials, with external randomisation given as an example for trials that cannot be blinded. The Institute stresses that in trials that cannot be blinded, adequate concealment of allocation is needed alongside outcomes that are assessed blind or independently of treating staff. Allocation concealment is assessed across outcomes together with generation of the randomisation sequence, and the risk of bias is then classified as high or low.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods prefer patient-reported anchors for deriving minimal important differences in principle, but note that published MIDs for one instrument vary widely with the anchor, observation period and analysis, and that no established standard exists to judge the quality of MID studies. For benefit assessments IQWiG therefore uses responder analyses without further checks only when the response criterion is at least 15% of the instrument's scale range, a value derived from systematic reviews of MIDs; prespecified MIDs below 15% are as a rule not used.
has perspective title Responder Thresholds of at Least 15% of the Scale Range Instead of Published MIDs

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Attributable Risk

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000225
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Attributable Risk
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods favour relative effect measures when grading the extent of added benefit, because a risk difference depends strongly on the baseline risk in the control group, which varies between regions, populations, comparator therapies and over time, and is capped by that baseline risk. A risk difference should therefore be read as a descriptive measure of a specific study, not a fixed property of a treatment. For health information, IQWiG converts pooled relative effects into absolute risk differences using a plausible baseline risk, usually the median control group risk of the included studies.
has perspective title Risk Differences Are Study-Specific and Derived From a Plausible Baseline Risk
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English version published 1 July 2026), Appendix A and section 7.7

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Attrition

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000227
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Attrition
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods assess missing data in two steps. Results are generally not used in a benefit assessment if more than 30% of the participants who should be analysed are left out entirely, or if the proportions left out differ between groups by more than 15 percentage points, which indicates non-random exclusion; these limits are guidance, with exceptions where exclusions are shown to be completely at random. Losses to follow-up among analysed participants have no fixed limit and are judged by their number, timing and reasons.
has perspective title Results Set Aside if Over 30% Are Excluded or Arms Differ by 15 Points
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English version published 1 July 2026), section 10.3.11

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Baseline Risk

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000260
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Baseline Risk
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods state that, when results from a meta-analysis are presented as absolute effects in its health information, a plausible baseline risk is first selected, typically the median control group risk across the included studies. In justified cases it may come from one suitable study or a valid external source such as a German prevalence study or registry, with large uncertainty handled by the Newcombe and Bender method. The relative pooled effect is then applied to it, and where included studies have heterogeneous baseline risks, absolute effects are shown for each assumed risk, for example low and high.
has perspective title Absolute Effects Built on the Median Control Group Risk
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English version published 1 July 2026), section 7.7

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Bayesian Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000276
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods set a standard approach by number of studies. With 2 studies a fixed-effect model is used. With 3 or 4 studies a random-effects model is fitted for standardised mean differences, odds ratios, relative risks and hazard ratios as a Bayesian meta-analysis with uninformative priors for the treatment effect and informative priors for the heterogeneity parameter, checked against a qualitative summary. With 5 or more studies the Knapp-Hartung method applies, and Bayesian approaches with other adequately justified priors remain an option.
has perspective title Bayesian Random-Effects Model as Standard for 3 or 4 Studies
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025, section 10.3.7 (Meta-analyses)

has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods treat bibliographic databases, alongside trial registries, as a main source of study results. Citing the Cochrane Handbook, they name MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL as the 3 most important databases, though a search may justifiably be limited to MEDLINE and CENTRAL depending on the question. Strategies combine subject headings and free-text terms and are quality assured with the PRESS checklist before searching, and reports document the databases, providers and interfaces, search period, last search date and full strategies with all limits.

has perspective summary IQWiG's methods make a budget impact analysis mandatory, from the statutory health insurance perspective, as a supplement to the health economic evaluation of drugs under German social law. has perspective summary IQWiG regards the randomised controlled trial as the gold standard and, in drug benefit assessments, uses non-randomised or observational studies only in justified exceptional cases. The study types able to give sufficient certainty for each question are fixed in advance in the report plan.

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Choice-Based Conjoint

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000330
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Choice-Based Conjoint
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/download/ga10-03_executive-summary-of-working-paper-11_conjoint-analysis.pdf
has perspective summary In a 2014 pilot project, IQWiG tested whether choice-based conjoint analysis could identify, weight and prioritise patient-relevant outcomes for its efficiency frontier method in chronic hepatitis C, using a discrete choice experiment, which it calls the choice-based variation of conjoint analysis. Patients and healthcare professionals chose between two fictitious treatments described by seven attributes, and the choices were analysed with logistic regression. IQWiG concluded that weighting patient-relevant outcomes in this way was feasible and that the linearity assumption could be tested, while some methodological issues remained unsolved.
has perspective title Pilot Found Choice-Based Weights Feasible for the Efficiency Frontier
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), executive summary of IQWiG working paper GA10-03, Choice-based Conjoint Analysis: pilot project to identify, weight, and prioritize multiple attributes in the indication hepatitis C, version 1.1 (23 July 2014, English translation), sections Research objective, Methods and Conclusion

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Cohen's d

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000333
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cohen's d
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG grades the extent of added benefit on continuous outcomes using the standardised mean difference, expressed as Cohen's d or Hedges' g, with thresholds guided by Cohen's classification of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 as small, medium and large effects. The lower limit of the 95% confidence interval must exceed 0.2 for a minor benefit, 0.3 for serious or 0.4 for non-serious outcomes for a considerable benefit, and 0.5 for a major benefit, which applies to serious outcomes only. When no suitable responder analysis exists, Hedges' g is assessed against an irrelevance threshold of 0.2.
has perspective title Cohen's d Thresholds for Minor, Considerable and Major Added Benefit
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 3.3.3 (Table 4) and section 10.3.3

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Comparator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000348
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Comparator
has display order 6
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary In a health economic evaluation, the base case compares the drug with the appropriate comparator therapy specified by the Federal Joint Committee (G-BA) and used to demonstrate added benefit. This should preferably be a treatment established in practice and not excluded by the efficiency principle. Where several treatment options are equally appropriate, sensitivity analyses cover the range of their costs, in particular the cheapest and the most expensive. Other comparators may be added depending on the commission, which may require a new benefit assessment.
has perspective title Appropriate Comparator Therapy Specified by the G-BA
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025, sections 3.3.3 and 4.3.2

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Conflict of Interest

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Conflict of Interest
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary Under German social law, external experts must disclose all connections to associations and contract organisations, particularly in the pharmaceutical and medical device industries, before IQWiG commissions them. IQWiG assesses whether the disclosures raise serious doubts about appropriate collaboration because of conflicts of interest, in which case collaboration on that commission is usually not possible or only possible under specific provisions. External reviewers must also disclose potential conflicts, and relationships are published only in summary form.
has perspective title Disclosure and Assessment of External Experts' Relationships

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Contamination

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Contamination
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG assesses the benefit of prevention programmes other than screening mainly through prospective comparative intervention studies, ideally with random allocation of participants to a strategy with or without the prevention measure, that report patient-relevant outcomes. Because of potential contamination between the intervention and control groups, it states that studies in which clusters were allocated to the study arms may also be eligible. Other designs, such as interrupted time series for mass-media campaigns, are judged case by case.
has perspective title Cluster Allocation Accepted Where Contamination Threatens Prevention Studies
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden 8.0), section 3.7 Prevention

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Contingency Table

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Contingency Table
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG treats binary outcomes as analyses of 2x2 tables and applies the usual effect and risk measures of such tables to categorical outcomes, with the statistical uncertainty described for every estimate. In meta-analyses with zero cells it adds a correction of 0.5 to each cell of the fourfold table, an approach it considers appropriate only while zero cells are few. For very rare events the Peto odds ratio needs no correction, but suits only effects that are not too large in a balanced design.
has perspective title Effect Measures and Zero Cells in 2x2 Tables
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden; German original authoritative), DOI 10.60584/General-Methods_V8.0, sections 10.3.1 and 10.3.7

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Continuous Data

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Continuous Data
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG uses pre-specified responder analyses whose response criterion is at least 15% of the instrument's scale range, and as a rule does not use criteria below that level. Where no suitable responder analysis exists but continuous data are available, it may use the standardised mean difference as Hedges' g, requiring the whole confidence interval to lie above an irrelevance threshold of 0.2, or a post hoc criterion of exactly 15%. When suitable responder analyses and continuous analyses are both available, the responder analyses are used.
has perspective title Responder Analyses at 15% of Scale Range Preferred Over Continuous Data
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden 8.0; the German original is authoritative), section 10.3.3

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000382
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost
has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary From the reference-case perspective of the community of statutory health insurance (SHI) members, direct reimbursable costs and insured persons' own expenses, including time costs, are counted, while transfer payments such as sickness allowance are left out. Resources are valued with standardised methods, using regulated prices such as per-case flat rates or negotiated drug prices. Under a societal perspective, productivity losses from paid work are valued by the friction cost approach, with friction costs set at 80% of wage costs. Costs from different years are adjusted with the German consumer price index.
has perspective title SHI Cost Components, Friction Costs and Consumer Price Index Adjustment
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025, sections 4.3.4, 4.7.1, 4.7.2 and 4.8

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Cost-Effectiveness

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000396
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG reports the cost-effectiveness ratio as the outcome of its health economic evaluations, which are cost-effectiveness or cost-utility analyses accompanied by a budget impact analysis. The ICER is the main result and is categorised, presented with the uncertainty from sensitivity analyses and alongside results of other evaluations of comparable questions. Because no generally accepted threshold exists for Germany, IQWiG applies no universal threshold, draws no dichotomous conclusion on cost-effectiveness and gives no single decisive price recommendation, leaving the decision-maker to weigh the information and judge affordability.
has perspective title ICER Is Categorised but No Universal Threshold Is Applied
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 1.4, 4.4 and 4.12

concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC)
has display order 5
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods call for a probabilistic sensitivity analysis in health economic evaluations, with its results presented as a scatter plot of incremental cost effectiveness. The result may additionally be presented as a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, termed a cost-effectiveness acceptance curve in the abbreviations list, or the scatter plot may be extended to include a confidence ellipse. The main result remains the ICER between the treatment alternatives, set out in tabular and graphical form.
has perspective title CEAC as an Optional Display of Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025, section 4.11 and table 5 (reference case components)

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Cost-Utility Analysis

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Utility Analysis
has display order 5
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's reference case for health economic evaluations of drugs in German statutory health insurance allows either a cost-effectiveness analysis based on selected benefit assessment outcomes or a cost-utility analysis using QALYs, each with an additional budget impact analysis. IQWiG describes the QALY as the most widely used preference-based outcome measure while acknowledging its limitations. Utilities should be based primarily on valuations by patients, and indirect valuation methods should be used only where a validated German tariff is available.
has perspective title Cost-Utility Analysis as a Reference Case Option

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Cross-Sectional Design

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cross-Sectional Design
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods state that the prevalence of diseases can be estimated from population-based cross-sectional studies. When diagnostic tests are compared on accuracy, the highest certainty of results comes from cohort and cross-sectional studies in which the tests and the reference test are conducted independently in the same patients under mutual blinding, whereas prognostic markers can be studied in cohort rather than cross-sectional studies. In assessments of potential, results of non-comparative studies, including cross-sectional studies, carry only minimum qualitative certainty of results.
has perspective title Cross-Sectional Studies for Prevalence and Test Accuracy
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 3.5.2, 3.8.1 and 10.1.2

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Cumulative Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000440
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cumulative Meta-Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG notes a continuing debate over whether meta-analyses in repeatedly updated systematic reviews should be calculated and presented as cumulative meta-analyses with correction for multiple testing. As a standard it applies the usual type of meta-analysis and normally does not draw on cumulative methods. It will consider cumulative meta-analysis with correction for multiple testing only if commissioned to update a review regularly until a decision can be made on the basis of a statistically significant result.
has perspective title Cumulative Meta-Analysis Not Used as Standard in Review Updates
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden 8.0), section 10.3.7 Meta-analyses, part E (Cumulative meta-analyses)

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Decision Criteria

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000450
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Decision Criteria
has display order 5
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary In benefit assessments of new drugs, IQWiG compares the drug with an appropriate comparator therapy in three steps. It first classifies the probability of an effect on each outcome as a hint, an indication or proof, then grades the extent of the effect as major, considerable, minor or non-quantifiable, and finally reaches an overall conclusion in one of six categories, from major added benefit to no added benefit proven or less benefit than the comparator. Its reports serve as recommendations to the G-BA, which can also weigh aspects beyond the benefit assessment.
has perspective title Added Benefit Graded by Probability and Extent
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of the authoritative German text), sections 1.3.2 and 3.3.3

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Decision Making

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000453
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Decision Making
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG submits the results of work commissioned by the Federal Joint Committee (G-BA) as recommendations, which the G-BA must by law consider in its decision-making. Where studies of adequate validity are lacking, IQWiG's task is to describe and classify the situation, while the G-BA takes the uncertainty into account and also weighs aspects such as the efficiency of interventions and the needs and values of people, which matter more when the evidence is uncertain. In health economic evaluations no universal threshold is applied, so the decision-maker weighs the information and judges affordability.
has perspective title Institute Assesses the Evidence, the Federal Joint Committee Decides
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 1.1, 1.3.4 and 1.4

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Dependent Censoring

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000469
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Dependent Censoring
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods note that adverse events and patient-reported outcomes in oncology studies are often recorded only during treatment, so observations are censored when treatment is discontinued or switched. Survival time methods are then needed for the different observation periods, but this incomplete data collection raises the problem of informative censoring, which may result in a high risk of bias. To avoid it, data on all outcomes relevant to the assessment should be collected completely, even after discontinuation or switching of treatment, since treatment policy and intention-to-treat analyses are required.
has perspective title Censoring at Treatment Switch Raises a High Risk of Bias
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.12
has wiki record identifier dependent-censoring

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Detection Bias

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000471
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Detection Bias
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG describes detection bias as the result of unequal observation of participants and treats blinding as an effective protection against it. Its risk-of-bias assessment of randomised trials, closely following the Cochrane tool, rates blinding of outcome assessors for each outcome. Where patients and physicians cannot be blinded, outcomes should be independent of the treating staff or assessed blind, and failing that a preferably objective outcome should be chosen. Results of unblinded trials are interpreted more cautiously than those of blinded trials.
has perspective title Blinded Outcome Assessment Where Treatment Cannot Be Blinded
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 10.1.4 and 10.3.13
has wiki record identifier detection-bias

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Diagnostic Accuracy

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000477
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Diagnostic Accuracy
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG assesses diagnostic tests primarily through comparative intervention studies with patient-relevant outcomes, because a test's benefit is in essence realised only through the treatment or prevention that follows. Studies of sensitivity and specificity are mainly relevant within the linked evidence approach, with the highest certainty from studies applying the index tests and reference test independently in the same patients under mutual blinding, appraised mainly with QUADAS-2. Meta-analyses of diagnostic accuracy are therefore of limited relevance; random-effects models are usually advisable, and bivariate models show advantages when a summary ROC curve is of interest.
has perspective title Test Accuracy Studies Mainly Relevant Through Linked Evidence
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 3.5, 3.5.1, 3.5.2 and 10.3.7
has wiki record identifier diagnostic-accuracy

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Differential Discounting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000485
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Differential Discounting
has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods require costs and benefits lasting longer than one year to be discounted after the first year at an identical constant rate of 3% per year in the base case, with identical rates of 0% and 5% in sensitivity analyses. Noting that the literature discusses differential discounting in certain cases, especially where the consumption value of health is assumed to rise over time, the Institute allows differential rates of 3% for costs and 1.5% for benefits to be examined in sensitivity analyses.
has perspective title Identical 3% Rate, With Differential Rates in Sensitivity Analysis
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 4.2 (Table 5) and 4.8
has wiki record identifier differential-discounting

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Distribution-Based MID

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000527
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Distribution-Based MID
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods state that anchor-based methods are preferred for determining a minimally important difference, with distribution-based methods also in use, but that no established standard exists for judging the quality of studies that derive such values. Because published values vary widely, the Institute accepts responder analyses only where the response criterion is at least 15% of the instrument's scale range. Otherwise it uses standardised mean differences (Hedges' g), treating an effect as at least small when the confidence interval lies wholly above an irrelevance threshold of 0.2.
has perspective title Fixed 15% Response Threshold Instead of Study-Derived MIDs
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.3
has wiki record identifier distribution-based-mid

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Dominance

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000538
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Dominance
has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary For health economic evaluations conducted outside the statutory framework of §35b SGB V, IQWiG states that when more than two treatments are considered, the cost-effectiveness ratios can be plotted as one or more efficiency frontiers. The treatments forming the frontier are those most efficient in benefits and costs, taking into account the criterion of absolute and extended dominance. IQWiG adds that the final segment of the frontier no longer needs to be extended, since that extension was previously intended for deriving a price recommendation.
has perspective title Efficiency Frontier Applying Absolute and Extended Dominance
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 4.15

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Efficiency Frontier

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000553
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Efficiency Frontier
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/en/about-us/methods/methods-paper/
has perspective summary When a formal cost-benefit assessment is undertaken, IQWiG uses an efficiency-frontier method rather than a fixed cross-indication threshold: existing interventions in the same indication are plotted with net cost on one axis and value of benefit on the other, the non-dominated options are linked to form the efficiency frontier, and the maximum reimbursable price for a new drug is inferred from its position relative to that frontier (its willingness-to-pay is indication-specific, derived from the slope of the frontier / the "proportional rule").
has perspective title Indication-Specific Efficiency Frontier Sets the Maximum Reimbursable Price
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods; Caro et al., efficiency frontier approach (Health Economics, 2010)
has wiki record identifier efficiency-frontier

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Evidence

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000571
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Evidence
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG normally bases its recommendations only on studies with sufficient certainty of results, judged by internal validity, external validity and statistical precision. Results on an outcome carry high qualitative certainty when they come from a randomised study with low risk of bias, moderate certainty from a randomised study with high risk of bias, and low certainty from a non-randomised comparative study. For each patient-relevant outcome the evidence then supports a proof, an indication or a hint of added benefit or harm, or none of these.
has perspective title Certainty of Results Graded by Study Design and Bias
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025, sections 1.3.4 and 3.1.4

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Focus Group
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG lists individual interviews and focus groups among its verbal methods for involving the perspectives of people affected. For benefit assessments with longer processing times, discussions with people affected take place as individual interviews or focus groups of no more than 6 people, conducted by specially trained staff with open-ended questions, ideally before the report plan is developed. IQWiG also counts focus groups among the instruments of qualitative research used to understand the experiences of people affected.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Grounded Theory
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods state that, when producing qualitative evidence syntheses for evidence reports, data from studies using different methodological approaches, such as grounded theory, ethnography and content analysis, must be included and summarised into synthesis findings. Aggregative synthesis methods such as content analysis, meta-summary or thematic synthesis are generally considered most suitable. Confidence in each synthesis finding is then assessed with the GRADE-CERQual tool.
has perspective title Grounded Theory Studies Included in Qualitative Evidence Syntheses
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English version published 1 July 2026), sections 10.4.3.1 and 10.4.3.2

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Hazard Ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000602
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Hazard Ratio
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary For time-to-event outcomes in drug benefit assessments, IQWiG uses the two-sided 95% confidence interval of the hazard ratio, or of the pooled meta-analytic hazard ratio, to determine the extent of effect. The same thresholds apply as for the relative risk: for all-cause mortality, the upper confidence limit must fall below 0.85 for a major, 0.95 for a considerable and 1.00 for a minor extent. If a hazard ratio cannot be interpreted meaningfully, for example because of relevant violation of the proportional hazard assumption, a relative risk at a meaningful time point should be examined.
has perspective title Hazard Ratio Confidence Interval Sets the Extent of Added Benefit

has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG holds that a diagnostic test realises its health benefit or harm mainly through the therapeutic or preventive procedures that follow it, and that diagnostic information without medical consequences as a rule has no benefit. It therefore assesses tests primarily through comparative intervention studies of the whole diagnostic and therapeutic chain with patient-relevant outcomes. Linked evidence, which joins test accuracy studies to treatment studies, is used only when direct evidence cannot be expected and is generally considered weaker.
has perspective title Benefit of Diagnostic Tests Judged on Patient Relevant Outcomes
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English version published 1 July 2026), sections 3.5, 3.5.1 and 3.5.1.2

has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods grade a result from a non-randomised comparative study as having low qualitative certainty in benefit assessments. In assessments of potential, where lower evidence requirements apply, historically controlled studies are listed among designs giving very low certainty, and one-arm studies compared with literature controls give minimum certainty. Benefit can also be inferred from well-documented case series when a dramatic effect reverses a certainly or almost certainly predictable disease course that no available treatment can influence.
has perspective title Historically Controlled Studies Give Very Low Certainty of Results

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000637
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)
has display order 5
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary In health economic evaluations of drugs, IQWiG treats the ICER, the difference in costs divided by the difference in the benefit assessment outcome or in QALYs, as the main result. The base-case ICER compares the drug with the appropriate comparator therapy, and the effect of varying the drug price is examined first. IQWiG applies no universal threshold, so it draws no dichotomous conclusion on cost-effectiveness. When more than two treatments are compared outside the §35b SGB V procedure, the ratios can be plotted as an efficiency frontier, which is no longer extended to derive a price recommendation.
has perspective title ICER Against the Appropriate Comparator Therapy as the Main Result
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), sections 1.4, 4.2 (Table 5), 4.10 and 4.15

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Indirect Treatment Comparison

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000649
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Indirect Treatment Comparison
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG regards indirect comparisons as resting on stronger assumptions than direct comparisons, so in benefit assessments they generally give only hints or indications rather than proofs and need adequate justification, although health economic evaluations of several interventions often require them. Only adjusted indirect comparisons via adequate common comparators, such as the Bucher method or network meta-analysis, are accepted; naive comparisons of single arms and modelling with strong assumptions about unknown effects are rejected. If serious doubts exist about similarity, homogeneity or consistency, indirect comparisons should not be used.
has perspective title Only Adjusted Indirect Comparisons via Adequate Common Comparators
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.8

has perspective summary IQWiG's comprehensive information retrieval is usually not limited to specific years, but searches may be restricted to English and German publications. IQWiG justifies this by evaluations showing that excluding non-English publications does not change the conclusion of most systematic reviews. Whether a language restriction can be expected to affect the result of a report is checked project by project, with complementary medicine given as an example. Focused information retrieval may also restrict languages.

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Loss to Follow-Up

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Loss to Follow-Up
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods generally exclude results from a benefit assessment if more than 30% of the participants who should be analysed are left out of the analysis altogether, or if the proportions left out differ between groups by more than 15 percentage points, which suggests non-random exclusion. These rules are guidance rather than rigid limits. For participants who are analysed but incompletely observed, no fixed limits apply: the risk of bias depends on the number, timing and reasons for losses to follow-up, and on differences between groups.
has perspective title Results Set Aside When Over 30% of Participants Are Not Analysed
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English version published 1 July 2026), section 10.3.11

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Mantel-Haenszel Method

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000681
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Mantel-Haenszel Method
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods set a standard meta-analysis approach that depends on the number of studies. With only 2 studies, IQWiG applies a fixed-effect model, using the Mantel-Haenszel method for binary data and the inverse variance method for continuous data, unless there are clear arguments against a fixed-effect model. With 3 or 4 studies it moves to a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis, since heterogeneity cannot be reliably estimated from fewer than 5 studies.
has perspective title Mantel-Haenszel Method for Binary Data When Only 2 Studies Are Pooled
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.7

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Meta-Regression

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000701
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Meta-Regression
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary Where studies are highly heterogeneous, IQWiG investigates potential causes and notes that meta-regression may identify study characteristics that explain differing effect sizes. Even when based on randomised studies, a meta-regression shows only an observed association, not a causal relationship. Analyses relating effects to average patient characteristics are especially difficult to interpret and share the limits of ecological studies; because their high risk of bias cannot be removed by adjustment, definite conclusions are possible only on the basis of individual patient data.
has perspective title Meta-regression Shows Association Only, Firm Conclusions Need IPD
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.7

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Minimal Clinically Important Difference

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000704
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Minimal Clinically Important Difference
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods prefer patient-reported anchors for determining a minimally important difference, but find that published values vary widely with the anchor, observation period, disease severity and direction of change, and that no established standard exists for judging their quality. The Institute therefore accepts prespecified responder analyses when the response criterion is at least 15% of the instrument's scale range. Otherwise it uses standardised mean differences (Hedges' g) with an irrelevance threshold of 0.2, or post hoc responder analyses at exactly 15%.
has perspective title Responder Thresholds of at Least 15% of the Scale Range
has primary source label Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG), General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation published 1 July 2026), section 10.3.3

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Multiple Regression

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Multiple Regression
has display order 3
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG's General Methods treat multifactorial methods mainly as a way to compensate for confounding in non-randomised studies, and set out what a report should usually give so that such a model can be judged. This includes an a priori specification of the outcome and all potential explanatory variables, how model assumptions and goodness of fit were checked, and estimates with standard errors and confidence intervals for every explanatory variable. Where variable selection cannot be avoided, IQWiG uses a form of backward elimination, which it prefers to forward selection.
has perspective title Reporting and Variable Selection in Multifactorial Regression Models
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.6

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Negative Study

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000726
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Negative Study
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG describes rating the non-significant result of a traditional significance test as evidence that the null hypothesis is true as one of the most common serious errors in interpreting medical data. Equivalence has to be shown with methods that test equivalence hypotheses, against an equivalence range defined in advance, because exact equivalence cannot be demonstrated statistically. A one-sided range of at most irrelevant inferiority gives a non-inferiority hypothesis, and the required sample size should be calculated before the study starts.
has perspective title Non-Significant Result Is Not Evidence of Equivalence
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden; German original authoritative), DOI 10.60584/General-Methods_V8.0, section 10.3.5

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG accepts network meta-analysis as an adjusted indirect comparison method, but indirect comparisons require stronger assumptions and generally provide only hints or indications of added benefit or harm, not proofs. Their use needs adequate justification, although they are often necessary in health economic evaluations that compare more than 2 interventions. A random-effects model should be the default, sufficient consistency between direct and indirect evidence is required, and non-adjusted comparisons of single arms from different studies are disapproved.
has perspective title Indirect Comparisons Give Hints of Added Benefit Rather Than Proof

has perspective summary In IQWiG benefit assessments, a result from a randomised study gives high or moderate qualitative certainty, while a result from a non-randomised comparative study gives low certainty. In assessments of potential, which carry lower evidence requirements, non-randomised controlled studies with active allocation following a preplanned rule count as low certainty when confounders are adequately controlled and as very low certainty otherwise. In classifying non-randomised studies, IQWiG primarily evaluates the control for potential confounders.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept One-Way Sensitivity Analysis
has display order 5
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG states that health economic evaluations should include both univariate and multivariate deterministic sensitivity analyses, alongside probabilistic sensitivity analysis, to account for parameter uncertainty. The deterministic analyses aim to identify the parameters with particular influence on the result, such as transition probabilities, utilities and costs. Each analysis is documented with the minimum and maximum values used and the underlying assumptions, the results are presented in tabular form, and the influence of the varied parameters can be shown in a tornado plot.
has perspective title Deterministic Sensitivity Analyses Reported in a Table and Tornado Plot
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 4.2 (Table 5) and section 4.11

has perspective summary IQWiG does not accept the QALY as its standard outcome for cost-benefit assessment, citing unresolved methodological and distributive-justice concerns. It assesses quality of life separately (e.g. standard gamble, time trade-off, or instruments such as the EQ-5D) and judges cost relative to benefit using an efficiency frontier within each therapeutic area.

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Pairwise Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000764
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Pairwise Meta-Analysis
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG chooses a random-effects model when heterogeneity cannot be excluded with sufficient certainty, and sets a standard approach by number of studies. With 2 studies it applies a fixed-effect model, using inverse variance for continuous data or Mantel-Haenszel for binary data. With 3 or 4 studies it uses, for common effect measures, a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis with informative priors for heterogeneity, checked against a qualitative summary. With 5 or more it uses the Knapp-Hartung method with the Paule-Mandel heterogeneity estimator, keeping the pooled estimate only if it is informative.
has perspective title Model Choice Set by the Number of Studies Pooled
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation), section 10.3.7

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Performance Bias
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG defines performance bias as bias caused by different types of care provided, apart from the intervention under investigation, and names blinding as an effective protection against it. Its risk-of-bias assessment of controlled studies, which closely follows the Cochrane tool, includes blinding of patients and treating staff as an item across outcomes. Results of unblinded trials, or of trials where unblinding may have occurred, are interpreted more cautiously than those of blinded studies.
has perspective title Performance Bias Defined as Unequal Care Beyond the Intervention
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation published July 2026; the German original is authoritative), sections 10.1.4 and 10.3.13

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Perspective
has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary In the reference case, the health economic evaluation takes the perspective of the community of people insured under statutory health insurance (SHI), as set out in German social law. This perspective counts direct reimbursable costs together with non-reimbursable time costs of insured persons or their relatives, while co-payments are shown separately and transfer payments such as sickness allowance are left out. Depending on the commission, the pure SHI, social insurance or societal perspective may also be considered, with those results provided separately.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Reference Standard
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG, which uses the term reference test, states that accuracy estimates for an index test may be biased if the reference test does not correctly distinguish sick from healthy participants, if only a non-random sample receives it, or if the reference test applied depends on the index test result. Including the index test within the reference test may overstate accuracy. For linked evidence, the same reference test should ideally verify results in the accuracy study and serve as the inclusion criterion in the treatment study.

has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden 8.0), sections 3.5.1.2 and 10.3.13
