concerns wiki concept Secondary Research
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG mostly uses systematic reviews to identify relevant primary studies, but an assessment can rest partly or solely on them if they show only minimal risk of bias and present the evidence completely, transparently and reproducibly. As a rule at least 2 independent high-quality reviews should be available, appraised with AMSTAR, AMSTAR 2 or ROBIS. If the reviews suggest that an assessment based on primary studies could reach different conclusions, IQWiG carries out that assessment instead.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf

has perspective summary IQWiG usually advises random-effects models for meta-analyses of diagnostic accuracy studies because heterogeneity is expected. Separate models for sensitivity and specificity may be used if evidence on bivariate models is insufficient, but when a summary ROC curve or a joint estimate of sensitivity and specificity is of interest, bivariate random-effects meta-analyses show advantages. Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Time-Lag Bias
has display order 1
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG defines publication bias as studies with a statistically significant negative difference, or no significant difference, being either not published at all or published later than studies with positive, statistically significant results. Pooling only published results can therefore bias the common effect estimate. Because funnel plots and meta-regression can neither confirm nor exclude this bias, IQWiG stresses searching for unpublished data and contacts authors or sponsors when studies have not yet been published at the time of its assessment.

has perspective summary IQWiG's reference case assumes that a benefit assessment under §35a SGB V already exists, and its comparison of the drug with the appropriate comparator therapy forms the basis of the decision-analytic model, for example to derive transition probabilities. The health economic evaluation does not call that result into question, so where no added benefit was shown, none is suggested by the model. Further data to determine transition probabilities for certain events, and background mortality, may come from exploratory searches of bibliographic databases and other sources.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 4
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary For benefit assessments, IQWiG's General Methods require analyses based on the treatment policy estimand, the effect of the whole treatment strategy regardless of discontinuation or switching, together with the intention-to-treat principle. Data on all relevant outcomes, including patient-reported outcomes and adverse events, should therefore be collected completely even after treatment is discontinued or switched. Censoring at a switch can make censoring informative and create a high risk of bias, and recording adverse events for only 30 days afterwards is insufficient.

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Unit of Allocation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000884
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Unit of Allocation
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG notes that simple standard procedures assume independent experimental units within a treatment arm, which does not hold in cluster-randomised studies or studies of eyes or teeth. Applying them anyway underestimates variance and gives p values that are too small. Results from such studies can still be considered only if the related error can be properly classified, and suitable methods such as generalised estimating equations or mixed models should be applied. For prevention programmes, IQWiG accepts studies allocating clusters to arms where contamination between groups is a concern.
has perspective title Clustered Data Need Methods for Dependent Observations
has primary source label IQWiG, General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation of Allgemeine Methoden; German original authoritative), DOI 10.60584/General-Methods_V8.0, sections 3.7 and 10.3.14
has wiki record identifier unit-of-allocation
is perspective of body Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care
isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

institutional perspective of IQWiG on Verification Bias

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000904
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Verification Bias
has display order 2
has institution label as shown IQWiG
has page URL https://www.iqwig.de/methoden/general-methods_version-8-0.pdf
has perspective summary IQWiG states that estimates of diagnostic accuracy may be biased if the reference test is conducted only in a non-random sample of participants who received the index test, which it calls partial verification bias. Bias may also arise when the reference test applied depends on the result of the index test, termed differential verification bias. IQWiG adds that all study participants, including those with unclear test results, need to be considered to avoid systematic bias.
has perspective title Partial and Differential Verification Bias in Diagnostic Studies
has primary source label IQWiG General Methods, Version 8.0 of 19 December 2025 (English translation published July 2026; the German original is authoritative), section 10.3.13
has wiki record identifier verification-bias
is perspective of body Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care
isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

has perspective summary The ISPOR-SMDM task force recommends that state-transition models be structured around the decision problem, with clearly defined states, transitions, cycle length, time horizon, rewards and assumptions. It emphasizes evaluating whether the Markov memory assumption is appropriate, using extensions when relevant history affects future outcomes, and documenting validation and uncertainty rather than treating the model as a purely mechanical calculation.

has perspective summary Under the Health Protection (Vaccination) Regulations 2009, the Secretary of State must, so far as reasonably practicable, implement JCVI recommendations on national programmes that rest on an assessment demonstrating cost effectiveness. JCVI applies NICE's methodology: a programme can be considered cost effective if its health benefits, both direct benefits to those vaccinated and indirect benefits to the unvaccinated population, exceed the opportunity costs of programmes that may be displaced. Reviewers of modelling are asked whether the approach to estimating indirect protection is appropriate.

has perspective summary Maryland law directs the Health Services Cost Review Commission to review hospital costs and rates so that each purchaser of hospital services is assured that total costs are reasonable, that aggregate rates are reasonably related to aggregate costs, and that rates are set equitably among all purchasers or classes of purchasers without undue discrimination or preference. Hospitals may charge only rates set under the statute and must comply with the all-payer model contract. The Commission may set rate levels and increases in aggregate or for each hospital, taking account of objective standards of efficiency and effectiveness.

has institution label as shown Medical Research Council and NIHR

has perspective summary The framework commissioned by the Medical Research Council and the National Institute for Health Research treats an intervention as complex because of features such as its number of components, the range of behaviours targeted, the skills needed to deliver and receive it, the groups, settings or levels targeted, and the flexibility permitted. Economic evaluation should be a core component of all phases of intervention research, and broad approaches such as cost benefit or cost consequence analysis will often suit complex interventions better than narrower cost-effectiveness or cost-utility analysis.

has perspective summary The Boards of Trustees of the Medicare trust funds make actuarial estimates for a 75-year period, 2026 to 2100 in the 2026 report, under intermediate assumptions, with low-cost and high-cost alternatives for Hospital Insurance, and show an illustrative alternative alongside the current-law projections. The 2026 report projects that the Hospital Insurance trust fund will be depleted in the second quarter of 2033, after which income would cover 89% of scheduled benefits, and puts the 75-year actuarial deficit at 0.56% of taxable payroll. has perspective summary The MHRA offers a national conditional marketing authorisation scheme for products that fulfil an unmet medical need, where the comprehensive clinical data normally required are incomplete but expected soon. The applicant must show a positive benefit-risk balance and the likelihood of providing comprehensive data after authorisation, and that the benefit of immediate availability outweighs the risk of data still being required. Authorisations are valid for one year, are renewable annually on application, and can convert to a standard authorisation once the specific obligations are fulfilled. Since 1 January 2025 the MHRA grants them UK-wide.

has perspective summary The MHRA asks for all serious suspected adverse drug reactions to established medicines and vaccines to be reported to the Yellow Card scheme, even if the effect is well recognised, and for all suspected reactions to new medicines and vaccines under additional monitoring, marked with an inverted black triangle. It is particularly interested in reactions in children, in patients over 65, to biological medicines and vaccines, from delayed effects and interactions, and to herbal and homeopathic remedies. A reporter needs only a suspicion, not proof of causality.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown MHRA
has page URL https://www.gov.uk/guidance/clinical-trials-for-medicines-collection-verification-and-reporting-of-safety-events
has perspective summary MHRA guidance under the amended Clinical Trials Regulations, which took full effect on 28 April 2026, defines an adverse event as any untoward medical occurrence in a participant given a medicinal product, whether or not caused by it. Sponsors and investigators should record adverse events from informed consent to the end of the trial unless the protocol says otherwise, and investigators report serious adverse events to the sponsor within 24 hours unless the protocol or investigator's brochure exempts them. Fatal or life-threatening SUSARs go to the MHRA within 7 days and other SUSARs within 15 days.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown National Association of Insurance Commissioners
has page URL https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/model-law-092.pdf
has perspective summary The NAIC Stop Loss Insurance Model Act bars an annual aggregate attachment point below the greater of USD 4,000 times the number of group members, 120% of expected claims or USD 20,000 for groups of 50 or fewer, and below 110% of expected claims for groups of 51 or more. Expected claims are those projected for the group's health plan in the absence of stop-loss or other insurance. An NAIC white paper describes the aggregate layer as protection against claim frequency, with claims paid under specific cover not counted towards the aggregate attachment point.

has perspective summary The National Cancer Institute's Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 6.0, published on 22 July 2025, gives a severity grading scale for each adverse event term. has perspective summary Australia's National Disability Insurance Scheme funds assistive technology that is directly related to a participant's disability, helps towards their goals, is safe and is supported by evidence. Low-cost, low-risk items under AUD 1,500 can be bought from the consumables budget without quotes, assessments or prior approval. Mid-cost items of AUD 1,500 to 15,000 need a recommendation from an assistive technology advisor, and high-cost items above AUD 15,000, such as powered wheelchairs and prosthetics, need an assessment by a qualified assessor and may first have to be trialled or rented.

has perspective summary Belgium's National Institute for Health and Disability Insurance (INAMI-RIZIV) states that a doctor can never charge fee supplements above the regulated fees to a hospital patient in a double or shared room, while in a single room a supplement can normally be charged. No supplement may be charged for a stay in a single room if the patient chose a double or shared room in the admission declaration. Room supplements follow the same pattern, so the room chosen on admission determines whether the patient can face charges above the regulated tariff.

has perspective summary Since 1 January 2025, doctors in Belgium, whether or not they have joined the national agreement, may not charge fee supplements for reimbursed ambulatory care to patients automatically entitled to increased reimbursement (BIM), and since 1 January 2026 the ban covers patients granted BIM after a means test. has perspective summary The budget impact test applies when the potential net budget impact of a medicine is expected to exceed £40 million per year in any of its first 3 financial years in the NHS. has perspective summary NHS England treats a simple confidential discount through a patient access scheme as the fastest and preferred route, and considers complex arrangements only once simple discounts are shown to be unsuitable. Commercial access agreements are confidential and at NHS England's discretion, using formats such as budget caps, price-volume agreements, outcomes-based rebates and indication-specific pricing. They are normally reserved for value propositions at or below the lower end of the standard NICE threshold range. Where net budget impact exceeds £40 million in any of the first 3 years, NHS England can negotiate to manage affordability.

has perspective summary The Universal Principles for Advance Care Planning, published by NHS England with partner organisations in March 2022, describe it as a voluntary process of person-centred discussion about preferences and priorities for future care. Six principles put the person at the centre, with personalised conversations, shared decision making, a shareable plan, the chance to review it, and freedom for anyone involved to speak up if the principles are not followed. Advance statements guide later decisions but are not legally binding, unlike valid and applicable advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting powers of attorney.

has perspective summary The NHS Payment Scheme defines the adjusted length of stay of an admitted patient care spell as the number of changes of calendar day from admission to discharge, after deducting days in critical care, rehabilitation, specialist palliative care and delayed transfers of care. Each healthcare resource group has a trimpoint of the upper quartile plus 1.5 times the interquartile range of adjusted stay, with a minimum of 5 days, beyond which excess bed days are paid daily. Adult emergency stays of zero or one day attract a reduced price when the group's average non-elective stay is 2 days or more.

has perspective summary NHS England's Quality, Service Improvement and Redesign tools present the balanced scorecard as a performance management tool for turning a team's vision and strategy into objectives, measures and targets. Design runs through eight stages, from a sound strategic foundation and cause-and-effect links between objectives to targets, strategic initiatives and full implementation, and the tool works best with buy-in across the organisation and involvement of a wide range of staff.

has perspective summary The NHS Standard Contract requires providers to follow national clinical coding guidance and bars local changes in counting and coding practice without the commissioner's agreement. has perspective summary The NICE Decision Support Unit treats the absolute natural history under the comparator as a separate component of a cost-effectiveness model, to which relative treatment effects from trials are then applied. Baseline response should be as specific as possible to the population of interest, which may favour recent trials, cohort studies or registers, and the choice of sources should be justified. The unit prefers a baseline model built independently of the relative effects model and does not recommend using the unweighted mean of trial baseline arms.

General-population life expectancy should come from ONS life tables for England, weighted by the sex mix of the patient group, with EQ-5D-5L population norms following NICE's adoption of that value set in August 2026. The 3.5% reference-case discount rate applies, and carer quality of life is excluded.

institutional perspective of NICE Decision Support Unit on Accelerated Failure Time Model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000023
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Accelerated Failure Time Model
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD14-Survival-analysis.updated-March-2013.v2.pdf
has perspective summary The NICE Decision Support Unit classifies the log-logistic and log normal distributions as accelerated failure time models and notes that the Weibull can be parameterised either as a proportional hazards or as an accelerated failure time model, whereas the Gompertz can only be a proportional hazards model. In an accelerated failure time model the treatment effect is an acceleration factor that acts multiplicatively on the time scale. Log-logistic and log normal models do not produce a single hazard ratio, so the proportional hazards assumption does not hold for them, although treatment group can still be included as a covariate.
has perspective title Accelerated Failure Time Models Report an Acceleration Factor
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 14: Survival analysis for economic evaluations alongside clinical trials, extrapolation with patient-level data (Latimer), June 2011, last updated March 2013, sections 2.2, 2.3, 2.4 and 2.9

institutional perspective of NICE Decision Support Unit on Administrative Censoring

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000088
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Administrative Censoring
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD14-Survival-analysis.updated-March-2013.v2.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 14 states that standard survival methods are suitable only if censoring is uninformative, and that extrapolation is required unless trial survival data are complete or very close to complete. When some patients remain event-free at the end of follow-up, only a mean restricted to that time can be estimated directly, so parametric models should be used rather than restricted means unless data are almost entirely complete. With substantial censoring, a scenario based only on observed data can show how far the extrapolated period drives the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio.
has perspective title Extrapolate Immature Survival Data With Parametric Models
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 14: Survival analysis for economic evaluations alongside clinical trials, extrapolation with patient-level data, June 2011, last updated March 2013, sections 2, 5 and 6.1

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis
has display order 3
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD2-General-meta-analysis-corrected-2Sep2016v2.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 2 sets out a single framework for synthesising aggregate data from randomised trials, mainly for probabilistic decision making, in which pairwise meta-analysis, indirect comparisons and network meta-analysis use the same core models with fixed or random effects. It uses Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo estimation and treats trial-specific baselines as nuisance parameters, because an incorrect baseline model would bias the relative treatment effects. Model fit is checked with the residual deviance, and fixed and random effects models are compared using the Deviance Information Criterion.
has perspective title Generalised Linear Model Framework for Aggregate Trial Data
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 2: A generalised linear modelling framework for pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, August 2011, last updated September 2016, sections 1, 2.1.1 and 2.1.2

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/nice-dsu/tsds/survival-analysis
has perspective summary TSD 14 states that AIC and BIC, unlike the negative 2 log likelihood, can compare parametric survival models that are not nested, and recommends presenting them alongside log-cumulative hazard plots and clinical plausibility. Model choice can rest on these tests only when survival data are very close to complete; with substantial censoring, external data, clinical plausibility and expert judgement are needed. TSD 21 adds that AIC and BIC give little information about how well a model extrapolates and should not be the sole basis for selection when the aim is to extrapolate.
has perspective title AIC and BIC Test Fit to Trial Data, Not Extrapolation

concerns wiki concept Anchoring Bias in Elicitation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/nice-dsu/tsds/expert-elicitation-tsd
has perspective summary NICE DSU Technical Support Document 26 recommends that standard training for experts judging long-term survival covers potential biases from anchoring, availability and overconfidence. When scenario testing is used, experts should give their own probability judgements about survival at the target time before any scenario is presented, so that their judgements are not anchored on it, and the scenario must be presented as an assumption, not a claim about the true hazard. The risk of an unduly influential expert should be discussed in training alongside anchoring effects.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000244
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Average Treatment Effect
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/nice-dsu/tsds/observational-data
has perspective summary TSD 17 states that the treatment effect typically of interest in NICE technology appraisals is the average treatment effect, the expected gain from treatment for a randomly selected individual and the effect a randomised trial would identify, although in some cases the effect on the treated may be the parameter of interest. It notes that the ATE needs more demanding, often untestable, assumptions than the alternatives, and that the ATE, ATT and local average treatment effect coincide only when effects are homogeneous. Analysts should state the parameter of interest and justify how their method estimates it.

has perspective summary TSD 21 states that none of the standard parametric survival models can accurately model survival where the hazard has two or more turning points, such as a hazard that rises soon after trial entry, falls as sicker patients die and rises again with age-related mortality. It describes flexible parametric, mixture, poly-hazard, piecewise and cure models for such shapes. Fitted and extrapolated hazard and survival functions should always be presented with general population functions plotted alongside, and background mortality incorporated to avoid extremely implausible projections.
has perspective title Standard Models Cannot Capture Two or More Turning Points
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 21: Flexible methods for survival analysis (Rutherford, Lambert, Sweeting, Pennington, Crowther, Abrams and Latimer, January 2020, updated version March 2022), sections 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 3.2 and 7.1

has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD6-Software.final_.08.05.12.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 6 sets out ways to embed evidence synthesis in probabilistic cost-effectiveness analysis, which it calls the preferred methodology for the NICE reference case. In a one-stage Bayesian approach, samples from the joint posterior go directly through the decision model with no assumption about their distributional form. In a two-stage approach the posterior samples are exported to another package, and all parameter values must come from the same Markov chain Monte Carlo iteration so that correlations are preserved. Frequentist alternatives sample from a multivariate normal distribution built from the estimates and their variance-covariance matrix.
has perspective title Posterior Samples Passed Directly Through the Decision Model
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 6: Embedding evidence synthesis in probabilistic cost-effectiveness analysis: software choices (Dias, Sutton, Welton and Ades, May 2011, last updated April 2012), executive summary and sections 2.1 to 2.3

has perspective summary TSD 14 recommends the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria for comparing the fit of alternative parametric survival models, which cannot be nested, and notes that the negative 2 log likelihood suits only nested models and was used erroneously in past NICE appraisals. Both criteria weigh improved fit against extra parameters, which BIC penalises more highly. They address internal validity, not the extrapolated portion of the curve, so with substantial censoring external data, clinical plausibility and expert judgement should guide model choice.
has perspective title AIC and BIC Compare Non-Nested Survival Models on Internal Fit Only
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 14: Survival analysis for economic evaluations alongside clinical trials: extrapolation with patient-level data (Latimer, June 2011, last updated March 2013), sections 3.3, 3.5 and 6.1

has perspective summary TSD 2 takes a Bayesian approach to pairwise and network meta-analysis using Markov chain Monte Carlo and recommends vague priors, such as N(0, 100²), for trial baselines and relative effects, with informative priors for relative effects needing special justification. It warns that routinely vague priors leave the between-trial variance poorly identified without many large trials and give posteriors biased upwards, so external data or elicited informative priors may help. Where all trials are two-arm, frequentist methods are acceptable if parameter uncertainty and correlations are propagated.

has perspective summary TSD 12 notes that preference-based quality of life data such as EQ-5D are typically skewed, bounded by the limits of the index and often include negative values, but that in most cases uncertainty in the mean can be adequately described by sampling from a normal distribution. If a lower limit is needed, such as minus 0.594 for the UK EQ-5D index, a standard beta distribution can be scaled up with a height parameter.

has perspective summary TSD 15 distinguishes patient heterogeneity, stochastic uncertainty and parameter uncertainty, and states that parameters reflecting patient heterogeneity should not be included within the probabilistic sensitivity analysis. Where patient characteristics relate non-linearly to model outcomes, a patient-level simulation that samples characteristics from population distributions should be used to obtain an unbiased estimate of mean outcomes, unless suitable subgroup analysis avoids the need. The estimate is unbiased only if enough patients are simulated and covariance between their characteristics is correctly taken into account.

has perspective summary TSD 14 states that the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria weigh the improved fit of alternative survival models against the potentially inefficient use of additional parameters, with BIC penalising extra parameters more heavily than AIC. has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD2-General-meta-analysis-corrected-2Sep2016v2.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 2 models the number of events in each trial arm as binomial, with a logit link to the arm's event probability, in its core models for pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomised trials. When trials report the proportion with an event at different follow-up times, it keeps the binomial likelihood but uses a complementary log-log link, assuming a constant event rate. Because zero cells are allowed, the occasional trial with a zero count needs no special precautions, whereas adding an arbitrary 0.5 biases effect estimates. Several small trials with zero cells can make the models numerically unstable.
has perspective title Binomial Likelihood Handles Zero Cells Without Continuity Corrections
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 2: A generalised linear modelling framework for pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Dias, Welton, Sutton and Ades, August 2011, last updated September 2016), sections 2.1.1, 3.2 and 6.3

has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD2-General-meta-analysis-corrected-2Sep2016v2.pdf
has perspective summary The DSU's evidence synthesis framework matches the likelihood and link function to the type of data, with a binomial likelihood and logit link as the core model for binary outcomes. For ordered categorical outcomes, such as the proportions reaching ACR-20, ACR-50 and ACR-70, it uses a multinomial likelihood with a probit link, treating the categories as cut-offs on an underlying continuous scale. This assumes the same treatment effect at every cut-off, which should be checked by comparing effects across cut-offs and by the residual deviance.
has perspective title Binomial and Multinomial Likelihoods for Categorical Trial Outcomes

has perspective summary TSD 20 reports that satisfying the Prentice criteria does not guarantee a causal relationship between treatment effects on a surrogate and on the final outcome. It favours a meta-analytic approach based on several trials, because associations between effects derived directly from randomisation are average causal effects. A single trial cannot show that an association confirmed under one treatment will hold for other interventions.

has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD2-General-meta-analysis-corrected-2Sep2016v2.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 2 notes that standardised mean differences allow trials that measured the same quantity on different continuous scales to be pooled, and names Cohen's d and Hedges' adjusted g as the best known, differing in how the pooled standard deviation is defined and in Hedges' small-sample correction. Dividing by the sample standard deviation introduces extra heterogeneity, because standard deviations carry sampling error and trials with narrow inclusion criteria tend to give larger values. Dividing estimates from an instrument by a standard deviation from an external representative population sample would give more interpretable results.
has perspective title Standardised Mean Differences Add Heterogeneity Across Trials

has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD15_Patient-level_simulation.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 15 defines a cohort model as one that estimates outcomes for a group of patients without explicitly considering each individual, although subgroups can be tracked separately, and asks that the choice between cohort-level and patient-level approaches be carefully considered and justified. Using only average characteristics gives a biased mean when heterogeneous characteristics relate non-linearly to outcomes, and replicate or tunnel states eventually make a cohort Markov model unwieldy. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis needs only one simulation loop in a cohort-level model, so it usually runs faster than in an equivalent patient-level model.
has perspective title Choice Between Cohort and Patient-Level Models Must Be Justified
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 15: Cost-effectiveness modelling using patient-level simulation (Davis, Stevenson, Tappenden and Wailoo, April 2014), sections 1, 2.1, 3.1, 3.2 and 3.6

has perspective summary TSD 8 defines construct validity as the extent to which a measure's scores agree with other measures or indicators of the dimensions of health-related quality of life relevant to the patient group. It names two common tests, known group differences and convergent validity, and states that validation is best performed at dimension level, although evidence is often available only for the index. Such tests can never prove validity, and groupings based on clinical measures such as visual acuity or respiratory function may relate only weakly to health-related quality of life.

has perspective summary The DSU notes that health-related quality of life data, particularly the EQ-5D preferred by NICE, are not normally distributed, being typically skewed, bimodal or trimodal, bounded by the index limits and often negative. It states that in most cases the uncertainty in the mean can still be described adequately by sampling from a normal distribution. has perspective summary TSD 15 describes a state-transition model as a discrete time approximation to clinical events that can occur at any point in time. Accuracy improves with continuity corrections such as the half-cycle correction and with shorter cycles, and reducing the cycle length until it has no appreciable effect on model outcomes is recommended. Incorrect discretisation can introduce bias, for example when several transitions can occur within one cycle, and where rapid events alternate with long quiet periods a discrete event simulation may be more efficient than very short cycles.
has perspective title Fixed-Cycle Models as Discrete Approximations to Continuous Processes
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 15: Cost-effectiveness modelling using patient-level simulation (Davis, Stevenson, Tappenden and Wailoo, April 2014), sections 2.6 and 3.3

has perspective summary TSD 8 names convergent validity, the extent to which a measure correlates with another measure of health, as one of two common tests of construct validity, alongside known group differences. It can be assessed by the strength of association between EQ-5D and another preference-based measure such as HUI3 or SF-6D, and a lack of association may suggest that EQ-5D is not valid in that group. Convergence with directly administered time trade-off, standard gamble or visual analogue scale values is a more limited test, because these reflect patient rather than general population values.

has perspective summary TSD 14 makes log-cumulative hazard plots, or suitable residual plots, the first step of its survival model selection algorithm, showing whether hazards are constant, monotonic or non-monotonic and whether proportional hazards is reasonable. Approximately straight plots identify parametric models to fit, parallel arms point to proportional hazards models, and curved plots call for piecewise or more flexible approaches. TSD 14 adds that such plots show fit to the observed data only and say nothing about the period beyond trial follow-up.

has perspective summary TSD 15 describes state-transition models as a discrete-time approximation in which patients are counted at fixed points set by the cycle length and time horizon. has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/68716099
has perspective summary TSD 24 states that simple methods, such as censoring patients at the time of switch or excluding switchers, are prone to bias and not recommended, because switching is often related to prognosis. Inverse probability of censoring weights can correct the bias introduced by censoring switchers, provided the switching model is appropriately specified and there is no unmeasured confounding. Adjusting censoring times only in switchers also creates informative censoring, so rank preserving structural failure time models, iterative parameter estimation and two-stage estimation should be applied with and without re-censoring in submissions to NICE.

has perspective summary TSD 2 assesses the fit of generalised linear models for pairwise and network meta-analysis through the posterior mean residual deviance, to which each data point should contribute about 1, so the total can be compared with the number of independent data points. Where the residuals suggest poor fit, plotting each point's contribution to the effective number of parameters against its signed deviance residual shows whether poorly fitting points materially affect the model, and points beyond the curve marking a contribution of 3 to the deviance information criterion generally indicate poor fit.

has perspective summary TSD 25 sets out meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy for NICE decision models, pooling sensitivity and specificity and discouraging the pooling of predictive values, which depend critically on prevalence. Its methods allow for heterogeneity between studies, the expected negative correlation between sensitivity and specificity and small cell counts, using the binomial bivariate random effects model, equivalent to the HSROC model, and a multiple thresholds model when studies report several cut-offs. Correlated posterior samples should feed a probabilistic decision model, since plugging in point estimates fails to carry the correlation through.

has perspective summary TSD 17 describes difference in differences as comparing the change in outcomes before and after a natural event between treatment and control groups, using longitudinal data or repeated cross-sections, which in general identifies the average treatment effect on the treated. The estimator assumes common trends across the groups and no selection on unobserved time-varying shocks, an assumption that fails if people change behaviour in anticipation of treatment. In its algorithm for choosing methods, patient-level data from a natural experiment suit such designs, which would be preferred in the first instance if their assumptions are reasonable.

has perspective summary TSD 15 advises that a patient-level simulation, such as a discrete event simulation, may be preferable to a cohort model when outcomes vary non-linearly with patient characteristics, when risks depend on time since an event or on past events, when bursts of events alternate with long quiet periods, or when patients compete for constrained resources. The choice of approach should be properly justified. Modellers are expected to justify the number of patients simulated, and probabilistic sensitivity analysis usually needs two nested simulation loops.
has perspective title When Patient-Level Simulation Suits NICE Appraisals and How to Size It
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 15: Cost-effectiveness modelling using patient-level simulation (Davis, Stevenson, Tappenden and Wailoo, April 2014), sections 1, 3.1 to 3.6 and 5.2

has perspective summary TSD 12 sets out the additive, multiplicative and minimum methods for estimating utility in a combined health state from single-condition data, and states that assuming a baseline of perfect health is inappropriate, with age and sex adjustment an absolute minimum. Where utilities for the combined condition are unavailable, the multiplicative method should be used. Submissions to NICE should justify including or excluding adverse event disutilities, treat decrements for grade 3 to 4 events as particularly important, and avoid double counting decrements for grade 1 to 2 events.

has perspective summary TSD 14 advises that proportional hazards modelling should only be used if the assumption can be clearly justified with log-cumulative hazard plots, external information and clinical expert opinion, and that the source of any hazard ratio should be clearly stated. It notes that log-logistic and log normal models do not produce a single hazard ratio. TSD 21 adds that assuming a proportional treatment effect is restrictive, that flexible parametric models can relax it through time-dependent effects, and that plotting the implied hazard ratio shows what is assumed beyond follow-up.

institutional perspective of NICE Decision Support Unit on Markov Chain

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000689
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Markov Chain
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD15_Patient-level_simulation.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 15 notes that state-transition models are often called Markov models, but that the term should strictly be limited to models with the Markovian property, in which transitions depend only on the current state and not on earlier events or time already spent in that state. A fixed transition matrix applied every cycle gives a time-homogeneous Markov chain, which can be extended to a Markov process with time-varying matrices. Once transitions depend on a patient's earlier history, the Markovian assumption no longer holds and the model cannot be called Markov.
has perspective title Markov Label Kept for Memoryless State-Transition Models
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 15: Cost-effectiveness modelling using patient-level simulation (Davis, Stevenson, Tappenden and Wailoo, April 2014), sections 2.4 and 4.6

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 4
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD15_Patient-level_simulation.pdf
has perspective summary NICE DSU Technical Support Document 15 describes state-transition models that assume the Markovian, or memoryless, property, in which transitions depend only on the current state, and notes that Markov models are so often used for cohorts that the two terms are treated as synonyms. Where transitions depend on time since an event or on earlier events, tunnel states can be added, but only up to a point before the cohort approach becomes unwieldy. A patient-level simulation of the same structure may then be preferable, as it may be where patient characteristics have a non-linear effect on costs and QALYs.
has perspective title When Patient-Level Simulation May Replace a Cohort Markov Model
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 15: Cost-effectiveness modelling using patient-level simulation (Davis, Stevenson, Tappenden and Wailoo, April 2014), sections 2.4, 3.1 and 3.2

institutional perspective of NICE Decision Support Unit on Meta-Regression

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000700
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Meta-Regression
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE Decision Support Unit
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD3-Heterogeneity.final-report.08.05.12.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 3 describes meta-regression as relating the size of a treatment effect to characteristics of the included trials in order to explain between-trial heterogeneity. Even with randomised trials, the study of effect modifiers is observational, so meta-regression shares the confounding of non-randomised studies and cannot show causality from association. Between-trial comparisons can show a highly significant but spurious relation when trials are few and precise, and they are open to ecological bias, which individual patient data avoid while giving far greater power.
has perspective title Meta-regression Is Observational and Open to Ecological Bias
has primary source label NICE DSU Technical Support Document 3, Heterogeneity: subgroups, meta-regression, bias and bias-adjustment (Dias, Sutton, Welton, Ades; September 2011, last updated April 2012), sections 1.1 to 1.1.3

has perspective summary The Decision Support Unit sets out one generalised linear modelling framework for fixed and random effects synthesis that applies to pairwise meta-analysis, indirect comparisons, multi-arm trials and network meta-analysis without distinction. Different likelihoods and link functions cover binomial, rate, continuous, competing risk and ordered categorical outcomes. Estimation is Bayesian, using Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation with WinBUGS code, and models are compared with the deviance information criterion while goodness of fit is judged by the residual deviance.

has perspective summary NICE DSU Technical Support Document 19 found partitioned survival analysis in 22 of 30 NICE cancer appraisals reviewed. It recommends justifying the choice of approach, using consistent terminology without calling the method Markov-like, and stating that every endpoint, including overall survival, is modelled and extrapolated independently. Because the curves lack a structural link, extrapolation may be more uncertain, so all relevant evidence should inform the extrapolation period, and a state transition model may have advantages where intermediate states are prognostic.

has perspective summary The Decision Support Unit recommends bivariate random-effects meta-analysis of test accuracy and adding a hierarchical summary ROC curve when implicit threshold effects are anticipated. It discourages the Moses-Littenberg approach now that exact methods are available and advises against extrapolating the curve beyond the range of the observed data. Because the model does not use threshold values, it cannot show which point on the curve a given threshold relates to. The DSU states its documents are not formal NICE guidance.

has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-02/TSD15_Patient-level_simulation.pdf
has perspective summary TSD 15 notes that state-transition models usually assume future events are independent of past events, which makes it hard to represent risks that depend on time since a previous transition. Replicate states that move the patient on each cycle, sometimes called tunnel states, record the passage of time even when the actual health state does not change. The document warns that only so many replicate states can be added before a cohort Markov model becomes unwieldy, and offers patient-level simulation with history-dependent transition matrices as one solution.
has perspective title Tunnel States Record Time Since the Last Transition

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE sets the reference-case perspective on costs as that of the NHS and personal social services, on the grounds that it does not set the NHS budget, and states that productivity costs should not be included. Costs of time lost from work through illness are therefore left out of the base-case cost-effectiveness estimate. They can be presented separately, as additional information for the committee, where they may be a critical component of a technology's value.
has perspective title Productivity Costs of Absence Excluded From the Reference Case

has perspective summary NICE's shared decision making guideline tells healthcare professionals to use absolute risk rather than relative risk when discussing options with people. Risks should be given as natural frequencies such as 10 in 100 rather than percentages, with the same denominator when comparing risks and over a defined period of time where relevant. The committee found absolute risks much clearer than relative risks, judged relative risks presented alone to be misleading and said relative risk should only supplement absolute risk.
has perspective title Absolute Risk and Natural Frequencies in Risk Discussions

has perspective summary NICE's shared decision making guideline asks healthcare professionals to describe a change in risk in absolute terms, for example that the risk of an event increases from 1 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000, rather than saying that the risk doubles. Comparisons should use natural frequencies with the same denominator, such as 7 in 100 against 20 in 100. The committee found absolute risks much clearer and said relative risk should only be introduced as a supplement to absolute risks.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE assesses severity in technology appraisals using both absolute and proportional QALY shortfall, and applies the QALY weight implied by whichever shows greater severity. An absolute shortfall of 12 to 18 QALYs or a proportional shortfall of 0.85 to 0.95 gives a weight of 1.2, and at least 18 QALYs or at least 0.95 gives 1.7; a result on a cut-off takes the higher level. Shortfall is discounted at the reference-case rate. Since August 2026, shortfall should be calculated with EQ-5D-5L utilities and population norms, with the cut-offs unchanged.
has perspective title Severity Modifier Using Absolute and Proportional QALY Shortfall

has perspective summary NICE recommends that commissioners and providers consider education-based programmes for health and social care practitioners, for example academic detailing, clinical education or educational outreach, as one of several antimicrobial stewardship interventions. These sit alongside review of prescribing by stewardship teams, promotion of antimicrobials recommended in local or national guidelines, and IT or decision support systems. In its medicines optimisation guideline, NICE separately recommends considering the principles of the PINCER intervention, which include educational outreach with regular reinforcement of educational messages, to reduce medicines-related patient safety incidents.

institutional perspective of NICE on Accelerated Approval

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000022
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Accelerated Approval
has display order 4
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2#modelling-methods
has perspective summary NICE treats final clinical end points as more informative than surrogate outcomes in cost-utility analysis, and expects any surrogate relationship to be supported by evidence and quantified. It recognises three levels of evidence, the strongest being randomised trials showing that a technology's effect on the surrogate corresponds to a commensurate effect on the final outcome. Uncertainty in the relationship must be quantified and included in probabilistic sensitivity analysis. Where a medicine is plausibly cost effective but the evidence is too uncertain, a committee can recommend it with managed access while data are collected for up to 5 years.
has perspective title Appraising Surrogate Evidence and Managed Access for up to 5 Years
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.5 to 4.6.11 and 6.4.6, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Access Negotiation

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Access Negotiation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/what-nice-does/patient-access-schemes-and-pricing-agreements
has perspective summary NICE states that a company unable to set a cost-effective NHS list price can offer a simple confidential discount through a patient access scheme, the preferred route because it needs less monitoring. Complex schemes, such as outcomes-based agreements, dose caps, rebates or upfront free stock, are non-confidential and are reviewed with an NHS expert panel over at least 12 weeks. Simple discount reviews take at least 4 weeks, or 10 working days on the fast track where requirements are met. NICE advises NHS England, which makes the final decision.
has perspective title Simple and Complex Patient Access Schemes Reviewed for NHS England
has primary source label NICE. Patient access schemes and pricing agreements (web page), sections 'What are patient access schemes?', 'How we assess patient access schemes' and 'The proposal review process', accessed 29 September 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case values technologies at prices that reflect as closely as possible those paid in the NHS, using price reductions when one is known to be available across the NHS, from sources such as patient access schemes, commercial access agreements, NHS Supply Chain, eMIT and the drugs tariff. Where the acquisition price varies substantially, costs should still reflect prices actually paid. The list price may be used when no NHS-wide reduction or nationally agreed price exists, and VAT is excluded from economic evaluations but included in budget impact.

has institution label as shown NICE

has perspective summary NICE's scope identifies all potentially relevant comparators that are established practice in the NHS, which may include branded and generic medicines, biosimilars and unlicensed technologies in established clinical use, while technologies recommended with managed access are not suitable comparators. In selecting the most appropriate comparators, the committee considers established NHS practice, the natural history of the condition without suitable treatment, existing NICE guidance, cost effectiveness and regulatory status. A cost-ineffective practice may remain a comparator if its use is embedded in clinical practice.

concerns wiki concept Addiction Treatment Economics
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's manual uses treatments to reduce drug misuse as its example of technologies with substantial benefits to other government bodies, such as reduced crime. Such benefits are counted only where agreed with the Department of Health and Social Care and set out in the remit, and are presented separately from the NHS and personal social services reference case. In the methadone and buprenorphine appraisal, reference-case ICERs against no treatment were £13,700 and £26,400 per QALY, and adding criminal justice and victim costs made methadone dominant. In the nalmefene appraisal, the wider perspective in the remit left nalmefene dominant.
has perspective title Crime Savings From Drug Misuse Treatment Reported Outside the Reference Case

institutional perspective of NICE on Additive Interaction Scale

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Additive Interaction Scale
has display order 3
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's manual asks for subgroup analyses that specify the choice of scale on which any effect modification is defined. It notes that the overall net treatment effect depends on baseline risk and on the relative effects of the technology, so subgroups may differ in one or more contributors to absolute treatment effects, and relative effects from randomised trials may be applied to baseline risk data for the subgroups of interest. Standard trial subgroup analyses test for differences in relative treatment effects through interactions, and post hoc data dredging for subgroup effects is viewed sceptically.
has perspective title Subgroup Analyses Must State the Scale of Effect Modification
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.16 and 4.9.4 to 4.9.8, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Adherence
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg76/chapter/Introduction
has perspective summary NICE's guideline on medicines adherence defines adherence as the extent to which the patient's action matches the agreed recommendations, and says non-adherence should not be seen as the patient's problem. It cites estimates that a third to a half of medicines prescribed for long-term conditions are not taken as recommended, with costs that include wasted medicines and extra demand for healthcare. Professionals should routinely assess adherence without judgement, may use prescription re-ordering records and returned medicines to identify non-adherence, and should tailor support because no single intervention suits all patients.
has perspective title Adherence Presumes Agreement Between Prescriber and Patient
has primary source label National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Medicines adherence: involving patients in decisions about prescribed medicines and supporting adherence (CG76), published 28 January 2009, last updated September 2019, Introduction and recommendations 1.2.1 to 1.2.5

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000089
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Administrative Censoring
has display order 3
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE notes that a lifetime time horizon often requires extrapolating data beyond the duration of the available studies, and asks for scenarios using different statistical models, including one in which the technology provides no further benefit beyond its use. When extrapolating time-to-event data, the clinical plausibility of the underlying hazard functions should routinely be assessed, and functions with stable or decreasing variance over time are likely to underestimate uncertainty. Simple adjustments for treatment switching, such as censoring patients who cross over, should be avoided as very susceptible to selection bias.
has perspective title Extrapolating Beyond Trial Follow-Up and Assessing Hazard Plausibility
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.24, 4.6.25 and 4.6.26, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Administrative Data

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Administrative Data
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9/chapter/introduction-to-real-world-evidence-in-nice-decision-making
has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework defines administrative data as data collected for administrative purposes by health and social care services, citing Hospital Episode Statistics, whose primary purpose is hospital reimbursement through payment by results, and treats claims data as a type of administrative data. Submissions should report the original purpose of data collection, the type of source, linkage methods and the completeness and accuracy of key variables, since imperfect linkage can exclude records or cause misclassification. NICE sets no minimum thresholds for completeness or accuracy.
has perspective title Administrative Data in the Real-World Evidence Framework

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng142/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's guideline on end of life care service delivery says providers should have policies so that advance care planning is offered to adults approaching the end of their life, taking account of under-served and vulnerable groups, and systems so that each person has a copy of their plan at home or with them if admitted. The committee found the evidence unclear but saw some benefit in helping people stay where they wish to be cared for and die, which may reduce the need for hospital services while increasing demand for community services.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng5/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's medicines optimisation guideline defines medicines-related patient safety incidents as unintended or unexpected incidents related to medicines use that could have or did lead to harm, including medication errors, near misses and potentially avoidable adverse events and hospital admissions. Organisations should support a fair blame culture, use several methods to identify incidents, such as health record review, patient surveys and direct observation of administration, and consider applying the principles of the PINCER intervention, including dedicated pharmacist support, educational outreach and information technology support.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Adverse Event Rate
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE asks that cost-comparison analyses capture the costs of differing health outcomes, such as managing adverse events, when relevant. Substantial differences between technologies in costs directly relating to health outcomes such as adverse events indicate that the technologies may not provide similar overall health benefits, so such differences must be clearly justified. For cost-utility analyses, results should include a table of disaggregated costs and of the decrements associated with further interventions and adverse events, presented with and without discounting.
has perspective title Adverse Event Costs in Cost Comparisons and Disaggregated Results
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.19, 4.2.20 and 4.10.4, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Age Weighting

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Age Weighting
has display order 3
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's manual sets no age weights for QALYs. Its reference case gives an additional QALY the same weight regardless of the other characteristics of the people receiving it, except in specific circumstances, and the committee regards all QALYs as being of equal weight. The main exception is the severity modifier, which weights QALYs by 1.2 or 1.7 according to absolute or proportional QALY shortfall, both measured against the general population with the same age and sex distribution as people with the condition.
has perspective title Equal QALY Weights, With No Age Weighting in the Reference Case
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), table 4.1, sections 6.2.10 and 6.2.12 to 6.2.18, and table 6.1, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000140
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Aggregate Data Meta-Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE asks that statistical pooling of study results be accompanied by an assessment of heterogeneity, which a random-effects model takes into account only to some extent, and that its degree and causes be explored as fully as possible, for example through subgroup analysis and meta-regression. Each included study should be described and a forest plot provided. If event risk differs substantially between control groups, submissions should assess whether the relative effect is constant over baseline risk, especially when the model's baseline rate is very different from the trial rates.
has perspective title Pooling With Heterogeneity Assessment and Baseline Risk Checks
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.4.9 and 3.4.10, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Alcohol Policy
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ph24/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's prevention guideline on alcohol-use disorders states that making alcohol less affordable is the most effective way of reducing alcohol-related harm. Its first policy recommendation asks government to consider a minimum price per unit, set by taking account of the health and social costs of alcohol-related harm and its effect on consumption, and to review it and alcohol duties regularly so that alcohol does not become more affordable over time. Further policy recommendations cover licensing and marketing, with final decisions left to government.
has perspective title Consider a Minimum Price per Unit and Review It Regularly
has primary source label National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Alcohol-use disorders: prevention (PH24), published 2 June 2010, 'Policy and practice' and recommendations 1 to 3

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng201/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's antenatal care guideline recommends offering a first antenatal booking appointment with a midwife by 10+0 weeks of pregnancy, and within 2 weeks if possible for women who contact or are referred to maternity services later than 9+0 weeks. It recommends planning 10 routine antenatal appointments with a midwife or doctor for nulliparous women and 7 for parous women, with additional or longer appointments offered according to the woman's medical, social and emotional needs.

For interventions with a social care focus, its reference case table lists capability or social care-related quality of life measures, such as ICECAP or ASCOT, for interventions that result in both health and capability or social care outcomes, alongside health effects measured in QALYs.

institutional perspective of NICE on Atkinson Index

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Atkinson Index
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/resources/support-document-health-inequalities-15313210669/chapter/distributional-cost-effectiveness-analysis-methods
has perspective summary NICE accepts distributional cost-effectiveness analysis only as supporting evidence of a technology's effect on health inequalities, and only where there is clear evidence of a significant burden of inequality in the eligible population. Its support document states that results should not weight costs or benefits differently by the social characteristics of those affected, including through mathematical functions that use health inequality aversion parameters. Outputs are instead the distributions of health benefits, health opportunity costs and net health benefit across deprivation quintiles, with descriptive metrics such as gaps, ratios or simple regressions.
has perspective title No Health Inequality Aversion Weights Applied to QALYs
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.12.1 to 4.12.8, last updated 31 March 2026; NICE support document: Health inequalities, chapter Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis methods, last updated 13 May 2025

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng15/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's antimicrobial stewardship guideline recommends that stewardship programmes consider regular feedback to individual prescribers in all care settings on their antimicrobial prescribing and related patient safety incidents, using professional regulatory numbers and cost centre codes, and integrating audit into existing quality improvement programmes. Organisations should consider updating individual prescribers and prescribing leads at least every year, with individual prescribing benchmarked against local and national rates and trends, and should support stewardship teams to give feedback and advice to prescribers who prescribe outside local guidelines without justification.

institutional perspective of NICE on Autonomy

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000236
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Autonomy
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/about-us/our-principles
has perspective summary NICE states that its committees balance the most overall benefit for the greatest number of people against fairness and respect for individual choice. One of the moral principles behind its guidance holds that people have the right to make informed choices about the care they receive. NICE adds that not everyone has the ability to make their own choices and that not everything people want will necessarily be available. Because resources are limited, decisions have to be made about which options are publicly funded.
has perspective title Right to Informed Choices Balanced Against Limited Resources
has primary source label NICE, Our principles (web page, replacing Social value judgements, second edition 2008), introduction and moral principles, accessed 14 October 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000238
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Average Cost-Effectiveness Ratio
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE frames cost-effectiveness for decisions in incremental terms. ICERs must be the ratio of expected additional total cost to expected additional QALYs compared with alternative technologies, following standard decision rules on dominance and extended dominance. Results should be presented in a fully incremental analysis with dominated and extendedly dominated technologies removed, with pairwise comparisons only when relevant and justified, and expected net health benefits should be reported alongside ICERs using values of £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY gained.
has perspective title Decisions Use Incremental Ratios in a Fully Incremental Analysis
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16 and 4.10.8, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Barrier to Implementation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000252
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Barrier to Implementation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg20/chapter/support-for-putting-the-guideline-recommendations-into-practice
has perspective summary NICE's guideline manual asks each guideline committee to consider factors that may help or hinder implementation, which it calls levers and barriers, and to judge how feasible its recommendations will be, taking account of the change in practice required, staff training needs, policy levers and funding streams. These judgements are documented in the guideline and its implementation resources. NICE's national implementation team then works with national partners, practitioners and commissioners to identify barriers to, and priorities for, implementation and develops support resources to help overcome them.
has perspective title Committees Weigh Levers and Barriers, and NICE Supports Implementation
has primary source label National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Developing NICE guidelines: the manual (PMG20), sections 1.5, 3.1, 9.1, 12.1 and 12.5, last updated 23 October 2025

institutional perspective of NICE on Base Case

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000254
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Base Case
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states that the committee's preferred cost-effectiveness estimate should be derived from a probabilistic analysis when possible unless the model is linear, and that any use of deterministic results must be clearly justified. Deterministic base-case or scenario analyses also need justification, although this matters less if the base case is shown to be linear or only moderately non-linear. All parameter values used in base-case, sensitivity, scenario and subgroup analyses should be clinically plausible and consistent with the data.
has perspective title Probabilistic Base Case Unless the Model Is Linear
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.27, 4.7.12 and 4.7.13, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Basket Trial

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000263
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Basket Trial
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE notes that some technologies suit alternative study designs, for example histology-independent cancer treatments studied in basket trials with a heterogeneous population. When basket trials are used, they should be appropriately designed and analysed, assess heterogeneity and allow borrowing between baskets. They should also include relevant comparators, allocate treatments randomly, use clinical endpoints with a validated relationship to overall survival and quality of life, and enrol all patient groups relevant to the indication.
has perspective title Basket Trials Should Assess Heterogeneity and Allow Borrowing
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.3.7 and 3.3.8, last updated 31 March 2026

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000266
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Bathtub Hazard
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states that standard parametric and more flexible approaches, such as spline-based and cure models, are available for extrapolating time-to-event data, and that their appropriateness and the validity of their extrapolations should routinely be considered. When alternative models are compared, the clinical plausibility of their underlying hazard functions should routinely be assessed and uncertainty in the extrapolated portion of the hazard explored. Hazard plots based on observed data and model predictions should be presented in graphs and tables alongside Kaplan-Meier and parametric curves.
has perspective title Clinical Plausibility of Extrapolated Hazard Functions
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.25 and 4.10.5, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Bayesian Analysis CEA

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000270
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Bayesian Analysis CEA
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE expects the committee's preferred cost-effectiveness estimate to come from a probabilistic analysis when possible, unless the model is linear. Parameter distributions should represent the available evidence rather than be chosen arbitrarily, and enough simulations should be run to minimise Monte Carlo error. Models should quantify decision uncertainty and report the probability of cost-effectiveness at £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained. Informative prior distributions for relative effectiveness are not recommended unless under very specific circumstances, such as very sparse adverse event data.
has perspective title Preferred Estimate From Probabilistic Analysis Unless the Model Is Linear
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.4.19, 4.7.2, 4.7.10 to 4.7.12 and 4.7.15, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Bayesian Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000274
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Bayesian Meta-Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE prefers the network meta-analysis methods of the DSU evidence synthesis series. External information should be used to help estimate between-study heterogeneity, and in networks with few included studies informative prior distributions for the heterogeneity parameter may be preferable, with distributions tailored to particular outcomes and disease areas. The source of the prior must be noted and justified, with sensitivity analysis over candidate priors. Informative priors for relative effectiveness are not recommended unless under very specific circumstances, such as very sparse adverse event data.
has perspective title Informative Heterogeneity Priors in Networks With Few Studies
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.4.11 and 3.4.16 to 3.4.19, last updated 31 March 2026
