institutional perspective of NICE on Before-and-After Study

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000279
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Before-and-After Study
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE names diagnostic before-and-after studies as a useful source of evidence on how clinical management changes after an index test is introduced into practice. It notes that such studies are often unavailable, particularly for a new test not yet in routine use, so expert clinical input on the usual care pathway is likely to matter. For relative treatment effects NICE strongly prefers randomised trials and regards non-randomised studies as tending to be at high risk of bias from confounding.
has perspective title Diagnostic Before-and-After Studies Inform the Care Pathway
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.3.2, 3.3.9 and 3.3.24, last updated 13 October 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Beta Distribution

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000283
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Beta Distribution
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE requires distributions to be assigned to characterise uncertainty in the precision of mean parameter values, and these should not be chosen arbitrarily but should represent the available evidence on each parameter, with their use justified. Where alternative plausible distributions exist, separate probabilistic analyses should explore them. Evidence on correlation between parameters should be reflected, avoiding both artificial restriction of ordered parameters and unsupported assumptions of perfect correlation. The manual does not name particular distributions such as the beta.
has perspective title Distributions Must Represent the Evidence, Not Be Chosen Arbitrarily
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.7.10 and 4.7.19, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Between-Subject Variation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000286
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Between-Subject Variation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE notes that for many technologies the level of benefit differs between patients with differing characteristics, and asks cost-utility analyses to give clinical and cost-effectiveness estimates separately for each relevant subgroup. Subgroups should rest on a clearly justified expectation of a differential effect, and post hoc data dredging will be viewed sceptically. Analysts should specify the scale on which effect modification is defined and reflect the statistical precision of all subgroup estimates in the analysis of parameter uncertainty.
has perspective title Separate Estimates for Each Relevant Subgroup When Benefit Differs
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.9.1, 4.9.3, 4.9.4 and 4.9.7, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Bibliographic Database
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg24/chapter/appendix-b-identification-selection-and-synthesis-of-clinical-evidence
has perspective summary NICE's user guide for company evidence submissions expects a systematic literature search in line with the systematic review sections of its methods manual. Companies must report enough detail for the results to be reproduced, including a full list of information sources and the full electronic search strategies for all databases, with any limits applied. Searches for published cost-effectiveness studies must also be described in enough detail to be reproduced, with the rationale for inclusion and exclusion criteria.

concerns wiki concept Biosimilar
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/what-is-a-biosimilar-medicine/
has perspective summary A biosimilar does not require a separate technology appraisal — a positive NICE recommendation for the reference biologic applies to the biosimilar. NICE conducts surveillance around loss of exclusivity and may produce an evidence summary where a review is warranted, with product choice for the NHS driven by overall value (cost, indications, formulation, pathway).
has perspective title No Separate Appraisal; Reference Product’s Recommendation Applies

institutional perspective of NICE on Break-Even Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000297
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Break-Even Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE allows threshold analysis to explore highly uncertain parameters when a switching value would inform decision makers: the value an input would need to take for the decision on whether a technology is a good use of NHS resources to change at a given threshold, such as £25,000 or £35,000 per QALY gained. The analysis should show how far the switching value is from the current best estimate. It is unsuitable for parameters highly correlated with other influential parameters and should not justify restricting the population to a subgroup. Implausible switching values are still reported with the plausible range.
has perspective title Switching Values at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY Gained
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.29, 4.7.22 and 4.7.23, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Capacity Planning

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000303
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Capacity Planning
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng94/evidence/39bed-occupancy-pdf-172397464704
has perspective summary NICE's emergency and acute care guideline asks providers to plan capacity to minimise the risks associated with occupancy rates exceeding 90%. Its committee found the convention of an 85% safe upper limit rested on a 1999 theoretical model unlikely to reflect current NHS practice, judged that optimal occupancy depends on case mix, hospital size, ward type and seasonal effects, and concluded that organisations would need to evaluate their own occupancy levels with dynamic modelling tools. Health systems may set local criteria for safe maximum occupancy while monitoring case mix, care processes and outcomes.
has perspective title Plan Bed Capacity Locally With Dynamic Modelling
has primary source label NICE guideline NG94, Emergency and acute medical care in over 16s: service delivery and organisation (published 28 March 2018), recommendation 1.3.1; evidence review 39 (Bed occupancy, March 2018), section 39.6

institutional perspective of NICE on Capacity Utilisation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000305
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Capacity Utilisation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng94/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's emergency and acute care guideline asks healthcare providers to monitor total acute hospital bed occupancy, capacity, flow and outcomes in real time and to plan capacity to minimise the risks of occupancy above 90%, a pragmatic maximum chosen because adverse outcomes rose at that level. For costing, NICE's methods manual bases the average cost of a multi-use technology initially on its expected throughput for the uses evaluated, and allows an additional marginal cost analysis where the technology is already recommended for another purpose and enough spare capacity exists.
has perspective title Monitor Bed Occupancy and Avoid Rates Above 90%
has primary source label NICE guideline NG94, Emergency and acute medical care in over 16s: service delivery and organisation (published 28 March 2018), recommendation 1.3.1 and evidence review 39 (Bed occupancy), section 39.6; NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.4.20 and 4.4.21, last updated 31 March 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary Where an intervention has a substantial and evidenced effect on carers, carer health-related quality of life can be included in the QALY calculation — most commonly as an additive carer disutility linked to the patient’s health state — and the committee decides case by case whether it belongs in the base case. This is the health-effect counterpart to carer costs, which sit outside the reference case.
has perspective title Carer HRQoL May Enter QALYs via Disutilities Where Evidenced

institutional perspective of NICE on Carer

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Carer
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE includes all relevant health effects for patients and, when relevant, for other people (mainly carers) in the reference-case perspective on outcomes, while costs take the NHS and personal social services (PSS) perspective. Carer health effects need evidence that the condition substantially affects carers' health-related quality of life and showing how the technology affects carers. When patients cannot report their own quality of life, measurements should come from their carer rather than healthcare professionals. Time spent by family carers may be costed only when the NHS or PSS might otherwise have provided the care, and such analyses are shown separately.
has perspective title Carer Health Effects Count in the Reference Case When Evidenced

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Case Weight
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE describes healthcare resource groups as standard groupings of clinically similar treatments that use common levels of healthcare resources, and calls them a valuable source of information for estimating resource use, with national average unit costs reported through the annual mandatory collection of reference costs. Analysts should consider all relevant HRGs, including critical care and unbundled costs outside the core HRG. HRG data may not be appropriate when the technology and its comparator fall in the same HRG, or when the mean cost does not reflect the technology's resource use; micro-costing may then be better.
has perspective title HRG Unit Costs Useful for Resource Use, With Stated Limits
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.4.9 and 4.4.10, last updated 31 March 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg51/chapter/statement-on-using-the-eq-5d-5l-value-set
has perspective summary NICE explains that EQ-5D levels are the multiple-choice options showing the extent of problems on each dimension, and that a value set is a mathematical model converting these questionnaire responses to utility values. Its interim methods statement makes the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and the new UK 5L value set the preferred approach for adults, and the UK 5L value set should derive all adult utility values in reference-case analyses. This applies to topics starting after 27 August 2026, while ongoing topics continue mapping 5L data to 3L utility values.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Causal Pathway
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's technology appraisal manual asks for the conceptual model behind a model structure to be transparent and justified, and says prior use of a structure is not enough. When surrogate end points stand in for final outcomes, it grades evidence from biological plausibility up to randomised trials showing a commensurate effect on the final outcome, and treats validation as specific to the population and technology. For diagnostics without direct outcome data, a linked evidence model should specify and review the links between diagnosis, treatment and final outcomes.
has perspective title Each Link From Surrogate or Test to Final Outcome Needs Evidence

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Clinical Algorithm Development
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/the-scope-2
has perspective summary NICE's technology evaluation manual treats the care pathway as the entire sequence of tests and treatments relevant to an evaluation, including the stages after diagnosis or treatment, and states that the range of treatment pathways must be understood to assess a technology's value. For diagnostic technologies used in sequence, every technology in the potential sequence should be included, and variants such as different thresholds may need separate evaluation. Where the technology and comparator both sit within a sequence, the evaluation may compare alternative sequences, counting all patient outcomes that change because of the test or sequence of tests.
has perspective title Evaluations Span the Whole Care Pathway and May Compare Alternative Sequences

has perspective summary NICE lists additional routine care, alongside patient characteristics, care setting and the year of the study, among the factors that can produce differences in relative effectiveness between studies in a systematic review. It asks for such potential effect modifiers to be identified before data analysis, either through a thorough review of the subject area or through discussion with experts in the clinical discipline.

institutional perspective of NICE on Comparator

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Comparator
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary The scope identifies all potentially relevant comparators that are established practice in the NHS, and identification at that stage should be inclusive. Branded, generic and biosimilar medicines can be comparators, as can unlicensed treatments that are established clinical practice, but technologies recommended with managed access cannot. When choosing the most appropriate comparators, the committee considers established NHS practice in England, the natural history of the condition, existing NICE guidance, the comparator's cost effectiveness and its regulatory status. A cost-ineffective established practice can remain a comparator if other NICE guidance recommends it or it is deeply embedded in practice.
has perspective title Established NHS Practice Identified Through the Scope
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 2.2.12, 2.2.13, 2.2.15 and 6.2.2 to 6.2.4, last updated 31 March 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://a.storyblok.com/f/243782/x/522b952db1/declaring-managing-interests-for-advisory-committees.docx
has perspective summary NICE's policy asks committee members and other contributors to declare any interest that a reasonable person would see as relevant, covering the preceding 12 months and updated before and at each meeting, and states that declaring an interest does not mean there is a conflict. Responses range from open declaration through partial exclusion to complete exclusion. A member with a specific financial interest leaves for the relevant item unless the interest has ended with no scope to benefit, and people likely to be excluded from more than 50% of discussions should not be appointed.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Construct Validity
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE prefers the EQ-5D for measuring health-related quality of life in adults. To argue that the EQ-5D is inappropriate, qualitative empirical evidence must show that key dimensions of health are missing, supported by evidence that the EQ-5D performs poorly on tests of construct validity, meaning it does not perform as would be expected, and on responsiveness in a particular patient population. This evidence should come from a synthesis of peer-reviewed literature, and any alternative measure must be accompanied by a detailed account of its methods.
has perspective title Poor Construct Validity Needed to Depart From the EQ-5D
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.3.6 and 4.3.10, last updated 31 March 2026

The suitability of an identified core outcome set is assessed with the Core Outcome Set Standards for Development (COS-STAD) and the Core Outcome Set Standards for Reporting (COS-STAR). The guidance sits in the manual's advice on outcomes for review questions about the effectiveness of interventions, and applies to the evidence reviews behind NICE guidelines.

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary Reference-case costs cover resources under the control of the NHS and personal social services, valued at the prices the NHS actually pays, including price reductions available across the NHS such as patient access schemes. National average HRG unit costs from reference costs are a valuable source, with micro-costing where HRGs do not reflect the technology. Costs from earlier years are adjusted with indices such as the NHS cost inflation index. Productivity costs are excluded from the reference case and may be presented separately.

institutional perspective of NICE on Cost per QALY

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000418
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost per QALY
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary Below a most plausible ICER of £25,000 per QALY gained, NICE normally recommends a technology on its cost-effectiveness estimate, and a negative decision must refer to the plausibility of the model inputs or the certainty of the ICER. Between £25,000 and £35,000, decisions refer explicitly to uncertainty, uncaptured benefits and health inequalities, and above £35,000 an increasingly stronger case is needed. Highly specialised technologies use a single level of £100,000 per QALY, and the usual £25,000 to £35,000 levels also apply to technologies giving less benefit at lower cost.
has perspective title Most Plausible ICER Read Against £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.3.4 to 6.3.9, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Consequence Analysis
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg20/chapter/incorporating-economic-evaluation
has perspective summary NICE's guidelines manual defines cost-consequences analysis as presenting costs and outcomes in discrete categories without aggregating or weighting them. It may be considered when a cost-utility analysis is not possible, and is useful when different outcomes cannot be incorporated into an index measure, ideally with a table summarising all costs and outcomes. For public health and social care interventions with multiple outcomes, a cost-consequences analysis is usually needed, although the base case should still be a cost per QALY analysis where possible.
has perspective title CCA When Outcomes Cannot Be Combined
has primary source label Developing NICE guidelines: the manual (PMG20), chapter 7 Incorporating economic evaluation, sections 7.3 (box 7.1) and 7.7, last updated 23 October 2025

institutional perspective of NICE on Cost-Effectiveness

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000395
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE does not use a precise maximum acceptable ICER above or below which a technology is automatically judged cost effective or not. Given the fixed NHS budget, the appropriate maximum reflects the opportunity cost of programmes displaced by new, more costly technologies, and because this cannot be defined precisely NICE uses a range, giving other factors more weight as the ICER nears the top. Results must follow standard decision rules on dominance and extended dominance, with expected net health benefits presented at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY.
has perspective title Range of Maximum Acceptable ICERs Reflecting Displaced NHS Care
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16 and 6.3.1, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC)

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000322
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (CEAC)
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE lists cost-effectiveness acceptability curves among the appropriate ways of presenting parameter uncertainty, alongside scatter plots and confidence ellipses on the cost-effectiveness plane when only 2 alternatives are compared. The presentation of CEACs should include a representation and explanation of the cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier, which shows the probability that the technology with the highest expected net benefit is cost effective. Submissions should also give the probability that the treatment is cost effective at £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained and the error probability, particularly when there are more than 2 alternatives.
has perspective title CEACs With the Acceptability Frontier and Probability at £25,000 to £35,000
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), section 4.7.15, last updated 31 March 2026

has perspective summary NICE lists cost-effectiveness acceptability curves among appropriate ways of presenting parameter uncertainty, and states that their presentation should include a representation and explanation of the cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier, the region showing the probability that the technology with the highest expected net benefit is cost effective. Alongside expected costs, outcomes and ICERs, analyses should report the probability that the treatment is cost effective at maximum acceptable ICERs of £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained, and the error probability, particularly when there are more than two alternatives.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE uses cost-effectiveness analysis in its cost-utility form to judge whether differences in expected costs between technologies are justified by changes in expected health effects, reflecting its focus on maximising health gain from a fixed NHS and personal social services budget. The reference case requires fully incremental analysis that follows standard decision rules on dominance and extended dominance, reporting ICERs alongside expected net health benefits valued at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY gained. Technologies likely to give similar or greater health benefits at similar or lower cost than their comparators are assessed by cost-comparison analysis instead.
has perspective title Reference Case Uses Fully Incremental Cost-Utility Analysis

has display order 1

has perspective summary NICE lists confidence ellipses and scatter plots on the cost-effectiveness plane, when the comparison is restricted to two alternatives, as appropriate ways to present parameter uncertainty, alongside cost-effectiveness acceptability curves and the acceptability frontier. Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness Threshold
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE does not apply a precise maximum ICER; because the NHS budget is fixed, the relevant benchmark is the opportunity cost of programmes displaced. Below a most plausible ICER of £25,000 per QALY gained (£100,000 for highly specialised technologies), a recommendation is normally based on the cost-effectiveness estimate. From £25,000 to £35,000 the committee makes explicit reference to factors such as uncertainty and benefits not captured in the QALY, and above £35,000 it needs an increasingly stronger case. This range replaced £20,000 to £30,000 in the manual update of 31 March 2026.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Minimisation Analysis
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE uses cost-comparison analysis in technology appraisals for technologies likely to provide similar or greater health benefits at similar or lower cost than comparators recommended in published NICE guidance for the same population. The analysis compares costs and resource use, while health effects are captured in the clinical-effectiveness evidence rather than in the analysis itself. Costs arising from differing health outcomes, such as managing adverse events, should be included where relevant. Substantial differences in outcome-related costs must be clearly justified because they suggest overall health benefits may not be similar.
has perspective title Cost-Comparison Analysis for Similar Health Benefits

has perspective summary When NICE reviews published economic evidence for a guideline, the review should usually focus on economic evaluations that compare both the costs and consequences of alternative interventions. Cost-of-illness studies, burden of disease studies and other non-comparative costing studies should usually be excluded. Some non-comparative costing studies may be included for service delivery questions or flagged for economic modelling, and inclusion criteria may be broadened when published economic evidence is extremely sparse.

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case expresses health effects in QALYs, combining health-related quality of life and length of life in a single index. Changes in health-related quality of life should be reported by patients, or by carers where that is not possible, and valued using public preferences from a representative UK sample through a choice-based method. institutional perspective of NICE on Cross-Sectional Design

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000436
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cross-Sectional Design
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9/chapter/methods-for-real-world-studies-of-comparative-effects
has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework describes cross-sectional studies as collecting information on current exposures and outcomes at a single time point. It accepts that they can be used to estimate intervention effects but regards them as less reliable than longitudinal designs such as cohort studies when a clear temporal separation of exposure and outcome is needed. When choosing a statistical model for a real-world evidence study, analysts should consider whether the data are cross-sectional or longitudinal, alongside the outcome distribution, sample size, clustering and heterogeneity.
has perspective title Cross-Sectional Studies Less Reliable Where Timing Matters
has primary source label NICE real-world evidence framework (ECD9), chapters on methods for real-world studies of comparative effects (types of non-randomised study design, cross-sectional studies) and conduct of quantitative real-world evidence studies (choosing study design and analytical methods), published 23 June 2022, last updated September 2025

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states that the proportional hazards assumption should always be assessed when relative treatment effects on survival or other time-to-event outcomes are measured with hazard ratios. It prefers log-cumulative hazard plots, as advised in Decision Support Unit Technical Support Document 14, together with visual inspection of hazard plots or hazard ratios over time and the proportional hazards tests reported in trial publications. If the assumption holds and is clinically plausible during extrapolation, hazard ratios may be pooled, and if it fails in some studies, the alternative methods in Technical Support Document 21 should be considered.
has perspective title Log-Cumulative Hazard Plots to Assess Proportional Hazards
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.22 to 4.6.24, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cure Rate Model
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's methods manual lists cure approaches, alongside spline-based models, among the more flexible options for extrapolating time-to-event data beyond standard parametric models. The appropriateness of each approach and the validity of its extrapolations should routinely be considered, the clinical plausibility of the underlying hazard functions assessed when comparing models, and uncertainty in the extrapolated portion explored. Where proportional hazards do not hold, the manual points to the alternative methods in NICE DSU technical support document 21.
has perspective title Cure Approaches Among Flexible Extrapolation Options

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Decision
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE committees normally choose between recommending a technology as an option, recommending it only in specific circumstances, recommending it with managed access for medicines, recommending use during an evidence generation period for HealthTech, recommending it only in a research context, or not recommending it. The type depends on how far the potential benefits are supported by evidence. When considering uncertainty, the committee should take into account the likelihood of decision error and its consequences for patients and the NHS, and it cannot make recommendations on pricing.
has perspective title Recommendation Types Matched to the Strength of the Case
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.1.15, 6.2.32, 6.4.1 and table 6.3, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Decision Criteria

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000446
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Decision Criteria
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE committees do not use a precise maximum acceptable ICER, and cost-effectiveness is necessary but not the only basis for decisions. Below a most plausible ICER of £25,000 per QALY gained the decision normally rests on the cost-effectiveness estimate; above it, the committee considers the certainty around the ICER, uncaptured benefits and non-health factors, and health inequalities, and above £35,000 it needs an increasingly strong case. Severity can add QALY weights of 1.2 or 1.7 based on absolute or proportional shortfall.
has perspective title Committee Factors Around a £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY Range
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.2.10 to 6.2.18, 6.3.1 and 6.3.4 to 6.3.8, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Decision Making
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's committee bases its recommendations on the evidence presented, stakeholder statements and expert views, considering the factors it judges most appropriate within the Health and Social Care Act 2012 and NICE's equality duties. It will not recommend technologies whose benefits are unproven or that are not a good use of NHS resources, and it uses a range rather than a precise maximum acceptable ICER. Above a most plausible ICER of £25,000 per QALY gained, decisions specifically consider uncertainty, uncaptured benefits and health inequalities, and the committee's reasoning must be explained so that the process is transparent.
has perspective title Committee Judgement Within a Structured and Transparent Process
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.1.1 to 6.1.3, 6.1.8, 6.3.1 and 6.3.5, last updated 31 March 2026

has institution label as shown NICE

has perspective summary In NICE's reference case the decision problem is defined by the scope developed by NICE, which covers the population, technology, care pathway, comparators, outcomes, costs and time horizon. The economic evaluation should start with a clear statement of the decision problem that defines the technologies compared and the relevant patient groups, and any differences from the scope must be justified. For medicines, the NICE technical lead and the external assessment group check whether a submission specifies the decision problem appropriately, and the committee considers whether the model reflects it.

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's committee does not use a precise maximum acceptable ICER, and cost-effectiveness is necessary but not the only basis for its decisions, so other factors carry more weight as the ICER nears the top of the range. Below a most plausible ICER of £25,000 per QALY gained (£100,000 for highly specialised technologies), the decision is normally based on the cost-effectiveness estimate. From £25,000 to £35,000 the committee makes explicit reference to factors such as the certainty around the ICER, uncaptured benefits and health inequalities, and above £35,000 it needs an increasingly stronger case.

institutional perspective of NICE on Dependent Censoring

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Dependent Censoring
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9/chapter/methods-for-real-world-studies-of-comparative-effects
has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework states that censoring can create bias if it is informative, that is, related to the outcomes and treatment assignment, as when people stop an experimental drug because of a perceived lack of benefit. Developers should consider this bias and address it where needed, using methods similar to those for time-varying confounding, such as marginal structural models with weighting, or methods for missing data. For trials with treatment switching, the technology appraisal manual advises against simply censoring or excluding patients who cross over, because these methods are very susceptible to selection bias.
has perspective title Informative Censoring Must Be Considered and Addressed
has primary source label NICE real-world evidence framework (ECD9), chapter on methods for real-world studies of comparative effects (analysis: informative censoring), published 23 June 2022, last updated September 2025; NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), section 4.6.26, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Detection Bias
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE lists detection bias, with limits in data quality and selection bias, among the reasons non-randomised studies tend to be at high risk of bias, and asks for the risk of bias in each such study to be assessed with a validated tool such as ROBINS-I. For randomised trials, internal validity includes blinding where appropriate, which prevents knowledge of treatment allocation from influencing behaviours, and the selection and measurement of outcomes. NICE notes that blinding is often not possible in trials of medical devices or diagnostics.
has perspective title Detection Bias Named Among the Risks of Non-randomised Evidence

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg48/chapter/methods-for-guidance-produced-in-the-nice-healthtech-programme
has perspective summary NICE's HealthTech programme manual notes that meta-analysis of test accuracy data is complicated by the correlation between sensitivity and specificity, by heterogeneity in setting, population, reference standard, equipment and operator skill, and by cut-off points that differ between studies, so the chosen method must be justified, with Decision Support Unit Technical Support Document 25 as the methods guide. Because most outcomes of testing follow from treatment started, modified or stopped, a linked evidence model should connect test results, care decisions and final outcomes, with test accuracy treated as an intermediate outcome.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE requires costs and health effects in the reference case to be discounted at the same rate of 3.5% per year. A rate of 1.5% may be considered only as a non-reference-case analysis, and it then applies to both costs and health effects, so NICE does not use differential discounting. The committee can consider the lower rate only if the technology is for people who would otherwise die or have a very severely impaired life, is likely to restore them to full or near-full health, and has benefits likely to be sustained over a very long period.
has perspective title Same 3.5% Rate for Costs and Health Effects

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE

has perspective summary NICE's evidence standards framework asks companies in all three evidence tiers to describe a digital health technology's expected uptake profile, meaning the proportion of the target population expected to use it and their usage rates. The profile should be calculated from pilot or other usage data, validated by relevant UK professionals and allow for subgroups whose uptake differs or changes over time. The company and evaluator should agree a plan to report ongoing usage against the usage profile agreed at commissioning, and for tier B and C technologies the budget impact analysis should include uptake estimates.

has perspective summary NICE's evidence standards framework says the expected uptake of a digital health technology may be affected by digital literacy within the intended user population, the availability of necessary connectivity and access to the necessary hardware or devices. Companies should show that their uptake profile is mindful of subgroups with different expected uptake rates and how these may change over time. The budget impact analysis should include any expected variations for different groups of service users, and the framework points companies to NHS Digital's guide on digital inclusion when considering health inequalities.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd7/chapter/how-to-meet-the-standards
has perspective summary NICE's evidence standards framework includes a design standard, applying to digital health technologies in all three evidence tiers, that asks companies to factor health inequalities into design and to describe expected positive impacts and efforts to reduce negative ones. A technology claiming to address a health or care inequality should also show that it challenges health inequalities or improves access to care among hard-to-reach populations, and that it promotes equality for people with protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. Data-driven technologies, including those using artificial intelligence, should describe design steps taken to mitigate algorithmic bias that could cause unequal impacts between groups.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd7/chapter/section-c-evidence-standards-tables
has perspective summary NICE's evidence standards framework sets 21 standards in 5 groups for the evidence a digital health technology should have to show its value in the UK health and care system. Technologies are classified by intended purpose into tiers A, B and C, with the evidence needed proportionate to the potential risk to service users. A budget impact analysis is expected in all tiers, and a cost-utility or cost-consequence analysis where the costs of commissioning, purchasing or implementing the technology are substantial for the relevant budget. The framework is not mandated, so commissioners are not required to use it.
has perspective title 21 Evidence Standards Tiered by Intended Purpose and Financial Risk

has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd7/chapter/section-b-classification-of-digital-health-technologies
has perspective summary NICE's evidence standards framework treats digital health technologies as digital products intended to benefit people or the wider health and social care system, such as smartphone apps, standalone software, online tools and programmes that analyse data from medical devices. It excludes software embedded in a medical device, training tools for professionals and tools for collecting research data. Technologies are classified by intended purpose into tier A for system services, tier B for communicating about health, health diaries and promoting good health, and tier C for technologies that inform or guide clinical management, diagnose or treat, where most regulated medical devices fall.

has perspective summary NICE's evidence standards framework for digital health technologies includes three deployment standards, which apply to all tiers and aim to ensure that claimed benefits can be realised in practice. Companies should set out a data flow map and minimum infrastructure requirements, describe their planned approach to training end users, and show that load testing matches expected uptake. For tier B and C technologies, the budget impact analysis should include all direct costs of implementing the technology, including staffing, training and supportive IT infrastructure.

concerns wiki concept Direct Cost
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case takes the perspective of the NHS and personal social services on costs, because its evaluations aim to support efficient use of those resources. Costs should relate to resources under NHS and PSS control and be valued at prices relevant to them, and productivity costs are excluded. Costs paid by patients may be included when the NHS or PSS reimburses them, and unreimbursed costs may be presented separately. Carer time may be costed when the NHS or PSS might otherwise have provided that care, in a separate analysis.
has perspective title NHS and PSS Perspective on Costs in the Reference Case

has perspective summary In the NICE reference case, costs and health effects are discounted at the same rate of 3.5% a year. The committee may consider a non-reference-case rate of 1.5% a year for both only if all stated criteria are met: the technology is for people who would otherwise die or have a very severely impaired life, is likely to restore them to full or near-full health, and has benefits likely to be sustained over a very long period. The committee must also be confident of long-term benefit and satisfied that irrecoverable costs are captured or mitigated.

has perspective summary In the reference case, NICE requires costs and health effects to be discounted at the same rate of 3.5% per year, so that results reflect present values over the time horizon. The committee must then see a highly plausible case that benefits are maintained.

has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/resources/support-document-health-inequalities-15313210669/chapter/distributional-cost-effectiveness-analysis-methods
has perspective summary NICE describes distributional cost-effectiveness analysis (DCEA) as a framework showing how costs and benefits vary across population groups and how a technology may affect the health inequality gap. A company should include one only with clear quantitative evidence of a significant burden of health inequalities in the eligible population, and only as supporting evidence. NICE's preferred methods stratify groups by Index of Multiple Deprivation, assume equal uptake unless evidence shows otherwise, apply no inequality aversion weights to QALYs, share opportunity costs equally with gradient scenarios, and report net health benefit by quintile.
has perspective title DCEA Only as Supporting Evidence, Without Inequality Aversion Weights

has perspective summary NICE recommends dupilumab for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in adults only if the disease has not responded to at least one other systemic therapy, such as ciclosporin, methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil, or these are contraindicated or not tolerated, and the company provides it according to the commercial arrangement. Dupilumab should be stopped at 16 weeks if the atopic dermatitis has not responded adequately, meaning at least a 50% reduction in the Eczema Area and Severity Index score (EASI 50) and at least a 4-point reduction in the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) from when treatment started.

has perspective summary NICE asks that costs and QALYs be combined using standard decision rules that reflect dominance or extended dominance where it exists, presented through incremental cost-utility analysis. Results should be shown in a fully incremental analysis with dominated technologies, meaning those more costly and less effective than another technology, and extendedly dominated technologies removed. Pairwise comparisons may be added when relevant and justified, and expected net health benefits should also be presented when appropriate, using values of £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY gained.

institutional perspective of NICE on ECOG Performance Status

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept ECOG Performance Status
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta638/chapter/1-Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE has recommended some cancer medicines only for adults with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1. In TA638 atezolizumab with carboplatin and etoposide for untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer is recommended only for this group, because the clinical trial evidence was in people with an ECOG score of 0 or 1. TA818 places the same condition on nivolumab with ipilimumab for untreated unresectable malignant pleural mesothelioma. The TA638 committee also asked healthcare professionals to take account of physical, sensory or learning disabilities, or communication difficulties, that could affect the ECOG score and to make appropriate adjustments.

has perspective summary NICE requires economic evaluations considered in its technology appraisals and highly specialised technologies evaluations to include an analysis using its reference-case methods, so that results are consistent across technologies and disease areas. Two forms are available: cost-utility analysis when a full analysis of costs and health benefits is needed, and cost-comparison analysis for technologies likely to provide similar or greater health benefits at similar or lower cost. Non-reference-case analyses may also be presented if they are justified and clearly distinguished.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Efficiency
has display order 3
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states that it does not set the NHS budget and that the objective of its evaluations is guidance representing an efficient use of available NHS and personal social services resources, so the reference-case cost perspective is that of the NHS and PSS. Its committees take into account the Health and Social Care Act 2012, which expects NICE to be aware of the broad balance between the benefits and costs of providing services. Committees consider how their advice may allow more efficient use of healthcare resources, requiring greater certainty as the impact on NHS resources increases.
has perspective title Guidance Aims at Efficient Use of NHS and PSS Resources

has perspective summary NICE guideline CG192 recommends considering two depression identification questions and the GAD-2 at a woman's first contact with primary care or her booking visit and in the early postnatal period. If she responds positively, is at risk or there is clinical concern, practitioners should consider using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or the PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or refer her to her GP or, where a severe problem is suspected, to a mental health professional. At later contacts the EPDS or the PHQ-9 can be used as part of monitoring.

has perspective summary NICE states that from 27 August 2026 the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and the UK value set should be used for all adult reference-case analyses, so the UK EQ-5D-3L value set no longer supplies reference-case utilities for adults in new work. has perspective summary NICE's interim methods statement makes the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and the UK value set by Rowen and colleagues its preferred approach for measuring and valuing health-related quality of life in adults. The UK value set should be used to derive all adult utility values in reference-case analyses, including general population utilities for QALY shortfall under the severity modifier. Utilities based on the EQ-5D-3L value set should not appear in sensitivity or scenario analyses, and 3L data should be mapped to 5L utility values. The statement replaces the 2019 position statement that rejected the 2018 England value set.

has perspective summary NICE describes the EQ-HWB (EQ Health and Wellbeing instrument) as a new standardised measure of health and wellbeing created following the Extending the QALY research project, to which NICE contributed. institutional perspective of NICE on Equity

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000560
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Equity
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary In the reference case NICE regards all QALYs as being of equal weight, and health inequalities are handled through structured decision making rather than as a decision-making modifier. Since a May 2025 update, if robust evidence shows a technology substantially affects health inequalities, the committee can apply flexibility to the range normally considered cost effective, but must consider healthcare displacement and opportunity cost. A distributional cost-effectiveness analysis is expected only where there is clear evidence of a significant burden of health inequalities, and it must not weigh costs or benefits differently by social characteristics.
has perspective title Equal QALY Weight With Structured Consideration of Health Inequalities
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.2.10, 6.2.35 to 6.2.38, 4.12.2, 4.12.3 and 4.12.7, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Equity-Efficiency Trade-off

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000563
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Equity-Efficiency Trade-off
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case gives all QALYs equal weight, but its committees may weight QALYs by 1.2 or 1.7 for severe conditions, judged by absolute or proportional QALY shortfall, whichever implies greater severity. To keep the opportunity cost visible, net health benefit must be shown at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY with and without the weighting. NICE's support document on health inequalities asks for results by deprivation quintile but rules out inequality aversion weights, leaving health inequalities to committee deliberation above £25,000 per QALY.
has perspective title Equal QALY Weights, a Severity Modifier and Visible Health Costs
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.2.10, 6.2.12 to 6.2.18, 6.3.2 and 6.3.5, last updated 31 March 2026; NICE support document: health inequalities, distributional cost-effectiveness analysis methods (last updated 13 May 2025)

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case gives an additional QALY the same weight whatever the characteristics of the person receiving it, except in specific circumstances. Decision-making modifiers can be applied through committee discussion or through QALY weighting, and the severity modifier weights QALYs by 1.2 or 1.7 according to absolute and proportional QALY shortfall. Net health benefits must be shown at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY with and without the weighting. Distributional analyses must not weight costs or benefits by social characteristics; where health inequality impacts are substantial, the committee can instead apply flexibility to the acceptable ICER range.
has perspective title Equal QALY Weights Apart From the Severity Modifier

institutional perspective of NICE on Evidence

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Evidence
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE considers all types of evidence, including unpublished and non-UK data, registries, real-world evidence and other observational sources, and the preferred source depends on the use being considered. For relative treatment effects there is a strong preference for high-quality randomised controlled trials, while real-world evidence may be preferred for natural history, treatment patterns or patient experiences. Evidence should be relevant to the patient groups, comparators, perspective, outcomes and resource use in the scope, and where empirical evidence is absent, structured expert elicitation is preferred.
has perspective title All Evidence Types Considered, RCTs Preferred for Effects
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.2.1, 3.3.1, 3.3.2 and 3.3.21, last updated 31 March 2026

concerns wiki concept Evidence Table
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg20/chapter/reviewing-evidence
has perspective summary NICE's guidelines manual says evidence tables help identify similarities and differences between studies, and that data from each study are extracted to standard templates for inclusion in them. Content depends on the study type and review question, typically covering design, population, intervention, comparator, outcomes, key findings with confidence intervals and quality comments. Example tables are given, but NICE states that no fixed template suits all topics, asks for headings to be agreed at the protocol stage, and requires extra calculations to be marked 'calculated by the review team'.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Evidence-Based Decision Making
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's technology appraisal committee bases its recommendations on the evidence presented, including stakeholder statements and expert views, and considers advice from NICE on scientific and social value decisions. The manual states that the credibility of NICE guidance depends on transparency, so each decision must be explained with reference to all the available evidence, expert contributions and consultation comments. Cost effectiveness is weighed without a precise maximum acceptable ICER, and below £25,000 per QALY gained the decision is normally based on the cost-effectiveness estimate.
has perspective title Committee Recommendations Must Be Explained Against All the Evidence
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), section(s) 6.1.3, 6.1.7, 6.1.8, 6.3.1 and 6.3.4, last updated 13 October 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta767/chapter/3-Committee-discussion
has perspective summary In the ponesimod appraisal the company used a Markov transition model with 20 health states, 10 EDSS states for relapsing-remitting MS, 9 for secondary progressive MS and death, with natural history from the British Columbia Multiple Sclerosis registry. Treatment effects from network meta-analyses adjusted progression through each EDSS state using 6-month confirmed disability accumulation. The committee noted that fatigue was not included explicitly in the model and was instead captured through measuring health-related quality of life by EDSS score.

institutional perspective of NICE on Expected Net Benefit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000577
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Expected Net Benefit
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states that the committee's preferred cost-effectiveness estimate should be derived from a probabilistic analysis when possible, unless the model is linear, and that any use of deterministic results must be clearly justified. ICERs must be the ratio of expected additional total cost to expected additional QALYs. Scenario analyses should in general also be probabilistic, and enough simulations should be run to minimise Monte Carlo error, which can be judged by reviewing the variance of outputs such as net benefits as the number of simulations rises.
has perspective title Preferred Estimate From Probabilistic Analysis Unless the Model Is Linear
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16, 4.7.11, 4.7.12 and 4.7.13, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Expected Value
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE requires reported incremental cost-effectiveness ratios to be the ratio of expected additional total cost to expected additional QALYs. The committee's preferred cost-effectiveness estimate should come from a probabilistic analysis when possible unless the model is linear, and any use of deterministic results must be clearly justified. Distributions for mean parameter values should reflect the available evidence, and submissions should present the expected value of each cost component, expected total costs and expected QALYs for each option compared, alongside expected net health benefits.
has perspective title Probabilistic Means Preferred Unless the Model Is Linear
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16, 4.7.10, 4.7.12 and 4.10.6, last updated 31 March 2026

has display order 1

has perspective summary NICE requires reported incremental cost-effectiveness ratios to be the ratio of expected additional total cost to expected additional QALYs, following standard decision rules for dominance and extended dominance, with expected net health benefits also presented. The committee's preferred estimate should come from a probabilistic analysis when possible unless the model is linear, and any use of deterministic results must be justified. Submissions should present the expected value of each cost component, expected total costs and expected QALYs for each option compared.

institutional perspective of NICE on Explanatory Trial

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000582
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Explanatory Trial
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE regards high-quality randomised controlled trials against relevant comparators as the most valid evidence of relative efficacy, but warns that results may not generalise to the population of interest because of the comparator, population, setting or treatment pathway used. Each trial is judged on internal validity and on external validity, meaning whether its results apply to wider patient groups and to routine clinical practice. When a randomised trial is not available or appropriate, the source and methods used to estimate relative effects must be justified.
has perspective title Trial Results Judged on Generalisability to Routine NHS Practice
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.3.6 and 3.3.8, last updated 13 October 2026

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000584
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Extended Dominance
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE requires economic evaluation results to be presented in a fully incremental analysis from which extendedly dominated technologies are removed. It defines a technology as extendedly dominated when a combination of 2 or more other technologies would be more cost effective. Standard decision rules for combining costs and QALYs should reflect extended dominance where it exists, and reported ICERs must be the ratio of expected additional total cost to expected additional QALYs. Expected net health benefits at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY should also be presented when appropriate.
has perspective title Extendedly Dominated Technologies Removed From Fully Incremental Analysis
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16 and 4.10.8, last updated 31 March 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/nice-dsu
has perspective summary Where trial data are censored, the base case should extrapolate survival using fitted parametric distributions (e.g. exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, log-logistic, log-normal, generalised gamma), selecting models by statistical goodness of fit and clinical/biological plausibility, and validating extrapolated hazards against background mortality and external data. TSD 21 cautions against over-relying on AIC/BIC beyond the observed follow-up.
has perspective title Parametric Survival Extrapolation With Fit and Plausibility Checks (DSU TSD 14/21)

has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework names constant comparison in a grounded theory approach as one of the common analytical approaches in qualitative health research, alongside thematic, content and framework analysis, and notes that each has strengths and limitations for particular research aims. Study reports should give the reasons for stopping data collection, whether data saturation or another reason.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta375/chapter/4-Evidence-and-interpretation
has perspective summary In its multiple technology appraisal of biological DMARDs for rheumatoid arthritis, NICE accepted data from the Early Rheumatoid Arthritis Study to estimate underlying disease progression on conventional DMARDs, in place of the linear HAQ progression assumed in earlier appraisals. The Assessment Group simulated a pain score for each patient from HAQ and estimated EQ-5D values with a mixture model developed by Hernández Alava and colleagues on data from 16,011 patients in the National Data Bank for Rheumatic Diseases. The group noted that this assumes treatments affect pain in proportion to their effect on HAQ.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Hazard Ratio
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE notes that studies with time-to-event outcomes often measure relative treatment effects as hazard ratios, which may be constant over time or change. The proportional hazards assumption should always be assessed, preferably with log-cumulative hazard plots, visual inspection of hazard plots or hazard ratios over time, and tests reported in the original trials. Hazard ratios may be pooled if proportional hazards hold within the trial and are clinically plausible during extrapolation; otherwise the alternative methods in DSU Technical Support Document 21 should be considered.
has perspective title Assess Proportional Hazards Before Relying on Hazard Ratios

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Health Economics
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE committees make recommendations on the clinical effectiveness and value for money of technologies for NHS use, and will not recommend technologies that are not considered a good use of NHS resources. Under the Health and Social Care Act 2012, NICE must have regard to the broad balance between the benefits and costs of health services or social care in England, alongside the degree of need and the desirability of promoting innovation. Because NICE considers the overall resources available to the NHS, decisions must account for the opportunity cost of programmes that a new technology may displace.
has perspective title Statutory Duty to Weigh the Benefits and Costs of NHS Services
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.1.1, 6.1.2 and 6.2.25, last updated 31 March 2026; Health and Social Care Act 2012, section 233(1)

If robust evidence shows that a technology substantially affects health inequalities, the committee considers this when judging whether it is an effective use of NHS resources, and can apply flexibility to the range normally considered cost effective, taking account of displacement and opportunity cost and giving stakeholders a rationale. has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/resources/support-document-health-inequalities-15313210669/chapter/distributional-cost-effectiveness-analysis-methods
has perspective summary NICE uses distributional cost-effectiveness analysis to show how a technology's costs and benefits vary across social groups and its effect on the health inequality gap, but only as supporting evidence and only where there is clear evidence of a significant burden of health inequalities in the eligible population. Groups are stratified by Index of Multiple Deprivation, and outputs cover health benefits, health opportunity costs and net health benefit for each quintile, with descriptive metrics such as gaps and ratios between the top and bottom of the distribution or simple regressions. Health inequality aversion weights are not applied.
has perspective title Distributional Analysis by Deprivation Quintile, Without Aversion Weights
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.12.1 to 4.12.3 and 4.12.7, last updated 31 March 2026; NICE support document: Health inequalities, chapter Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis methods, last updated 13 May 2025

has perspective summary NICE's support document names socioeconomic status, level of deprivation and ethnicity as social characteristics related to health inequalities, and its preferred analysis stratifies by the Index of Multiple Deprivation, with other stratification allowed where inequalities concentrate in groups such as ethnic or inclusion health groups and there is an evidence-based rationale. Where robust evidence shows that structural or social barriers to accessing care or taking part in research cause uncertainty or bias in the inequality evidence, committees may accept a higher level of uncertainty. This consideration is separate from NICE's legal obligations under the Equality Act 2010.

has perspective summary NICE's resource impact process manual says its resource impact tools usually cover 3 years after guidance is published and state when maximum implementation is assumed to be achieved. Costs are not discounted, and predictions of future uptake should not rely on a single source where possible, drawing on company submissions and previous uptake of similar technologies. The budget impact test is exceeded if the net annual NHS cost could be greater than £40 million in any of the first 3 years of use, and NHS England may then seek special arrangements with the company.

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg48/chapter/methods-for-guidance-produced-in-the-nice-healthtech-programme
has perspective summary NICE states that diagnostic technologies may bring some direct benefit from the knowledge gained and some direct harm from testing, but that most outcomes come after testing, when treatment or preventive measures are started, modified or stopped. Trials of tests are unusual, so where direct data on final outcomes are lacking a linked evidence modelling approach should be used. The links between test results, care decisions and final outcomes must be specified and justified, and companies relying on intermediate outcomes such as test accuracy should supply supporting evidence for their use.

has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework recognises external controls formed from real-world data or from data from previous clinical trials. Earlier trials may offer greater similarity in inclusion criteria, follow up and outcome determination, but often provide only aggregate data. Differences in patients, settings, care, data collection and time periods can limit comparability, so developers should select and curate data to minimise these differences, design studies to emulate a target trial and consider bias analysis.

institutional perspective of NICE on Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000633
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE requires the ICER to be the ratio of expected additional total cost to expected additional QALYs, presented through incremental cost-utility analysis that reflects dominance and extended dominance, with expected net health benefits at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY alongside it. Committees then work from the most plausible ICER. Below £25,000 per QALY, a decision not to recommend must state the committee's view on the plausibility of the modelling inputs or the certainty around the ICER, and as the ICER rises from £25,000 to £35,000 committees refer explicitly to uncertainty, uncaptured benefits and health inequalities.
has perspective title Expected Costs Over Expected QALYs, Judged as the Most Plausible ICER
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16 and 6.3.4 to 6.3.8, last updated 31 March 2026
has wiki record identifier icer
is perspective of body National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
isDefinedBy heiro-wiki.owlexternal

institutional perspective of NICE on Incremental Cost-Utility Ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000642
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Incremental Cost-Utility Ratio
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE asks for results through incremental cost-utility analysis, with each incremental cost-effectiveness ratio calculated as expected additional total cost divided by expected additional QALYs, after removing dominated and extendedly dominated options. Below a most plausible ratio of £25,000 per QALY gained, a recommendation normally rests on the cost-effectiveness estimate. Between £25,000 and £35,000, committees refer explicitly to uncertainty, uncaptured benefits and health inequalities, and above £35,000 they need an increasingly stronger case. Expected net health benefits should be presented alongside the ratio.
has perspective title Ratio of Expected Costs to Expected QALYs, Judged at £25,000 to £35,000
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16, 4.10.8 and 6.3.4 to 6.3.8, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Indirect Treatment Comparison
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary Where technologies have not been compared within a single randomised trial, NICE expects the head-to-head trials to be presented with a network meta-analysis if appropriate, a term that includes adjusted indirect comparisons through a common comparator, and the committee weighs the extra uncertainty of indirect evidence. Trial randomisation must be preserved: comparing single arms from different trials is not acceptable, and such data are treated as observational. Population adjustment needs individual patient data from at least one trial, and inconsistency between direct and indirect evidence must be reported and explored.
has perspective title Adjusted Indirect Comparisons That Preserve Randomisation

has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE

has perspective summary NICE's shared decision making guideline asks healthcare professionals to share and discuss the information people need to make informed decisions and to make sure they understand the choices available, including doing nothing. Discussions should cover the risks, benefits and consequences of each option, including choosing no treatment. Professionals should check understanding and check that the person's choice is consistent with what matters to them. Patient decision aids support informed, values-based decisions and do not advise people to choose one option over another.

has perspective summary NICE's scope specifies the technology being evaluated, where it will be used and how and in what circumstances, particularly when this differs from alternatives or standard care. Diagnostic technologies must be described precisely because variants such as different thresholds may need separate evaluation, and when the technology and comparator are part of a sequence in the care pathway, alternative sequences may be compared. A treatment continuation rule should be analysed as an additional treatment strategy alongside the base-case interventions and comparators, not as a subgroup.

has institution label as shown NICE

has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework asks researchers collecting qualitative data to consider the content, tone, order and phrasing of their questions, and to take care that questions are not leading. It treats reflexivity, meaning how a researcher's own values and preferences may affect the findings, as important throughout data collection, and recommends a clear statement on researcher reflexivity in study reports. Rapport between researcher and participant is also described as important for participants to express their views openly.
