has perspective summary The NICE guideline on primary brain tumours and brain metastases uses the Karnofsky Performance Status as a condition in its glioma recommendations. Radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for newly diagnosed grade 4 glioma (glioblastoma) is offered to people aged around 70 or under who have a Karnofsky score of 70 or more, and best supportive care alone is to be considered for people aged around 70 or over with a score under 70. For recurrent high-grade glioma the guideline lists the Karnofsky score among the factors to take into account when choosing treatment.

has perspective summary In the appraisal of empagliflozin for chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the company model moved people between quartiles of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire clinical summary score, each with a specific utility and cost. The committee considered whether the KCCQ is an appropriate measure of quality-of-life outcomes and heard clinical experts describe it as well validated for heart failure. It noted that there may be some inconsistencies in how the size of effect translates from trial data into modelled quality-of-life effects, and concluded that the company's model structure was appropriate for decision making.

has perspective summary NICE builds planned updating into technology appraisal guidance. NICE updates that guidance at the end of the data collection period, or earlier if the joint managed access governance group agrees. Other guidance is updated when changes to the evidence, clinical pathway or economic case are likely to have a material effect on recommendations.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 4
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9/chapter/methods-for-real-world-studies-of-comparative-effects
has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework lists loss to follow up among the causes of censoring in longitudinal studies and warns that informative censoring causes bias if censoring depends on outcomes and differs across interventions. Developers should compare patterns of missingness across groups and over time. Complete records analysis is sufficient if the amount of missing data is low and likely to be missing completely at random. Otherwise, methods such as imputation, inverse probability weighting or maximum likelihood estimation are available, with sensitivity or bias analysis if data are not missing at random.
has perspective title Informative Censoring and Missing Data in Real-World Evidence Studies
has primary source label National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NICE real-world evidence framework (ECD9), published 23 June 2022, last updated September 2025, chapter 'Methods for real-world studies of comparative effects', sections on study design, informative censoring and missing data

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/what-nice-does/patient-access-schemes-and-pricing-agreements/managed-access
has perspective summary Beyond ordinary managed-entry deals, NICE can recommend a medicine "with managed access" funded from two ringfenced NHS England pots — the Cancer Drugs Fund (since 2016) and the Innovative Medicines Fund (from June 2022), each about £340 million a year. Eligible patients get immediate, time-limited access while a data collection agreement (often real-world data such as SACT) resolves the specific uncertainties NICE identified, up to a maximum of five years. A mandatory re-appraisal at the end routes the medicine to routine commissioning or out of the fund; entry requires high unmet need and uncertainty that the planned evidence can plausibly resolve.
has perspective title Ringfenced CDF/IMF Funds Back a "Recommended With Managed Access" Route Ending in Re-appraisal

concerns wiki concept Meta-Regression
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE asks that statistical pooling be accompanied by an assessment of heterogeneity, which a random-effects model can address only in part, and that the degree of heterogeneity and its reasons be explored as fully as possible. Known clinical heterogeneity, for example from patient characteristics, may be explored using subgroup analyses and meta-regression. Potential effect modifiers should be identified before data analysis, and where control-group event risks differ substantially, it should be assessed whether the relative effect is constant across baseline risks.

has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework describes misclassification as measurement error in categorical variables and lists it among data quality limitations that can affect eligibility criteria, outcomes, exposures and covariates and create information biases. Differential measurement error generally biases comparative effects in a direction that can be hard to predict. NICE notes it is often recommended to define outcomes for high specificity, and suggests sensitivity or bias analyses that can be propagated through to cost-effectiveness analyses.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000713
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Modified Rankin Scale
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary In its guideline on stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, NICE selects people with acute ischaemic stroke for thrombectomy using, alongside earlier criteria, a pre-stroke functional status of less than 3 on the modified Rankin scale and a score of more than 5 on the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale. Clinicians should also take into account the person's overall clinical status and the extent of established infarction on initial brain imaging. NICE states that the thresholds were included so that the recommendation could be implemented in practice and to be consistent with the NHS England clinical commissioning policy on mechanical thrombectomy.
has perspective title Pre-Stroke Modified Rankin Score Below 3 Is a Thrombectomy Selection Criterion
has primary source label NICE guideline NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management, recommendation 1.4.8 [2019] and the committee's rationale in the Recommendations chapter, last updated 13 April 2022

institutional perspective of NICE on Monetary Valuation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000717
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Monetary Valuation
has display order 4
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case uses cost-utility analysis with health effects expressed in QALYs, justified by its focus on maximising health gains from a fixed NHS and personal social services budget. Its maximum acceptable ICER is framed as the opportunity cost of programmes displaced by new, more costly technologies, and it uses a range of £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained rather than a precise figure. Net health benefits are presented using values of £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY gained.
has perspective title Health Measured in QALYs Against an Opportunity Cost Range
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.14, 4.2.15, 6.3.1, 6.3.2 and 6.3.4 to 6.3.8, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Moving Target Problem

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000721
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Moving Target Problem
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg48/chapter/methods-for-guidance-produced-in-the-nice-healthtech-programme
has perspective summary NICE allows evidence on predecessor versions of a health technology to be considered, particularly when evidence on the current model or version is limited, and expects the assessment report to comment on how far that evidence applies. For technologies likely to have rapid iteration and several new versions after guidance is published, threshold analyses can identify a switching value for the performance parameters that drive cost-effectiveness results. Guidance may then state the performance ranges or values that a recommended technology needs to maintain to remain cost effective.
has perspective title Switching Values for HealthTech That Iterates Rapidly
has primary source label NICE HealthTech programme manual (PMG48), chapter 2, sections 2.2.8, 2.3.27 and 2.4.31, last updated 17 December 2025

institutional perspective of NICE on Narrative Review

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Narrative Review
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE expects evidence on outcomes to come from a systematic review that follows a pre-defined protocol and uses explicit, valid and replicable methods to minimise biased selection of studies. When there is not enough relevant and valid data for pairwise or network meta-analysis, the analysis may have to be restricted to a narrative overview that critically appraises individual studies and presents their results. In those circumstances the committee is particularly cautious when drawing conclusions about relative clinical effectiveness.
has perspective title Narrative Overview Only When Data Cannot Support Meta-Analysis
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.3.4, 3.4.2 and 3.4.21, last updated 13 October 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Net Benefit Approach

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000730
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Net Benefit Approach
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary When several technologies are compared, NICE allows cost-effectiveness rankings to present probabilistic results, showing the probability that each technology is ranked highest, meaning it produces the highest net benefit, and possibly every other rank, for example in rankograms shown alongside each technology's expected net benefit. The manual also suggests reviewing how the variance of probabilistic outputs, such as net benefits, changes as simulations increase, to judge whether the model has been run enough times to minimise Monte Carlo error.
has perspective title Ranking Technologies by the Probability of Highest Net Benefit
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.7.11 and 6.3.3, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Net Health Benefit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000731
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Net Health Benefit
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE asks for expected net health benefits alongside ICERs, using values of £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY gained, and sees them as particularly informative with several comparators, small differences in costs or QALYs, subgroup considerations, or technologies giving less benefit at lower cost. When decision-making modifiers apply, net health benefits should be presented with and without the QALY weighting to show the effect on opportunity costs. A positive value means population health rises, and a negative one means health displaced elsewhere exceeds the gain, though such technologies may still be recommended under modifiers.
has perspective title Net Health Benefit at £25,000 and £35,000, Weighted and Unweighted
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16, 4.10.8 and 6.3.2, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Net Monetary Benefit
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states that expected net health benefits should be presented as well as ICERs, using values placed on a QALY gain of £25,000 and £35,000. Net health benefit is described as particularly informative when decision-making modifiers are applied, when there are several technologies or comparators, when differences in costs or QALYs are small, or when a technology provides less health benefit at lower cost. Results are expected in a fully incremental analysis, and net monetary benefits can also be shown alongside ICERs and net health benefits.
has perspective title Expected Net Health Benefit Alongside ICERs at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.16 and 4.10.8, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Network Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000735
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Network Meta-Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary When technologies have not been compared within a single randomised controlled trial, NICE asks for the pairwise head-to-head trials to be presented together with a network meta-analysis if appropriate, and it prefers the methods in the Decision Support Unit evidence synthesis series. External information should inform the between-study heterogeneity, and informative priors for that parameter may be preferable in networks with few studies. Trial randomisation must be preserved, so single arms from different trials may not be compared.
has perspective title Network Meta-Analysis Alongside Head-to-Head Trials Using DSU Methods
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.4.11, 3.4.16 and 3.4.20, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Non-Randomised Controlled Trial

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000741
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Non-Randomised Controlled Trial
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE has a strong preference for high-quality randomised controlled trials for relative treatment effects, but non-randomised studies may complement them when evidence is limited or form the primary source when there is no trial evidence. Non-randomised studies can be interventional without randomisation or observational, and tend to be at high risk of bias because factors influencing treatment assignment may predict outcomes. Each study's risk of bias should be assessed with a validated tool such as ROBINS-I, and extensive sensitivity analyses should cover all key risks of bias.
has perspective title Non-Randomised Studies at High Risk of Bias from Confounding
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.3.2, 3.3.9, 3.3.12 and 3.3.13, last updated 13 October 2026

has perspective summary NICE recommends sacubitril valsartan as an option for treating symptomatic chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction only in people with New York Heart Association class 2 to 4 symptoms, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35 per cent or less, and a stable dose of an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker. Treatment should be started by a heart failure specialist with access to a multidisciplinary heart failure team. The NYHA class therefore sets the population for which the appraisal found the drug an acceptable use of NHS resources.

institutional perspective of NICE on Occupancy Rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000746
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Occupancy Rate
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng94/chapter/Recommendations
has perspective summary NICE's emergency and acute care guideline asks healthcare providers to monitor total acute hospital bed occupancy in real time, taking account of changes over 24 hours and the occupancy levels of specific wards and units, and to plan capacity to minimise the risks of occupancy rates above 90%. Its committee distinguished capacity, the number of beds, from occupancy, the proportion of beds filled, and chose 90% as a pragmatic maximum because adverse outcomes rose at that level. Local flexibility is allowed, with higher rates for efficiently managed elective pathways and lower rates where harm is evident.
has perspective title Monitor Bed Occupancy in Real Time and Plan to Avoid Rates Above 90%
has primary source label NICE guideline NG94, Emergency and acute medical care in over 16s: service delivery and organisation (published 28 March 2018), recommendation 1.3.1; evidence review 39 (Bed occupancy, March 2018), section 39.6

institutional perspective of NICE on One-Way Sensitivity Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000747
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept One-Way Sensitivity Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE treats univariate and best- or worst-case sensitivity analysis as an important way of identifying parameters with a substantial effect on cost-effectiveness results and explaining the drivers of a model, and suggests 'tornado' histograms for presenting them. Such analyses become increasingly unhelpful for representing combined uncertainty as the number of parameters grows, and deterministic analysis is less appropriate for decision making when a model is non-linear. Threshold analysis can identify a switching value, for example at £25,000 or £35,000 per QALY gained, and should show how far it lies from the current best estimate.
has perspective title Tornado Diagrams for Key Drivers and Switching Values for Uncertain Inputs
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.7.17, 4.7.21 and 4.7.22, last updated 31 March 2026
has wiki record identifier one-way-sensitivity-analysis

institutional perspective of NICE on Opportunity Cost

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Opportunity Cost
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE states that, given the fixed NHS budget, decisions about a new technology must consider the programmes for other patient groups that may be displaced by its adoption, including those not evaluated by NICE. The appropriate maximum acceptable ICER is that of the opportunity cost of programmes displaced by new, more costly technologies, but because NICE lacks complete information on competing programmes it uses a range of £25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained. When decision-making modifiers apply, net health benefits at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY should show the effect on opportunity costs.
has perspective title Maximum Acceptable ICER Set by the Opportunity Cost of Displaced Care
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.2.25, 6.3.1, 6.3.2 and 6.3.4 to 6.3.8, last updated 31 March 2026

In the reference case an additional QALY receives equal weight regardless of who receives the benefit.

institutional perspective of NICE on Pairwise Meta-Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000763
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Pairwise Meta-Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE considers combining outcome data through meta-analysis appropriate when there are enough relevant and valid data using comparable outcome measures. Each study's characteristics and limitations should be reported with a forest plot, and pooling should come with an assessment of heterogeneity, which a random rather than fixed effects model accounts for only to some extent, so its reasons should be explored through subgroup analysis, meta-regression or sensitivity analysis. Where a network meta-analysis is presented, pairwise meta-analyses of the direct comparisons should be shown alongside it.
has perspective title Pool Comparable Trials With a Forest Plot and an Assessment of Heterogeneity
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.4.8 to 3.4.10 and 3.4.20, last updated 31 March 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Parameter Input

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000767
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Parameter Input
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE expects all model parameter values used in base-case, sensitivity, scenario and subgroup analyses to be clinically plausible and estimated with methods consistent with the data, and every parameter to be tabulated with its data source. The effect of choosing different data sources for key parameters, such as costs, utilities and relative effectiveness, should be explored with alternative data sets. Distributions for probabilistic analysis must represent the available evidence and be justified, formal elicitation can be used when data are lacking, and uncertainty about a parameter is not, in general, a reason to leave it out of the probabilistic analysis.
has perspective title Parameters Tabulated, Plausible and Fully Represented in PSA
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.6.27, 4.6.28, 4.7.8, 4.7.10, 4.7.12 and 4.10.1, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Patient Time Cost
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE sets the reference-case perspective on costs as that of the NHS and personal social services (PSS), because its evaluations aim at efficient use of NHS and PSS resources. Costs paid by patients may be included when the NHS or PSS reimburses them, averaged across patients when reimbursement rates vary, and unreimbursed patient costs may be presented separately. Productivity costs are excluded from the reference case. The manual does not mention the value of patients' own time, which therefore falls outside the reference case.
has perspective title Reference Case Costs Exclude Unreimbursed Patient Costs
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.7, 4.2.9 and 4.4.23, last updated 13 October 2026

has perspective summary In its appraisal of adalimumab, etanercept and ustekinumab for plaque psoriasis in children and young people, NICE noted that the trials did not collect the EQ-5D-Y, a generic preference-based measure for young people, and reported only the Children's Dermatology Life Quality Index and the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL). Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Performance Bias
has display order 4
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE states that blinding, when applied, prevents knowledge of treatment allocation from influencing behaviours in randomised controlled trials. Its manual lists blinding among the features used to assess a trial's internal validity, together with the method of randomisation, concealment of allocation and completeness of follow up. NICE notes that blinding is often not possible in trials of specific medical devices or diagnostics, and requires all evidence to be critically appraised and potential biases identified.
has perspective title Blinding Counted in the Internal Validity of Trial Evidence

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Perspective
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary The reference case takes the perspective of the NHS and personal social services (PSS) on costs and counts all relevant health effects on outcomes, whether for patients or, when relevant, other people such as carers. NICE gives the reason that it does not set the NHS budget and aims to guide efficient use of available NHS and PSS resources. Productivity costs are excluded from the reference case, and costs to other government bodies are included only by agreement with the Department of Health and Social Care and reported separately.
has perspective title NHS and PSS Perspective on Costs, All Relevant Health Effects
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.2.7, 4.2.9, 4.2.10, 4.4.22 and 4.4.23, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Population
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/the-scope-2
has perspective summary NICE states that the scope defines the population for whom a technology is evaluated as precisely as possible, including where, why and how the technology is used in the care pathway, and may highlight subgroups whose clinical or cost effectiveness might differ. For medicines the relevant population is normally informed by the expected marketing authorisation, and people left out of a scope to keep the evaluation manageable are not thereby judged unsuitable for the technology. Cost-utility analyses should give separate estimates for each relevant subgroup, defined preferably by an expected difference in effect with a clear and plausible rationale.
has perspective title Scope Defines the Population as Precisely as Possible
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 2.2.9 to 2.2.11 and 4.9.1 to 4.9.3, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Preference Elicitation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case asks for the valuation of health-related quality of life measured by patients or their carers to be based on public preferences from a representative sample of the UK population, using a choice-based method. Health effects are expressed in QALYs, with the EQ-5D preferred in adults, so the preference elicitation behind the value set supplies reference-case utility weights. From 27 August 2026 the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system and the UK value set apply to adult reference-case analyses, and the manual's EQ-5D sections are due for revision.

concerns wiki concept Primary Research
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary When evidence on clinical effectiveness is absent, weak or uncertain, NICE committees may recommend that a technology is used only while more research is done, after weighing the value of further evidence, the feasibility of the research and how long findings will take. Managed access, for medicines only, applies when new evidence is expected from ongoing or planned trials or from patients in clinical practice and could be collected within at most 5 years without undue burden. A research-only recommendation carries no requirement for NHS funding.

has perspective summary Probabilistic sensitivity analysis is preferred in the reference case, characterising parameter uncertainty through assigned distributions so it is reflected simultaneously in results; NICE has required PSA in cost-effectiveness models since 2004, with results typically shown via cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept QALY Shortfall
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE defines severity as the future health lost by people living with a condition with standard care in the NHS. It compares remaining lifetime QALYs under current treatment with those of a general population of the same age and sex distribution, as absolute and proportional QALY shortfall. Whichever measure implies greater severity sets a QALY weight of 1, 1.2 or 1.7. NICE's interim methods statement PMG51 (paragraph 1.12) says the EQ-5D-5L value set should also be used for general population utilities in the shortfall, for topics that start evaluation after its publication on 27 August 2026; evaluations already under way keep EQ-5D-3L values.
has perspective title Severity Measured as QALY Shortfall Against a Matched General Population
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), section 6.2 and table 6.1, last updated 13 October 2026; interim methods statement PMG51, Statement on using the EQ-5D-5L value set, paragraph 1.12, published 27 August 2026

has perspective summary NICE's guidelines manual appraises each economic evaluation with a methodology checklist and then reaches two overall categorical judgements instead of a summed score. Applicability is classed as directly, partially or not applicable, and methodological quality as minor, potentially serious or very serious limitations. Each category depends on how likely it is that failing one or more criteria would change the conclusions about cost effectiveness. Studies judged not applicable would usually be excluded from further consideration.

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case requires health effects to be expressed in QALYs, with changes in health-related quality of life reported by patients and valued using choice-based public preferences from a representative UK sample. The EQ-5D is the preferred adult measure, and for new topics starting after 27 August 2026 utilities come from the EQ-5D-5L and the new UK 5L value set instead of mapping to the 3L value set. All QALYs carry equal weight in the reference case, although committees may weight QALYs by 1.2 or 1.7 for more severe conditions, judged by absolute and proportional QALY shortfall.

concerns wiki concept Reference Case
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary Economic evaluations considered by NICE should include an analysis using reference-case methods, and any additional analyses must be justified and clearly distinguished from it. The reference case covers all health effects for patients and, when relevant, carers; NHS and personal social services costs; cost-utility analysis with QALYs; a time horizon long enough to reflect all important differences; and a 3.5% annual discount rate for costs and health effects. From 27 August 2026 the EQ-5D-5L and its UK value set are preferred for adults in new topics, under an interim methods statement (PMG51) that takes precedence over the manual.

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE states its reference case as a table in which each row pairs one element of the analysis with the expected method. Health effects for patients and, when relevant, carers are counted, costs take the NHS and personal social services perspective, the time horizon reflects all important differences in costs or outcomes, health effects are expressed in QALYs with the EQ-5D preferred in adults, and costs and health effects share an annual discount rate of 3.5%, with 1.5% considered only as a non-reference case under three conditions in section 4.5.3. Departures are allowed in additional analyses when justified and kept apart from the reference case. The EQ-5D row is due for revision after PMG51.

has institution label as shown NICE

has perspective summary NICE's technology appraisal manual describes diagnostic test accuracy studies as evaluating one or more index tests against a reference standard that classifies people as having or not having the target condition. Comparative accuracy studies assess two or more index tests against a single reference standard, usually in the same people. The manual lists differences in reference standard among the likely sources of heterogeneity in meta-analysis of test accuracy, and asks for the choice of synthesis method to be justified.

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary For the reference case, NICE requires costs to relate to resources under the control of the NHS and personal social services, valued at prices relevant to the NHS and PSS, with evidence that resource use and cost data were identified systematically. Resource use estimates should include changes in infrastructure, use and maintenance and, where appropriate, staff training. For technologies with several uses, average costs are identified first and a marginal cost analysis may be added when an already recommended technology has spare capacity, and carers' time may be considered when the NHS or PSS might otherwise have provided that care.

institutional perspective of NICE on Scarcity

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Scarcity
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE considers the overall resources available to the NHS when judging value for money, so decisions about a new technology must weigh the healthcare programmes for other patient groups that its adoption may displace, including those NICE has not evaluated. The manual treats the NHS budget as fixed, so new, more costly technologies displace other programmes. When decision-making modifiers are applied, net health benefit is presented to show this opportunity cost, and a negative value means health gains too small to prevent an overall health loss from care not funded elsewhere.
has perspective title Adoption Weighed Against Care Displaced From a Fixed NHS Budget
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 6.2.25, 6.3.1 and 6.3.2, last updated 31 March 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Secondary Research
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/evidence-2
has perspective summary NICE requires evidence on outcomes to come from a systematic review, defined as systematically locating, including, appraising and synthesising the evidence for a clearly formulated question, and carried out to a pre-defined protocol. Synthesis of the included studies is allowed but not required. Attempts should be made to find evidence outside the public domain, such as unpublished or abstract-only trial data. Where an economic evaluation rests on new analyses, a review of published, relevant economic evaluations should also be done.
has perspective title Outcome Evidence Must Come From a Systematic Review
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 3.3.4, 3.3.25, 3.3.26 and 3.4.2, last updated 13 October 2026

has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case takes the NHS and personal social services perspective on costs, while counting all relevant health effects for patients and, when relevant, carers. Costs to other government bodies may be included only exceptionally, when agreed with the Department of Health and Social Care, and must be reported separately from the reference case. Productivity costs are excluded from the reference case but can be presented separately when they may be a critical component of a technology's value, and the time of family carers can be costed and shown separately.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9/chapter/methods-for-real-world-studies-of-comparative-effects
has perspective summary NICE's real-world evidence framework states that some propensity score methods allow the similarity of intervention groups on observed covariates to be examined, and that absolute standardised differences of less than 0.1 are generally considered to indicate good balance. Small absolute differences may still matter if the variable has a strong effect on the outcome. The framework also lists absolute standardised mean differences as one way to compare an analytical sample with the target population when assessing external validity.

concerns wiki concept Strict Dominance
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case calls for cost-utility analysis with fully incremental analysis, following standard decision rules that reflect dominance and extended dominance. Results should be presented with dominated technologies, defined as more costly and less effective than another technology in the analysis, and extendedly dominated technologies removed. Acceptability curves should be accompanied by the cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier, and expected net health benefits at £25,000 and £35,000 per QALY should also be presented when appropriate.
has perspective title Dominated Technologies Removed From a Fully Incremental Analysis
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), table 4.1 and sections 4.2.16, 4.7.15 and 4.10.8, last updated 31 March 2026

has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249/chapter/Rationale-and-impact
has perspective summary In its falls guideline NICE records that community studies of gait and balance assessment, such as the Timed Up and Go test, were identified, and that although the committee agreed these tests help in observing gait and balance problems, they do not predict a person's risk of falling. The guideline recommends against using falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Case-finding people who have had a previous injury from a fall or multiple falls, are living with frailty, or have gait or balance problems was judged useful for identifying those who may need a more detailed assessment.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Treatment Administration Cost
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's manual asks for all relevant costs, including treatment, monitoring, staffing and facilities, and calls Healthcare Resource Groups a valuable source, while warning that they may not suit technologies sharing an HRG with the comparator, when micro-costing may be more appropriate. It gives an administration cost as an example of a direct, intrinsic consequence of a technology. In the amivantamab appraisal, the committee rejected a community nursing code for subcutaneous dosing as unsuitable for an outpatient procedure and concluded that the SB12Z code should be used.
has perspective title Administration Costs Included and Costed With the Right HRG Code

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Treatment Switching
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE accepts that statistical methods adjusting for treatment switching can be presented when control patients move onto the technology and an intention-to-treat analysis is considered inappropriate. Simple methods such as censoring or excluding data from patients who cross over should be avoided because they are very susceptible to selection bias. The chosen method should be justified against the trial's switching mechanism, the available baseline and time-dependent data and the expected treatment effect, and the resulting uncertainty should be explored and quantified.
has perspective title Avoid Censoring or Excluding Switchers When Adjusting Survival
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), section 4.6.26, last updated 13 October 2026

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Unmet Need
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary In NICE technology appraisals the extent of unmet health need is reflected within the severity of the condition, defined as the future health lost by people living with it under standard care in the NHS. Severity is measured by absolute and proportional QALY shortfall, and the committee may weight QALYs by 1.2 for a proportional shortfall of 0.85 to 0.95 or an absolute shortfall of 12 to 18, and by 1.7 at 0.95 or 18 and above. The modifier is not initially applied to appraisals of HealthTech.
has perspective title Unmet Health Need Reflected Within the Severity Modifier

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Utility
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case expresses health effects in QALYs, giving each health state a utility that reflects its health-related quality of life and multiplying it by the time spent in that state. Patients should report changes in quality of life, valued using public preferences from a representative UK sample and a choice-based method, since different methods produce utility values that cannot always be compared. Under NICE's August 2026 interim methods statement, the UK EQ-5D-5L value set should be used to derive all adult utility values in reference-case analyses.
has perspective title Utility Values From Public Preferences, Now on the UK EQ-5D-5L Value Set
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.3.1 to 4.3.5, last updated 31 March 2026; NICE Interim methods statement: implementing the EQ-5D-5L value set (PMG51), section 1.7, published 27 August 2026

institutional perspective of NICE on Value of Information

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000899
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Value of Information
has display order 2
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary The NICE manual does not name value of information analysis or require EVPI, but asks models to quantify decision uncertainty: the probability that a different decision would be reached if true cost effectiveness were known. Before recommending a technology for use while more research is done, the committee weighs the potential value to the NHS of additional evidence and what could be gained by reconsidering the decision, balancing net benefits to current patients against those to current and future patients. Managed access for medicines needs resolvable uncertainty that data could address within 5 years.
has perspective title No Formal VOI Requirement, but Research Recommendations Weigh Evidence Value
has primary source label NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36), sections 4.7.2, 6.2.27, 6.4.6 and 6.4.14, last updated 31 March 2026

has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg51
has perspective summary NICE's interim methods statement PMG51, published 27 August 2026, requires the UK EQ-5D-5L value set for all new topics, so utilities are calculated directly from EQ-5D-5L data. When only EQ-5D-3L data are available, they are mapped to 5L utility values using the mapping model developed by the Decision Support Unit and the Economic Evaluation Policy Research Unit. Topics started before publication continue to map 5L data to the 3L value set. PMG51 replaces NICE's 2017 position statement on the 5L value set.

concerns wiki concept Vertical Equity
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/committee-recommendations-2
has perspective summary NICE's reference case gives an additional QALY the same weight regardless of the other characteristics of the people receiving the health benefit, except in specific circumstances. In technology appraisals the committee may apply a greater weight for severity, judged by absolute and proportional QALY shortfall with current care, whichever implies greater severity: 1.2 for proportional shortfall of 0.85 to 0.95 or absolute shortfall of 12 to 18, and 1.7 for at least 0.95 or at least 18. The modifier is not initially applied to appraisals of HealthTech, and highly specialised technologies receive no severity weight.

concerns wiki concept Welfare Economics
has display order 3
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
has perspective summary NICE justifies cost-effectiveness analysis by its focus on maximising health gains from a fixed NHS and personal social services budget, and states that its evaluations aim to represent an efficient use of available NHS and PSS resources. Health effects are measured in QALYs valued from the preferences of a representative sample of the UK population, and productivity costs are excluded. In the reference case an additional QALY has the same weight whoever receives it, except in specific circumstances, and distributional cost-effectiveness analysis may be used only as supporting evidence on health inequalities.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Wellbeing or Capability Instrument
has display order 1
has institution label as shown NICE
has page URL https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg20/chapter/incorporating-economic-evaluation
has perspective summary The NICE guidelines manual sets a reference case that varies with the decision problem and notes that for interventions with a social care focus the intended outcomes are broader than health. In table 7.1 the column for interventions with a social care focus names capability or social care-related quality of life measures, such as ICECAP or ASCOT, when an intervention results in both health and capability or social care outcomes. For public-sector interventions with health and non-health outcomes the measure is decided case by case. The manual says section 7.4, which holds table 7.1, will be updated.

has perspective summary The panel appointed by NOAA under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 concluded that contingent valuation studies can produce estimates reliable enough to be the starting point of a judicial process of damage assessment, including lost passive-use values, provided they follow its guidelines. It recommended the willingness to pay format in place of compensation required, because it is the conservative choice, with the valuation question posed as a vote on a referendum. Where design choices are ambiguous, the option that tends to underestimate willingness to pay is preferred, since hypothetical markets tend to overstate it.

has perspective summary Pharmacies in Norway may substitute generic, biosimilar or parallel-imported medicines only when the Norwegian Medical Products Agency has placed them on its substitution list, which has the status of a regulation. Listed products must contain the same active ingredient at the same strength in the same pharmaceutical form, be bioequivalent or biosimilar, and be judged medically equivalent; notes can limit substitution, for epilepsy medicines to the start of treatment. A physician may reserve a prescription against substitution only for compelling medical reasons recorded in the patient's record; otherwise a patient who declines substitution pays the price difference.

has perspective summary The System of Health Accounts records administration under function HC.7, split into governance and health system administration, and administration of health financing. has perspective summary The System of Health Accounts treats current health expenditure by disease as comparable with the direct health cost component of cost-of-illness accounts. Direct non-health costs, such as family travel, lodging or childcare during a hospital stay, fall outside it, as do the indirect productivity costs and intangible costs that cost-of-illness studies may add. Disease accounts use top-down allocation so that spending across all diseases sums to current health expenditure, whereas specific cost-of-illness studies usually build estimates bottom-up from patient-level data.
has perspective title Disease Expenditure Accounts Cover Direct Health Costs Only

has perspective summary In its July 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, the OBR projects UK health spending in its baseline scenario to rise from 8% of GDP in 2030-31 to 13% by 2075-76, real growth of 2.5% a year, drawing on the ONS 2024-based population projections. Demographic factors explain 0.4 percentage points of annual real growth, income effects 1.2 points (an income elasticity of 0.8) and other cost pressures 1 point. Without the other cost pressures health spending would reach around 9% of GDP, and healthy life expectancy scenarios give 12% and 15%.

has perspective summary The OBR projects UK health spending from demographic change, income effects and other cost pressures, which add 1 percentage point a year to real growth. Its 2024 report attributed 0.72 points of this to the Baumol effect, multiplying projected economy-wide productivity growth of 1.5 per cent a year by an OECD coefficient of 0.48. The July 2026 report keeps these assumptions, projecting health spending rising from 8 per cent of GDP in 2030-31 to 13 per cent by 2075-76, but calls future relative productivity growth in health very uncertain; without these pressures spending reaches about 9 per cent.

has perspective summary Health at a Glance 2025 reports that on average across 28 OECD countries, 3.4% of the population had unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024, up from 2.7% in 2019. The report states that policies need to secure an adequate supply and distribution of health workers and services and address financial barriers to care.

has perspective summary The OECD reports that member countries spent on average around 3% of health spending on administration in 2014, double that level in France and higher still in the United States. Single-payer systems had lower administrative costs than multi-payer systems, and among multi-payer systems those with free choice of insurer tended to cost more than those with automatic affiliation. Private insurance schemes spent from 9% of their spending on administration in Australia to more than 30% in Spain, the United Kingdom and Austria. The OECD cautions that some countries value private insurers' administration as the sum of costs, leaving out profits and brokerage fees.

has perspective summary The OECD treats average length of stay as an indicator of efficiency in health service delivery: all else equal, a shorter stay reduces the cost per discharge and shifts care to less expensive settings, although some patients may be discharged too early. Its 2025 edition reports 6.5 days for acute care across 36 OECD countries in 2023, from 4.7 days in Türkiye and Mexico to 15.7 days in Japan.

has perspective summary The OECD's 2010 report on health care systems states that patients who do not bear the full cost of care may consume more than necessary, and that providers may prescribe more for well insured patients. Higher out-of-pocket payments can cut demand for necessary care as well as care of limited value, and the RAND experiment found harm to people who were both poor and sick. Provider payment design and evidence-based practice are named as other remedies.

has perspective summary The Private Health Insurance Act 2007 sets a principle of community rating so that everybody who chooses has access to health insurance. has perspective summary The PBAC guidelines ask applicants to use individual-level models only when a model cannot feasibly be built as a cohort model, and say more complex techniques are unnecessary if simpler models give plausible sensitivity and scenario analyses. has institution label as shown PBAC

has perspective summary For economic models that extrapolate time-to-event data, the PBAC guidelines ask submissions to fit a range of parametric survival models, such as exponential, Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic, gamma and Gompertz, and more flexible approaches such as piecewise spline models. Goodness of fit should be assessed and discussed using visual inspection, Akaike's information criterion and the Bayesian information criterion. The most appropriate model for the base case must be justified, a number of the best-fitting models tested in sensitivity analysis, and the plausibility of predictions in the unobserved period addressed.

has display order 3
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/content/information/files/pbac-guidelines-version-5.pdf
has perspective summary The PBAC submission guidelines state that for patient-relevant outcomes measured on a scale, such as a quality of life instrument or the 6-minute walk distance test, the minimal clinically important difference may be established using an anchor approach, with statistical or consensus approaches less preferred. The MCID can then serve as the threshold beyond which an individual patient counts as a responder. Submissions tabulate each proposed MCID with its source, its method of derivation and any differences in population, outcome definition or baseline value.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/content/information/files/pbac-guidelines-version-5.pdf
has perspective summary The PBAC guidelines ask each submission to tabulate important differences between the trial setting and the Australian setting after listing, covering the population, disease severity, circumstances of use, concomitant treatments and the health care system. Each difference is judged either unlikely to have an effect or as needing further investigation, which is then addressed through translation analyses in the economic evaluation. Differences that may affect comparative effectiveness or safety can undermine the assumptions needed for a cost-minimisation approach and then call for a supplementary analysis.
has perspective title Tabulate Trial Versus Australian Setting Differences and Test Those That Matter

has display order 2
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/content/information/files/pbac-guidelines-version-5.pdf
has perspective summary The PBAC recommends to the Minister which medicines should be subsidised and, under the National Health Act 1953, must consider effectiveness and cost against alternative therapies. It cannot recommend a medicine that is substantially more costly than an alternative unless satisfied that it also provides a significant improvement in health. Its decisions weigh five quantitative factors, including comparative health gain, cost-effectiveness and projected net cost to the PBS, with less readily quantified factors such as confidence in the evidence, equity, clinical need and severity.
has perspective title No Positive Advice for a Costlier Medicine Without a Significant Health Gain

has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/content/information/files/pbac-guidelines-version-5.pdf
has perspective summary The PBAC guidelines ask that a model capture all relevant health states and clinical events, stay consistent with the clinical management algorithms, be informed by the literature and be checked for face validity. Submissions must justify excluding any potentially relevant state or event, discuss its effect on outputs and explain departures from existing models. Plausible alternative structures should be tested, structural assumptions parameterised where evidence or expert opinion allows and otherwise explored in scenario analyses, since probabilistic analysis cannot address structural uncertainty.

has display order 2

has perspective summary The PBAC guidelines ask submissions to report dichotomous outcomes and important adverse events as both relative risks and risk differences with 95% confidence intervals, and to present relative risk, odds ratio and risk difference separately in meta-analyses. For indirect comparisons, the outcome measure showing the least heterogeneity across trials should be applied; where the desired final outcome is an absolute risk difference but a relative measure is more consistent across trials, the comparison should be run on odds ratios and converted to a risk difference.

has perspective summary The PBAC asks submissions whose models go beyond the clinical data to show, step by step, how the comparative trial results are transformed into the modelled base-case estimate of incremental cost-effectiveness. Each step undertaken, such as applicability adjustments, translation of surrogate to clinical outcomes, extrapolation over time and conversion to QALYs, is presented with re-estimated costs and outcomes, and the final step must correspond to the base-case ICER. The stepped presentation identifies the assumptions that need fuller sensitivity analysis.

has perspective summary The PBAC guidelines tell applicants to take care when converting relative treatment effects across jurisdictions with different baseline risks, and to ensure that the baseline risk, meaning patients' prognostic characteristics, does not differ between the trial evidence and the target population. has perspective summary The PBAC Guidelines ask submissions to use commonly adopted statistical standards to represent uncertainty around the true value of each uncertain model input. As an example, they describe beta distributions as a natural match for transition probabilities, with log-normal distributions for relative risks or hazard ratios and gamma or log-normal distributions for costs and utility parameters. The use of alternative distributions should be justified, and interval estimates from the fitted distributions should define the ranges tested in deterministic sensitivity analyses.

has institution label as shown PBAC

has perspective summary PBAC submissions present budget impact analyses giving the most likely extent of use of the proposed medicine and its financial impact on the Australian Government. Sponsors justify an epidemiological or market-share approach and use a standardised Excel workbook to estimate net changes for the PBS or RPBS, the MBS and the wider government health budget over six years. Unlike the economic evaluation, these financial analyses exclude health outcomes, apply no discounting and exclude costs from outside the identified budget. Where a special pricing arrangement is offered, costs are shown with and without it.

has perspective summary For meta-analyses of trial results, the PBAC Guidelines ask submissions to report the extent of statistical heterogeneity using the Cochran Q statistic, its degrees of freedom, the chi-square test for heterogeneity and the I-squared statistic with its 95% uncertainty interval. The example results table places the chi-square (Q) value, degrees of freedom and P value beside each pooled estimate. Group-level trial data are pooled with a DerSimonian-Laird random effects model, and any other method must be explained and justified.

institutional perspective of PBAC on Cohort Simulation

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cohort Simulation
has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-3a/3a-2-computational-methods-and-structure-of-economic_analysis.html
has perspective summary The PBAC Guidelines ask for the least complicated modelling technique that can implement the model structure, moving from decision trees to cohort-based state transition models and then to individual-level models. Cohort-based state transition, or Markov, models suit longer time horizons when a manageable number of health states can represent the condition under the memoryless assumption, with tunnel states for time-varying transitions. A half-cycle correction is the default, and individual-level models are used only when a structure cannot feasibly be implemented as a cohort-based model.
has perspective title Cohort Models Preferred Unless the Structure Cannot Be Implemented
has primary source label Guidelines for preparing a submission to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee, version 5.0 (September 2016), subsection 3A.2.3

has display order 3
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-1/1-1-clinical-issue-addressed_by-the-submission.html
has perspective summary The main comparator is the therapy that prescribers would most replace with the proposed medicine, judged on what would be likely to happen in practice rather than what should happen. Where pharmacological analogues are already listed, the main comparator is usually the analogue prescribed on the PBS for the largest number of patients in the target population. Where no PBS medicine is listed for the population, or the medicine is used in addition to existing treatment, the comparator is usually clearly defined standard medical management.

institutional perspective of PBAC on Comparator Selection

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000351
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Comparator Selection
has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-1/1-1-clinical-issue-addressed_by-the-submission.html
has perspective summary The submission must nominate as its main comparator the therapy prescribers would most replace with the proposed medicine — judged on what would likely happen in practice, not what should happen. A defined hierarchy applies (usually the pharmacological analogue already listed for the largest number of PBS patients in the target population). The comparator is not merely current best practice, and the PBAC can reject a sponsor’s nominated comparator and substitute another, which resets the entire clinical and economic evaluation built on it.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/appendixes/appendix-6-including-nonhealth-outcomes-in-a-supplementary-analysis.html
has perspective summary The PBAC Guidelines allow direct patient benefits that are not health outcomes, such as a more convenient form of administration, to be valued in a supplementary analysis. Methods to estimate the monetary or other value of the nonhealth benefit may include a conjoint analysis or a discrete choice experiment with a monetary attribute. Where health outcomes do not otherwise differ substantively from the main comparator, the resulting estimate, such as willingness to pay, can enter a supplementary cost-benefit analysis, and any consumer surplus needs a nominated basis for sharing between the sponsor and the taxpayer.

has display order 3
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-3a/3a-6-health-care-resource-use-and-costs.html
has perspective summary Submissions identify each direct health care resource item whose use changes when the proposed medicine replaces the main comparator, and quantify it in natural units such as packs dispensed or admissions. The amount provided, not the amount consumed, is the relevant measure, so wastage is costed. Unit costs are in Australian dollars for a stated year close to the submission date, using the Manual of resource items and their associated costs, and historical costs are inflated with a relevant Australian health price index. Productivity impacts appear only in supplementary analyses.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-3b-cost-minimisation.html
has perspective summary A cost-minimisation approach is appropriate where the therapeutic claim is non-inferiority (or superiority) with an equivalent or superior safety profile in both nature and magnitude, and the medicine costs the same or less; the comparison is then reduced to costs. The non-inferiority assumption must be well justified, and where adverse-effect profiles differ significantly a full economic evaluation is required instead.

has perspective summary The PBAC Guidelines state that a probabilistic sensitivity analysis may be provided in addition to deterministic sensitivity analysis, and note that it can characterise parameter uncertainty but cannot address translational or structural uncertainty. Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Minimisation Analysis
has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-3b-cost-minimisation.html
has perspective summary PBAC guidance treats a cost-minimisation approach as appropriate where the therapeutic claim is non-inferiority or superiority, the safety profile is equivalent or superior in nature and magnitude, and the proposed medicine is expected to cost the health system the same or less. The non-inferiority assumption for both effectiveness and safety must be well justified. If adverse effect profiles differ significantly in nature, the approach is unlikely to suffice and a full economic evaluation is expected. Submissions must establish equi-effective doses and identify differences in prescribing, administration, monitoring and adverse-event costs.

has institution label as shown PBAC

has perspective summary The PBAC Guidelines prefer a cost-utility analysis to a cost-effectiveness analysis, particularly where a submission claims incremental life-years gained, where quality but not quantity of life improves, or where direct randomised trials report a multiattribute utility instrument. Where transformations or external data are needed to estimate QALYs, a stepped transformation from the cost-effectiveness analysis to the cost-utility analysis should be presented. Australian-based preference weights are preferred when scoring utility instruments.

Values from all sources of evidence should be adjusted to the model structure, for example by translating reported rates or cumulative probabilities into probabilities for the timeframe of a model cycle.

has display order 4
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-3a/3a-8-results-of-the-base-case-economic-evaluation.html
has perspective summary The PBAC asks submissions to present the base-case incremental cost, incremental effectiveness and ICER, with the ICER calculated as the incremental costs divided by the incremental health outcomes. The ICER is built up in steps from the trial data and recalculated after each transformation, such as surrogate to clinical outcome, translation to the Australian setting, extrapolation and conversion to QALYs, so that the steps with the largest effect on the ICER are visible. An ICER based on an outcome other than life-years or QALYs gained should be compared with earlier PBAC decisions using the same outcome.
has perspective title Stepped Derivation of the Base-Case ICER

has institution label as shown PBAC

has perspective summary PBAC's guidelines prefer a cost-utility analysis, with outcomes measured in QALYs, over a cost-effectiveness analysis, particularly where life-years are gained, where quality but not quantity of life improves, or where direct randomised trials report a multiattribute utility instrument. Where another outcome is chosen, sponsors must justify why it is not translated into QALYs. The base case must present the incremental cost, incremental effectiveness and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, calculated as incremental costs divided by incremental health outcomes, with a stepped derivation from the trial data.

has perspective summary The PBAC guidelines ask submissions relying on an indirect comparison to identify the trials used, draw a network diagram and justify excluding trials whose differences may affect transitivity. The method should be described: the Bucher method for trials sharing a common reference arm is widely used, and network meta-analyses may be presented as supplementary analyses. Naive comparisons of single arms are difficult to interpret and reduce the PBAC's confidence, and where patient-level data exist for at least one study, matching-adjusted indirect comparisons or simulated treatment comparisons should be used to correct for trial differences.

institutional perspective of PBAC on Markov Assumption

has display order 1
has institution label as shown PBAC
has page URL https://pbac.pbs.gov.au/section-3a/3a-2-computational-methods-and-structure-of-economic_analysis.html
has perspective summary PBAC guidelines reserve cohort-based state transition models for longer time horizons that can be represented with a manageable number of health states under the constraints of the Markovian, or memoryless, assumption. Submissions should consider whether transition probabilities from each state can reasonably be treated as independent of states experienced earlier, using pathway health states to carry the effects of previous events and tunnel states where probabilities vary with time spent in a state. Individual-level models are used only when a cohort model cannot feasibly be implemented, for example because previous events influence later event rates.

has display order 3

has perspective summary New Zealand's PHARMAC prefers to report cost-utility results as incremental utility-cost ratios, the incremental QALYs gained per NZD 1 million of net expenditure, because they reflect opportunity cost within a fixed budget. Incremental cost-utility ratios, the incremental cost per QALY gained, are described as the long-established international unit and in effect the inverse of the utility-cost ratio, and should be reported alongside it. QALYs in these ratios should not be weighted for health need or disease severity, to keep the ratios as value free as possible.

has page URL https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_briefs/RB9174.html
has perspective summary RAND's Health Insurance Experiment (1971 to 1982) randomly assigned more than 7,700 people to free care or to 25, 50 or 95 per cent coinsurance. Spending was 20 per cent lower under 25 per cent coinsurance and about 30 per cent lower under 95 per cent coinsurance than under free care. Cost sharing reduced highly effective and less effective care in roughly equal proportions, and the poorest and sickest 6 per cent fared better under free care on 4 of 30 conditions. RAND describes cost sharing as a blunt tool that should be minimal or nonexistent for the poor.
has perspective title Evidence from the Health Insurance Experiment
has primary source label RAND Corporation, The Health Insurance Experiment: A Classic RAND Study Speaks to the Current Health Care Reform Debate, research brief RB-9174-HHS, published 6 December 2006, sections Effects on Use of Health Services, Effects on Appropriateness of Care and on Quality of Care, Effects on Health, and Implications for Today's Health Care Reform Discussion

institutional perspective of TLV on Value-Based Pricing

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000897
Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown TLV
has page URL https://www.tlv.se/in-english/medicines/pricing-and-reimbursement-of-medicines.html
has perspective summary Sweden applies value-based pricing without price negotiation: the company states its requested price in the reimbursement application, and TLV grants inclusion at that price if the health-economic analysis shows it is justified by the value delivered (cost-effective, with marginal benefit over the most cost-effective existing therapies). In practice there is no price bargaining — prices can be set freely under this value-based ceiling; a product rejected as too expensive can reapply at a lower price or with new evidence. This contrasts with the negotiation-based models used in most other jurisdictions (a three-party managed-entry route with the regions now supplements it).
has perspective title Accept/Reject at the Company’s Requested Price; Value-Based Pricing Without Negotiation

has perspective summary The Social Security Act requires the HHS Office of Inspector General to compare each Part B drug's ASP with its AMP and notify the Secretary when ASP exceeds AMP by 5% or more. has perspective summary Federal regulations assign a health plan to the bronze, silver, gold or platinum level of coverage when its actuarial value is 60%, 70%, 80% or 90%, within a de minimis variation. Silver plan variations with cost-sharing reductions must reach 73%, 87% or 94% for the three groups eligible for those reductions.

has perspective summary Federal rules require health insurance issuers to pay rebates when their medical loss ratio falls below 85% in the large group market or 80% in the small group and individual markets, and a state may substitute a higher standard. The rebate equals premium after taxes and fees, adjusted for the risk programmes, multiplied by the shortfall. Administrative services, including cost containment that is not quality improvement, broker fees and general administration, are reported as non-claims costs, and all retrospective and concurrent utilisation review, fraud prevention and marketing cannot count as quality improvement.

has perspective summary The federal criteria for designating primary care health professional shortage areas define a rational service area as a county or group of counties whose population centres lie within 30 minutes' travel time of each other, or an area with limited access to neighbouring resources, measured generally by travel time over 30 minutes. has perspective summary The Department of Labor describes stop-loss cover that pays claims above an attachment point set for a single member or for aggregate claims over a set period, citing 125% of expected claims per plan year as an aggregate example, with the employer self-insuring claims below it. has perspective summary The UK National Screening Committee states that all approved screening programmes should aim to facilitate a personal informed choice, its overarching and guiding principle. has page URL https://amr-review.org/sites/default/files/160518_Final%20paper_with%20cover.pdf
has perspective summary The Review, commissioned by the UK government and chaired by Jim O'Neill, names externalities, imperfect information and an unwillingness to pay for public goods as the main market failures behind antimicrobial resistance. It places antibiotic consumption among goods with negative externalities: individuals take and may benefit from the drugs, but the resistance they contribute to affects all of society. It accepts some positive externality from curing infections that would otherwise spread, but judges the resistance externality more pronounced and weakly regulated, leading to overuse in patients and animals.

institutional perspective of UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights on Acceptability of Healthcare

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000024

has display order 1
has institution label as shown UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
has page URL https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/g00/439/34/pdf/g0043934.pdf
has perspective summary The Committee treats acceptability as one of four interrelated elements of the right to health, alongside availability, accessibility and quality. All health facilities, goods and services must be respectful of medical ethics and culturally appropriate, sensitive to gender and life-cycle requirements, and designed to respect confidentiality and improve the health status of those concerned. States must ensure that privatisation of the health sector does not threaten acceptability, and that health services are culturally appropriate, with staff trained to respond to the needs of vulnerable or marginalised groups.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Access to Care
has display order 2
has institution label as shown UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
has page URL https://docs.un.org/en/E/C.12/2000/4
has perspective summary The Committee holds that the right to health contains four interrelated elements: availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality, applied according to the conditions in each State party. Accessibility has four overlapping dimensions: non-discrimination, physical accessibility, economic accessibility (affordability) and information accessibility. Payment for health services must follow the principle of equity, so that poorer households are not disproportionately burdened with health expenses compared with richer households. Acceptability requires services that respect medical ethics and are culturally appropriate, while quality requires scientifically and medically appropriate care.
has perspective title Right to Health: Availability, Accessibility, Acceptability and Quality

Heads of State and Government committed to prioritise budget allocations for primary health care, recalling the recommended target of an additional 1 per cent of gross domestic product or more.
