has display order 1
has institution label as shown United Nations Statistics Division
has page URL https://unstats.un.org/unsd/demographic/sources/surveys/Handbook23June05.pdf
has perspective summary The UN Statistics Division's household survey handbook sets three requirements for probability sampling, namely that each element has a known chance of selection, that the chance is greater than zero and that it can be calculated, although chances need not be equal. It strongly recommends always using probability sampling, even when it costs more, because only then can estimates be inferred to the population and sampling errors be estimated. Quota, convenience, purposive and random walk samples give biased estimates whose size and often direction are unknown.

has perspective summary Under the Affordable Care Act, the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute may not develop or use a dollars-per-QALY measure, or a similar measure that discounts the value of a life because of disability, as a threshold for deciding what care is cost effective or recommended. has perspective summary HHS rules define the attachment point as the threshold of an issuer's claims costs for one enrollee in a benefit year after which those costs become eligible for reinsurance payments. Under the transitional reinsurance programme for 2014 to 2016, each payment was the coinsurance rate multiplied by claims costs between the attachment point and the reinsurance cap. In the current risk adjustment programme, the high-cost risk pool pays 60% of an enrollee's claims above USD 1 million, a threshold HHS kept for the 2027 benefit year, funded by a charge on premiums.

has perspective summary EPA's Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses state that iterative bidding in stated preference surveys has been shown to suffer from starting point bias, with respondents' maximum willingness to pay systematically related to the opening dollar amount. They record concerns that the range and intervals of amounts on payment cards may influence answers, and that second responses to double-bounded dichotomous choice questions may not be independent of the first. EPA notes that researchers have generally turned from direct questions to other stated preference formats.

institutional perspective of US Environmental Protection Agency on Cost-Benefit Analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000390
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Benefit Analysis
has display order 4
has institution label as shown US Environmental Protection Agency
has page URL https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/chapter-1-guidelines-for-preparing-economic-analyses_final_508-compliant.pdf
has perspective summary The EPA Guidelines focus on benefit-cost analysis and economic impact analysis, which they describe as the two mainstays of the agency's economic analyses. Benefit-cost analysis assesses economic efficiency using the Potential Pareto criterion: a policy moves towards efficiency when those who gain could fully compensate those who lose and remain better off, so net benefits are positive. Benefits and costs that cannot be quantified or monetised should still be described, and distributional effects are assessed separately from the efficiency analysis.
has perspective title Benefit-Cost Analysis and the Potential Pareto Criterion

has display order 3
has institution label as shown US Environmental Protection Agency

has perspective summary The EPA values mortality benefits using estimates of what people are willing to pay for small reductions in their risk of dying, and states that it does not place a dollar value on individual lives. It recommends a central estimate of USD 7.4 million in 2006 dollars, updated to the year of the analysis, for all benefits analyses of mortality risk reduction, regardless of the age, income or other characteristics of the affected population, until revised guidance is available. The agency has proposed replacing the term value of statistical life with one that better describes small changes in mortality risk.

institutional perspective of US Environmental Protection Agency on Welfare Economics

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000912
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Welfare Economics
has display order 2
has institution label as shown US Environmental Protection Agency
has page URL https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/appendix-a-guidelines-for-preparing-economic-analyses_final_508-compliant.pdf
has perspective summary The EPA guidelines set out the welfare theory underlying the agency's economic analyses, starting from the two fundamental theorems of welfare economics: every competitive equilibrium is Pareto optimal, and every Pareto optimal allocation can be reached as a competitive equilibrium after suitable redistribution. Judging the fairness of net gains would need a social welfare function, on which there is no general agreement, so the guidelines apply the Kaldor-Hicks test: winners could compensate losers and remain better off, and losers could not pay winners to forgo the change. Whether compensation is paid is a separate value judgement for government.
has perspective title Fundamental Welfare Theorems and the Kaldor-Hicks Compensation Test
has primary source label US Environmental Protection Agency, Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses, 3rd edition (2024), EPA-240-R-24-001, Appendix A Economic Theory, sections A.1 (Market Economy) and A.3 (Benefit-Cost Analysis)
has wiki record identifier welfare-economics

institutional perspective of US Environmental Protection Agency on Willingness to Pay

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000918
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Willingness to Pay
has display order 2
has institution label as shown US Environmental Protection Agency
has page URL https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/chapter-7-guidelines-for-preparing-economic-analyses_final_508-compliant.pdf
has perspective summary EPA guidelines name willingness to pay as the preferred measure of benefits, because it accounts for individual trade-offs between wealth and benefits in monetary terms and so allows net benefits to be calculated; the term is used to cover willingness to accept compensation as well. Mortality risk reductions are valued from individuals' willingness to pay for small reductions in the risk of dying, aggregated as the value of statistical life (VSL), which EPA stresses is not the value of life itself. EPA policy applies a single VSL estimate across all its programmes, and willingness to pay is also the preferred measure for morbidity effects.
has perspective title Willingness to Pay as the Preferred Benefit Measure, Including the VSL
has primary source label US Environmental Protection Agency, Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses, 3rd edition (EPA-240-R-24-001, 2024), Chapter 7 introduction and footnote 1, sections 7.2.1.1 and 7.2.1.2

has perspective summary The WHO and UNODC International Standards for the Treatment of Drug Use Disorders require resource allocation for treatment to be guided by evidence on the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of treatment interventions. From a public budget perspective, the Standards call evidence-based treatment a smart investment because treating drug use disorders costs much less than untreated dependence, citing a NIDA estimate that savings can exceed investment by 12 to 1 through lower crime, justice, law enforcement and healthcare costs. Systems built on the service delivery pyramid, with most care in outpatient and community settings, are described as more cost-effective.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO and World Bank
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240117808
has perspective summary The 2025 global monitoring report defines financial protection as the absence of both financial barriers to needed care and financial hardship from out-of-pocket spending. It states that the SDG financial hardship indicator does not capture people kept from care by financial barriers, so the population without financial protection is underestimated. Forgone care is defined as a recognised need left unmet because of barriers at any point in the care pathway. Across 38 low- and middle-income countries, a median of 58.6% of women reported problems accessing health care in 2014 to 2023, down from 67.8%.

institutional perspective of WHO on Acceptability of Healthcare

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Acceptability of Healthcare
has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240094765
has perspective summary WHO's handbook for assessing barriers to effective coverage defines acceptability coverage as the proportion of the population for whom services are acceptable, a domain of the Tanahashi framework that follows availability and accessibility and precedes contact. It adopts the right to health definition and adds that acceptability is shaped by perceptions, expectations, personal beliefs and past experiences with providers. Listed barriers include discriminatory attitudes of health personnel, perceptions of low quality, gender norms, low trust, weak confidentiality and poor fit with cultural beliefs. Effective coverage depends on the acceptability domain first being achieved.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Access Barrier
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241564021
has perspective summary The World Health Report 2010 identifies reliance on direct payments, including user fees, as by far the greatest obstacle to universal coverage, since people who must pay on the spot are deterred from using services. WHO states that removing these charges helps poorer people obtain care but does not guarantee it. Transport costs and lost income can be even more prohibitive than service charges, and services that are unavailable or far away cannot be used even when free. The report also cites cultural and language barriers, such as settings where women are prevented from travelling alone.
has perspective title Direct Payments and Other Barriers to Accessing Health Services
has primary source label World Health Organization, The World Health Report: Health Systems Financing: the Path to Universal Coverage (2010), Message from the Director-General (page vi); Executive summary, Removing financial risks and barriers to access and Other barriers to accessing health services (pages xiv to xvi); Chapter 3, Other barriers to access (pages 51 to 52)

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Access Policy
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241564021
has perspective summary The World Health Report 2010 frames the move towards universal coverage along three dimensions: who is covered, which services are covered and what proportion of the costs is met from pooled funds. A country can extend coverage to more people, include other services or reduce cost sharing and fees, trading these choices off within limited pooled funds. The report names reliance on direct payments, including user fees, as by far the greatest obstacle to progress. It warns that abolishing fees without planning for extra demand and replacement funding can leave staff unpaid and dispensaries empty.

has perspective summary WHO's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), endorsed by all 191 WHO Member States at the World Health Assembly in May 2001, defines activity limitations as difficulties an individual may have in executing activities, an activity being the execution of a task or action. Disability is an umbrella term for impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions, which sit at the levels of the body, the whole person and the person in a social context. The ICF distinguishes capacity, what a person can do in a standard environment, from performance in the person's usual environment.

has perspective summary WHO's technical report on patient safety incident reporting and learning systems states that reporting systems should yield learning to improve safety rather than simply communicate failure. A single report seldom gives a definitive view of causation, so further investigation and analysis are needed to establish why an incident happened.

has page URL https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/gho-documents/global-health-estimates/ghe2023_daly_methods.pdf
has perspective summary WHO's methods for its Global Health Estimates record that the standard DALYs of the original Global Burden of Disease study and earlier WHO updates used non-uniform age weights, giving less weight to years of healthy life lost at young and older ages. With the DALY defined purely as a measure of population health loss, WHO states that age weights are difficult to justify. After informal consultations in 2012, WHO adopted the GBD 2010 approach of no age weighting and a 0% discount rate, which raised the absolute number of DALYs and the share at younger and older ages.
has perspective title Age Weights Dropped From DALYs Since 2012
has primary source label World Health Organization, WHO methods and data sources for global burden of disease estimates 2000-2023, Global Health Estimates Technical Paper GHE/2026.3 (September 2026), sections 2 and 2.3

has perspective summary WHO's guide to economic evaluation of immunisation programmes treats agent-based models as individual-based models, in which each person has characteristics such as age, susceptibility, location and household that govern transmission. It notes their flexibility for dynamic stochastic transmission but also their computing demands and outcomes that are harder to validate and interpret, and suggests them when infection risks differ substantially between many small groups. Its recommendations call for a dynamic model when vaccination is likely to change the force of infection.
has perspective title Individual-Based Models for Vaccines When Risks Differ Across Small Groups

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/373421
has perspective summary WHO's overview of regulatory considerations on AI for health, which it presents as a discussion document rather than guidance, sets out 18 considerations. It advises documenting intended use and training data, and showing performance beyond the training and testing data through external validation on an independent dataset representative of the intended population and setting. Clinical validation should be graded by risk: randomised trials for the highest-risk tools, prospective real-world validation with a comparator elsewhere, and a period of more intense post-deployment monitoring.

institutional perspective of WHO on Allocative Efficiency

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Allocative Efficiency
has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020689
has perspective summary WHO's principles for health benefit packages state that all countries must ensure, through their package selection process, that available resources are used in the most efficient manner by achieving the greatest possible health benefits within the budget constraint. Every decision within a finite budget carries an opportunity cost, because funding one intervention means that other services, which may have produced more health, protected the most vulnerable from impoverishment or improved access for the least advantaged, will not be provided. Where other criteria are prioritised, the resulting health loss must be clearly communicated.
has perspective title Benefit Packages Should Secure the Greatest Health Gain Within the Budget
has primary source label World Health Organization, Principles of health benefit packages (2021, ISBN 978-92-4-002068-9), principle 3, page 8

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/337641
has perspective summary WHO and UNICEF's operational framework for primary health care, requested by the World Health Assembly to turn the Astana commitments into action, sets out 14 levers, of which funding and allocation of resources is one of four core strategic levers. It calls primary health care the most efficient route to universal health coverage but finds funding insufficient: in 2016 none of 16 low-income countries with data spent more than US$50 per capita on it. Funds should be rationally allocated across primary care, public health interventions and community engagement, and tertiary facilities often receive disproportionately large shares of health budgets.
has perspective title Funding and Allocation of Resources as a Core Lever for Primary Health Care

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/antimicrobial-resistance
has perspective summary WHO states that antimicrobial resistance drives health care costs largely through longer hospital stays and greater need for intensive care, along with more use of second-line antibiotics and extra diagnostic testing. It reports a projection that treating resistant bacterial infections alone could cost USD 412 billion a year up to 2035, with productivity losses of USD 443 billion a year. On 23 May 2026 the World Health Assembly adopted an updated global action plan on antimicrobial resistance for 2026 to 2036, which aims to enable the UN target of a 10% fall in bacterial AMR-associated deaths by 2030.
has perspective title Costs Driven by Longer Stays and a Global Action Plan for 2026 to 2036
has primary source label World Health Organization, Antimicrobial resistance fact sheet (16 July 2026), 'A global concern' and 'WHO response'; World Health Assembly decision WHA79(19), Global action plan on antimicrobial resistance 2026 to 2036 (23 May 2026)

has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/42699
has perspective summary The WHO guide to cost-effectiveness analysis defines capital goods as inputs lasting more than a year and says their cost must be spread over the study period. The economic cost combines the opportunity cost of the investment with depreciation, and where rental markets work poorly the item should be annualised from its purchase value net of resale value, the interest rate and its useful life. Start-up costs should be annualised over the programme's lifetime, with a 10-year period recommended where technologies are not expected to change over a short period.

has perspective summary WHO's guidance on the ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health sets six consensus principles covering autonomy; human well-being, safety and the public interest; transparency, explainability and intelligibility; responsibility and accountability; inclusiveness and equity; and AI that is responsive and sustainable. Under the autonomy principle, humans should remain in full control of health care systems and medical decisions, and AI systems should be designed to help providers and patients make informed decisions, with meaningful human oversight that may depend on the risks of the system.

has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240096745
has perspective summary WHO's global status report on alcohol defines alcohol-attributable fractions as the contribution of alcohol as a risk factor, interpreted as the proportion of deaths or disease burden that would disappear if there had been no alcohol consumption in a population. WHO quantifies the burden for 31 health conditions and estimates that 2.6 million deaths, 4.7% of all deaths, were attributable to alcohol in 2019. The fractions can be negative: for ischaemic stroke and diabetes mellitus the estimated net effect of alcohol was beneficial.

has perspective summary WHO's pricing guideline conditionally recommends that countries use tendering for pharmaceutical products, with price considered alongside product quality, product characteristics, availability, supply security, supply reliability and supply chain charges, and with tendering combined with other pricing policies and complemented by price negotiation. Its implementation considerations ask purchasers to explore options for structuring the tender, such as single versus split tenders, to exploit market size and purchasing power while ensuring supply security, to base order quantities on reliable estimates of need, and to penalise intentional failure to supply.

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/e09a9dc3-4f57-4eb0-ad36-828df6ba8c68/content
has perspective summary The WHO guide to cost-effectiveness analysis recommends that analysts evaluate all interventions initially against the null, the situation if none of a set of interacting interventions were implemented, so that currently funded services can be assessed as well as new options. In the league table, the option with the lowest ratio against the null in each set of mutually exclusive interventions comes first and the others follow by incremental ratios, with weakly dominated options left out. A background paper in the guide warns that ranking interventions by average cost-effectiveness alone will in general give suboptimal allocations.
has perspective title Interventions Evaluated First Against the Null, Then Incrementally

has perspective summary WHO's guide to economic impact studies in health states that isolating the share of a disease's or risk factor's economic costs that effective policies or interventions could avoid is a highly relevant undertaking that should be strongly encouraged. Every estimate must be measured against a stated counterfactual, and because the theoretical minimum risk can differ from the feasible minimum, the choice should follow the policy question. The guide adds that the size of an economic burden cannot set priorities on its own, which also need the costs of reducing it and the marginal effect of extra spending.

has perspective summary The WHO handbook for guideline development treats feasibility as a determinant of recommendation strength: the greater the barriers to implementing an option, the less likely the intervention is to be strongly recommended, with feasibility shaped by available resources, programme considerations, infrastructure and training. Implementation should be considered from the start of guideline development, and the basic steps for national or subnational implementers include analysing local needs, identifying potential barriers and facilitating factors, and designing an implementation strategy. Qualitative evidence can inform questions on contextual barriers and facilitators.

has perspective summary WHO's World Health Report 2010 states that financing labels can mislead, because two systems described as tax-based, or two based largely on insurance, may pool and use funds very differently, so the traditional division into tax-based and social health insurance systems, or Beveridge versus Bismarck, is no longer useful for policy-making. WHO's current health financing guidance instead analyses revenue raising, pooling and purchasing in every system, irrespective of whether it is labelled tax-based or health insurance.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Capacity Planning
has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/373473
has perspective summary WHO's WISN method sets staffing requirements from the workload of a health facility rather than from population-to-staff ratios or fixed facility standards, which ignore local variation in demand and the work staff actually do. It estimates each cadre's available working time, sets standard workloads for its main activities, adds allowance factors for support and additional activities, and compares current with required staff, a smaller WISN ratio meaning greater work pressure. Using the workloads of planned future services allows the staff needed for those services to be calculated.
has perspective title Workload-Based Staffing Requirements With the WISN Method
has primary source label World Health Organization, Workload indicators of staffing need (WISN): user's manual, second edition (ISBN 9789240070066, October 2023), sections 1.1, 1.2, 3.2 to 3.8 and 4.4

institutional perspective of WHO on Concentration Curve

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000352
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Concentration Curve
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240102606
has perspective summary WHO's 2024 handbook on health inequality monitoring uses the concentration curve to show how the absolute and relative concentration indices are calculated. Subgroups are ranked by an ordered social dimension, with the cumulative population share on the x-axis and the cumulative share of the health indicator on the y-axis. With no systematic difference in health across the dimension, the curve runs along the 45-degree diagonal, and the further it lies from that line, the greater the inequality. If health does not follow the subgroup ordering, these measures may suggest little inequality.
has perspective title Curve Plots Cumulative Health Share Against Ranked Population
has primary source label World Health Organization, Health inequality monitoring: harnessing data to advance health equity (2024), ISBN 978-92-4-010260-6, Chapter 21 (Complex summary measures of health inequality: ordered disproportionality measures) and Annex 17
has wiki record identifier concentration-curve

institutional perspective of WHO on Concentration Index

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000353
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Concentration Index
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/379703
has perspective summary WHO's 2024 book on health inequality monitoring treats the concentration index as an ordered disproportionality measure, weighted by population size, for dimensions with a natural order such as wealth or education. The absolute concentration index is twice the area between the line of equality and the concentration curve, and the relative index divides it by the setting average, bounding it between minus 1 and plus 1. Zero means no inequality and positive values show concentration among advantaged subgroups. WHO notes the measures can suggest low inequality when health does not follow the subgroup ordering.
has perspective title Absolute and Relative Concentration Indices for Ordered Inequality
has primary source label World Health Organization, Health inequality monitoring: harnessing data to advance health equity (ISBN 9789240102606, December 2024), chapter 21, summary measures based on ordered inequality dimensions

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cross-Price Elasticity
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240019188
has perspective summary WHO advises policy-makers to know the own-price, cross-price and income elasticities of demand for tobacco products in their country, and to update the estimates regularly, so that the effect of a tax rise on consumption and revenue can be anticipated. It defines cross-price elasticity as the change in demand for one product when the price of another changes, with a positive value signalling substitutes, such as hand-rolling tobacco and manufactured cigarettes. Most studies find e-cigarettes and conventional cigarettes to be partial substitutes, while several studies in India found bidis and manufactured cigarettes to be complements.
has perspective title Cross-Price Elasticity Needed to Forecast Tobacco Tax Effects
has primary source label World Health Organization, WHO technical manual on tobacco tax policy and administration (2021), ISBN 978-92-4-001918-8, sections 2.2.3 (Key takeaway 14) and 2.4.2

has perspective summary The WHO Consultative Group on Equity and Universal Health Coverage recommends that countries sort services into high, medium and low priority classes using criteria related to cost-effectiveness, priority to the worse off and financial risk protection. It suggests starting with cost-effectiveness estimates and then integrating the concern for the worse off and other relevant criteria, and finds an exclusive focus on cost-effectiveness generally indefensible. The criteria should be specified and balanced through public deliberation and participatory procedures.

has perspective summary WHO holds that decisions on health benefit packages should be evidence-based, unbiased, impartial and fair, and seen as fair by all affected parties. Package design should respect the difference between data, dialogue and decision: rigorous scientific assessment free of conflicts of interest, a transparent deliberative appraisal involving all appropriate stakeholders, and a final political decision by those accountable for it, who may weigh considerations beyond expert evaluation. Deliberations, reasoning and trade-offs should be made public and communicated to decision makers and citizens.

has perspective summary WHO's global strategy on digital health, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2020, sets a vision of accelerating the development and adoption of appropriate, accessible, affordable, scalable and sustainable person-centric digital health solutions. It states that digital health will be valued and adopted if it supports equitable and universal access to quality health services, makes health systems more efficient and sustainable, and strengthens services from health promotion to palliative care while protecting the privacy of patient information. A strategic objective calls for inclusive approaches to adoption, including digital health literacy and preparing health workers to use the technologies.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020924
has perspective summary WHO's global strategy on digital health defines the digital divide as the gap between demographics and regions that have access to modern information and communications technology and those that do not or have restricted access, including the telephone, television, personal computers and the internet. The strategy is designed for use by all Member States, including those with limited access to digital technologies, goods and services. It promotes digital technologies as adaptable digital public goods that support equity in access to digital resources so that no one is left behind, and lists improving digital health literacy at population level among possible actions.

has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020924
has perspective summary WHO's global strategy on digital health asks that, when digital health interventions are planned and prioritised, relevant factors of inequality are assessed so that introducing the technologies does not aggravate them, a "do no harm" test, and that access for specific population groups is guaranteed. It calls for stronger gender equality and health equity approaches and accessibility for people with disabilities, to promote an inclusive digital society with better digital health skills. The strategy adds that, designed properly, digital solutions can promote inclusiveness because digital connectivity can transcend physical barriers.

has perspective summary WHO's global strategy on digital health, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2020, understands digital health as the field of knowledge and practice associated with the development and use of digital technologies to improve health. The definition encompasses eHealth and extends it to digital consumers with a wider range of smart and connected devices, and to the Internet of Things, advanced computing, big data analytics, artificial intelligence including machine learning, and robotics. WHO states that digital health should be an integral part of health priorities and benefit people in ways that are ethical, safe, secure, reliable, equitable and sustainable.

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240010567
has perspective summary WHO's Digital Implementation Investment Guide sets out a process for countries to produce a costed implementation plan for integrating digital interventions into health programmes. It warns that the full costs of digital health implementations are frequently underestimated because budgets focus on the initial demonstration or deployment and omit long-term operation and maintenance. Planners are asked to estimate the total cost of ownership across development and setup, deployment, integration and interoperability, scale and sustained operations, identifying the cost drivers for each phase.

has perspective summary WHO's Global Health Estimates compute years lived with disability using disability weights on a scale from 0 for perfect health to 1 for a state equivalent to death. WHO holds that the weights should reflect general population judgements about the healthfulness of defined states, not judgements of quality of life, the worth of persons or stigma. Its estimates for 2000 to 2021 draw on Global Burden of Disease 2021 weights, derived from large population surveys of paired comparisons, with WHO's own revisions for conditions including infertility, intellectual disability, vision and hearing loss, dementia and low back pain.

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241564021
has perspective summary WHO defines efficiency as the quality or quantity of output, such as health outcomes or services, for a given level of input, and states that seeking efficiency gains does not mean simply cutting costs. It estimates that 20% to 40% of all health spending is wasted through inefficiency, describing this as a conservative, indicative figure based on relatively limited data. It identifies ten leading causes of inefficiency and argues that the resources released could be used to extend coverage towards universal health coverage.

has perspective summary WHO's principles for health benefit packages list cost-effectiveness and equity, including priority to the worse off, among possible selection criteria alongside burden of disease, financial risk protection and budget impact. WHO states that trade-offs between conflicting goals may be necessary and that explicit priority setting makes them transparent. Packages should achieve the greatest possible health benefit within the budget, and where other criteria are prioritised, the health loss resulting from the trade-off must be clearly communicated to decision makers and the public.

has perspective summary WHO describes health equity as achieved when everyone can attain their full potential for health and well-being, and equity as the absence of unfair, avoidable or remediable differences among groups defined socially, economically, demographically, geographically or by other dimensions such as sex, gender, ethnicity, disability or sexual orientation. It states that health and health equity are determined by the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, play and age, and that monitoring health inequality, with data disaggregated by age, sex, education, income, disability and other factors, must be central to national health information systems.

has perspective summary WHO's annual global spending report measures health spending as current health expenditure reported by Member States under the System of Health Accounts 2011, excluding capital expenditure, and compiled in the Global Health Expenditure Database with a two-year lag. Global spending fell in 2022 to US$ 9.8 trillion, or 9.9% of global GDP, while average health spending across countries was 6.7% of GDP. WHO distinguishes the two measures: the average is taken across countries, whereas the global share divides total health spending by total GDP.

institutional perspective of WHO on Moral Hazard

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Moral Hazard
has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241564021
has perspective summary The World Health Report 2010 identifies reliance on direct payments, including user fees, co-insurance, co-payments and deductibles, as the greatest obstacle to universal coverage. Charges at the point of use discourage use of services, particularly prevention, and encourage overuse by people who can pay and underuse by those who cannot. The report notes that OECD countries raised cost sharing to limit government spending and discourage unnecessary use, but that these payments cause financial hardship and reduce access. Financial catastrophe becomes negligible only when direct payments fall to 15 to 20 per cent of total health expenditure.
has perspective title Direct Payments and Cost Sharing as Barriers to Access
has primary source label World Health Organization, The World Health Report: Health Systems Financing: the Path to Universal Coverage (2010), Message from the Director-General; Executive summary; Chapter 1, Direct payments and Box 1.2 (page 5); Chapter 3, The problems with direct payments (pages 41 to 42) and The retreat from direct payments (pages 45 to 47)

has display order 3
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020689
has perspective summary WHO's principles for health benefit packages state that every decision within a finite budget carries an opportunity cost, since funding one intervention means that other services, which might have produced more health, protected the most vulnerable from impoverishment or improved access for the least advantaged, will not be provided. Countries should therefore use available resources in the most efficient manner, achieving the greatest possible health benefits within the budget constraint. Where other criteria are given priority, the health loss resulting from the trade-off must be clearly communicated.
has perspective title Every Benefit Package Decision Carries an Opportunity Cost

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/317ba614-5295-4f6f-baba-56f281f228f9/content
has perspective summary The WHO describes a tax that internalises costs to bring consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages to socially optimal levels as a Pigouvian tax. It rests the economic case on negative externalities, including lost productivity from diet-related noncommunicable diseases and treatment costs where health care is publicly funded, and on internalities, where people do not account for the future costs of current consumption. It treats excise taxes as the most important form of consumption tax for health objectives, and notes that taxes levied on sugar content can also encourage producers to reformulate.

has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/924156198X
has perspective summary WHO identifies three principal health system inputs, namely human resources, physical capital and consumables, bought with financial resources of both a capital and a recurrent character. It treats human resources as the most important input and notes that labour accounts for two-thirds or more of recurrent health expenditure in many countries. It notes that investment decisions are generally irreversible, and that new investment choices must be made carefully and the existing mix of inputs monitored regularly to reduce imbalances that impair performance.

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Scarcity
has display order 2
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241507158
has perspective summary A WHO report setting out the collective views of its Consultative Group on Equity and Universal Health Coverage states that available resources in every country fall short of what is required to meet all needs. Universal health coverage is therefore taken to require a comprehensive range of key services, not every beneficial one, and countries must choose which services to expand first. Ranking services by cost-effectiveness usually gives the largest sum of health benefits for a given budget, and the same criteria can guide displacing less important services within a fixed budget.
has perspective title No Country Can Cover Every Beneficial Service, So Priorities Must Be Set

has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/329389
has perspective summary WHO's guide to economic evaluation of immunisation programmes holds that vaccine impact in a population includes indirect effects in unvaccinated or unsuccessfully vaccinated people, whose exposure falls as circulation of the pathogen declines, and that these effects should be estimated from empirical data integrated in a mathematical model. Ignoring herd immunity is described as not best practice. A static model suits cases where vaccination is unlikely to change the force of infection in susceptibles, while a dynamic model is called for where it is likely to and a static model would not give a conservative estimate.

has primary source label World Health Organization, WHO guide for standardization of economic evaluations of immunization programmes, second edition (WHO/IVB/19.10, October 2019), sections 5.2, 5.4, 6.2 and 6.6

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Willingness-to-Pay Threshold
has display order 4
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5153921/
has perspective summary WHO staff writing in the WHO Bulletin trace GDP-based thresholds to the Commission on Macroeconomics and Health's estimate of the economic value of a year of healthy life, and compare them with value-of-life measures of willingness to pay for an extra healthy year. WHO-CHOICE authors called an intervention very cost-effective if it averted a DALY for less than average per capita income, and cost-effective below three times that level. None of these thresholds should be used alone as a funding rule or as a measure of affordability, and WHO-CHOICE has never recommended such use.

institutional perspective of WHO on Years Lived with Disability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000925
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Years Lived with Disability
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/gho-documents/global-health-estimates/ghe2023_daly_methods.pdf
has perspective summary WHO's Global Health Estimates calculate years lived with disability as the prevalence of each sequela multiplied by its disability weight, replacing the incidence-based method of the original Global Burden of Disease study and earlier WHO updates. WHO gives the reasons: an incidence count misses current burden when incidence has fallen, needs estimates of duration as well as incidence, and assigns all health loss to the age of onset. YLDs carry no discounting or age weighting and are adjusted for independent comorbidity, with disability weights combined multiplicatively for people with several conditions.
has perspective title Prevalence-Based YLDs Without Discounting or Age Weights
has primary source label World Health Organization, WHO methods and data sources for global burden of disease estimates 2000-2023, Global Health Estimates Technical Paper WHO/DSA/DDA/GHE/2026.3 (September 2026), sections 1.4, 2, 2.1 and 2.3 to 2.5

institutional perspective of WHO on Years of Life Lost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000926
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Years of Life Lost
has display order 1
has institution label as shown WHO
has page URL https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/gho-documents/global-health-estimates/ghe2023_daly_methods.pdf
has perspective summary WHO's Global Health Estimates calculate years of life lost as deaths at each age multiplied by a standard loss function giving the years lost for a death at that age. Because even the lowest observed death rates include avoidable deaths, WHO bases the standard on the frontier national life expectancy implied by the lowest projected age-specific mortality rates for 2050 in the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024, giving life expectancy at birth of 92.7 years. Since consultations in 2012, WHO has used a 0% discount rate and no age weighting.
has perspective title Standard Loss Function From Projected Frontier Life Expectancy
has primary source label World Health Organization, WHO methods and data sources for global burden of disease estimates 2000-2023, Global Health Estimates Technical Paper WHO/DSA/DDA/GHE/2026.3 (September 2026), sections 2, 2.2 (Table 2.1) and 2.3

has perspective summary The WHO Regional Office for Europe finds that the countries with the strongest financial protection apply user charges very sparingly, citing the United Kingdom, or protect people through exemptions for poor people and regular users of health services, annual caps on all co-payments per person, and low fixed co-payments in place of percentage co-payments. Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
has display order 2
has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/42699
has perspective summary The WHO guide to cost-effectiveness analysis sets out generalised CEA, in which a set of related interventions is first evaluated against a null scenario, the situation that would exist if none of those interventions were implemented. Because currently funded and new interventions are assessed together, the approach can identify existing allocative inefficiencies instead of taking the current mix of care as given. Results are first presented in a single league table, and WHO-CHOICE measures health effects in DALYs, recommending that other analysts do the same for comparability.

concerns wiki concept Cost-of-Illness Study
has display order 1
has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598293
has perspective summary WHO does not recommend the cost-of-illness approach for estimating the economic impact of disease or injury at the societal level. It describes traditional cost-of-illness studies as static, partial and inconsistent, citing an undefined quantity of interest, an unclear counterfactual, neglect of capital and human capital effects, and unrealistic human-capital valuation of lost production. Direct-cost elements may still answer narrower questions, such as spending on a given disease by households, firms or government.

has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020689
has perspective summary WHO states that one overarching goal of health benefit package design is to maximise population health within the available budget. Cost-effectiveness, meaning the value for money of an intervention, is listed as one possible selection criterion alongside burden of disease, equity, financial risk protection, budget impact, feasibility and political acceptability. Trade-offs between criteria should be explicit, and where other criteria are prioritised the resulting health loss should be clearly communicated.
has perspective title Cost-Effectiveness as One Criterion for Benefit Packages
has primary source label World Health Organization. Principles of health benefit packages (2021), ISBN 978-92-4-002068-9, principle 3 and table 2, pages 7 to 8

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://www.who.int/health-topics/health-equity
has perspective summary WHO defines equity as the absence of unfair, avoidable or remediable differences among groups of people, whether those groups are defined socially, economically, demographically, geographically or by dimensions such as sex, ethnicity or disability. It states that monitoring health inequality must be central to national health information systems, beginning with data disaggregated by age, sex, education, income and disability. It calls for services that are available, accessible and acceptable to everyone, and for action on the structural determinants that shape the distribution of power and resources.
has perspective title Identifying and Eliminating Unfair Health Differences

institutional perspective of World Health Organization on Externality

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1
has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/who-guide-for-standardization-of-economic-evaluations-of-immunization-programmes-2nd-ed
has perspective summary WHO defines externalities as costs or benefits of an individual's production or consumption decision that indirectly affect the well-being of others. Its guide counts indirect effects in unvaccinated or unsuccessfully vaccinated people, arising from reduced pathogen circulation, as part of total vaccine effectiveness, and states that ignoring effects such as herd immunity, serotype replacement or antimicrobial resistance is not best practice. Where vaccination directly reaches epidemiologically influential groups and negative externalities could exceed positive ones, its model-choice flow chart requires a dynamic transmission model.
has perspective title Include Indirect Vaccination Effects
has primary source label WHO Guide for Standardization of Economic Evaluations of Immunization Programmes, 2nd Edition (WHO/IVB/19.10), October 2019, Glossary (Externalities), section 5.2 and section 6.3.2.1 (Figure 5)

Type institutional perspective record

has display order 1

has perspective summary WHO analyses health financing through the functions of revenue raising, pooling and purchasing, with benefit design as a fourth policy area, whatever label a system carries, such as tax-based or health insurance. Its Health Financing Progress Matrix sets nineteen desirable attributes as benchmarks for progress towards universal health coverage, including funding that is predominantly public or compulsory, pooling that enhances redistribution of prepaid funds, purchasing that reflects population health needs and keeps budgetary control, and benefit changes preceded by cost-effectiveness and budget impact assessments.

has perspective summary WHO's 2025 guidance adopts the 2020 international definition of HTA and places HTA between regulatory approval for market access and the management of a technology across its lifetime. Regulators focus on quality, safety and performance, whereas HTA must also consider effectiveness, value for money, equity, acceptability to patients and providers, organisational impact and ethical issues. The guidance is aimed mainly at policy-makers in low- and middle-income countries and applies HTA from pre-market approval through procurement to reassessment and disinvestment.

institutional perspective of World Health Organization on Market Failure

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000685
Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Market Failure
has display order 1
has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240034204
has perspective summary WHO's normative guidance defines common goods for health as population-based functions or interventions, such as disease surveillance and health regulation, whose provision is subject to specific market failures because they are public goods, being non-rival and non-exclusionary, or have large social externalities. Because they will not arise through market forces alone and also suffer collective action failures, they are often underfunded, and WHO holds that they require public financing and public action. It treats this as distinct from the market failures of information asymmetry, risk selection and moral hazard that justify pooled financing of individual services.
has perspective title Market Failures Make Common Goods for Health a Case for Public Financing
has primary source label World Health Organization, Financing common goods for health (guidance, ISBN 9789240034204, 14 September 2021), chapters 1 and 2 and Box 1
has wiki record identifier market-failure

has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://www.who.int/publications-detail-redirect/analytical-guide-to-assess-a-mixed-provider-payment-system
has perspective summary WHO's analytical guide notes that in nearly all countries several payment methods co-exist as a mixed provider payment system, each creating incentives, chiefly towards over-provision or under-provision, shaped by the payment unit, rate, basis and timing. Misaligned methods and rates send incoherent signals that can undermine universal health coverage objectives. The guide proposes a five-step assessment: mapping purchasers, providers and payment methods; assessing incentives and their effects on provider behaviour; other health system effects; governance arrangements; and policy options to align payment methods within and across purchasers.
has perspective title Assessing Mixed Provider Payment Systems in Five Steps
has primary source label World Health Organization, Analytical guide to assess a mixed provider payment system (Mathauer and Dkhimi), Health Financing Guidance No. 5, WHO/UHC/HGF/Guidance/19.5 (2019), Part 1 and Box 1.4

institutional perspective of World Health Organization on Universal Health Coverage

has display order 1
has institution label as shown World Health Organization
has page URL https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/universal-health-coverage-(uhc)
has perspective summary WHO defines universal health coverage as all people having access to the full range of quality health services they need, when and where they need them, without financial hardship, from health promotion to palliative care. Under definitions revised in 2025, progress is tracked by a service coverage index scored from 0 to 100 and by the share of people whose out-of-pocket health spending exceeds 40% of the household discretionary budget. The 2025 monitoring report with the World Bank put the index at 71 in 2023 and financial hardship at 26% in 2022.

has perspective summary Productivity losses belong in the Dutch reference case, which takes a societal perspective, and paid and unpaid work count equally. For paid work the guideline separates absence from work (absenteeism) from reduced productivity while at work (presenteeism), noting that both may be important, and names the iMTA Productivity Cost Questionnaire as a frequently used instrument. Valuation must use the friction cost method, which assumes that staff absent for an extended period can be replaced, so losses arise mainly during the friction period an employer needs to replace them.

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland measures disease burden with proportional shortfall, which sets the reference value for the maximum acceptable cost per QALY. Its disease burden method also reports absolute shortfall, the total quality-adjusted future life years lost to the condition, together with the remaining QALYs with the condition. Absolute shortfall is presented as a proxy for the fair innings view, which gives younger patients more priority, so that conflicts with the proportional measure stay visible and can be weighed as separate arguments in the final advice.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/heiro/HEIRO_6000127
Type institutional perspective record

has display order 3

has page URL https://www.zorginstituutnederland.nl/financiering/fondsbeheer-zvf-en-flz/zorgverzekeringsfonds/wat-is-risicoverevening
has perspective summary ZIN explains that Dutch health insurers must accept everyone for the basic insurance and charge the same basic premium to all, so they may not offer lower premiums to young, healthy people to attract them, a practice it calls risk selection. Because some insurers carry more high-risk enrolees, ZIN administers risk equalisation, paying each insurer a contribution from the Health Insurance Fund based on its enrolees' risk profiles. The profiles use age, sex, region and health indicators such as medicine use and hospital visits, with norm amounts set each year by the health minister.
has perspective title Risk Equalisation Supports Open Enrolment and Uniform Premiums

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland describes a lock under which the Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport can temporarily keep new, expensive hospital medicines out of the basic health insurance package. A medicine becomes a candidate if it would cost €20 million or more a year across one or more new indications, or €10 million or more a year in one indication at €50,000 or more per patient per year, counting drug costs only. The institute then assesses necessity, effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and feasibility, and the medicine leaves the lock only after successful price negotiation.

has perspective summary ZIN requires all standard parametric distributions to be evaluated and reported when trial time-to-event data are extrapolated, with spline and cure models allowed only if these are insufficient. Statistical fit must be evaluated using the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, after visual fit and the proportional hazards assumption, and the AIC and BIC for each distribution studied must be reported. ZIN states that these steps address internal validity only, so clinical and external plausibility of the extrapolation matters more.

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland's guideline requires validation of a model-based economic evaluation to cover the conceptual model, the input data, the software implementation and the model outcomes, reported with the AdViSHE checklist. The conceptual model needs at least cross validation against other models and earlier institute assessments, with expert face validation where differences are found, and operational validation compares model results with input data and with empirical data not used as input.

has perspective summary In the Netherlands, the National Health Care Institute assesses whether care can be reimbursed from the basic health insurance package and receives advice from two independent committees. The Scientific Advisory Board reviews whether the Institute's conclusions on how well care works, for which patients, and on the quality of the cost-effectiveness assessment are scientifically well founded. The Insured Package Advisory Committee then advises from a societal perspective against the criteria of necessity, effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and feasibility, mainly where social impact is high, and the Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport decides.
has perspective title Scientific Board Checks the Assessment Before the Package Committee Advises

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Attrition
has display order 3
has institution label as shown ZIN
has page URL https://english.zorginstituutnederland.nl/site/binaries/site-content/collections/documents/2024/01/16/guideline-for-economic-evaluations-in-healthcare/guideline-for-economic-evaluations-in-healthcare.pdf
has perspective summary The Dutch guideline for economic evaluations requires missing data to be handled in the statistical analysis, since ignoring it can distort estimates and precision. Simple methods such as complete case analysis usually suffice only when under 5% of data are missing or data are missing completely at random; where data are missing at random, multiple imputation must be used, with scenario analyses testing that assumption because it cannot be told apart from missing not at random. Reports should state the amount of missing data, the likely mechanism and any imputation methods.
has perspective title Complete Case Analysis Only Below 5% Missing, Otherwise Multiple Imputation
has primary source label Zorginstituut Nederland, Guideline for economic evaluations in healthcare (2024 version, published 16 January 2024), sections 4.3 and 5.2.1

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Background Mortality
has display order 1
has institution label as shown ZIN

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland's guideline for economic evaluations requires survival curves extrapolated beyond trial follow-up to be checked for clinical and external plausibility against longer trials, registries or clinical experts. If an extrapolation implies higher survival than that of the general Dutch population, it must be adjusted, so general population mortality sets a limit on modelled survival. Where data are immature, the base case uses the most conservative plausible curve, giving the smallest incremental difference in life expectancy, with scenario analyses for other distributions and shorter time horizons.
has perspective title Extrapolated Survival Must Not Exceed That of the General Dutch Population

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland's guideline requires the results of both the base case analysis and scenario analyses to be based on the probabilistic analysis, a change from the 2016 version, and now includes medical costs in life years gained in the base case. has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland's guideline names heterogeneity in the baseline risk of events, with heterogeneity in the effectiveness of an intervention, as a type that can currently enter reimbursement decisions. has perspective summary The Dutch guideline for economic evaluations requires the results of both the base case and the scenario analyses to be based on the probabilistic analysis, which varies all uncertain inputs at once by Monte Carlo simulation. has perspective summary The intervention must be compared with the standard or usual intervention in Dutch practice at the time. The standard intervention is the first choice under clinical guidelines or practice; where none exists, the usual intervention, meaning the one used most frequently, applies and may be watchful waiting with supportive or palliative care. If the standard or usual intervention is not the most cost-effective option available in the Netherlands, the most cost-effective intervention must also be compared, using a fully incremental analysis.

has perspective summary All relevant costs are included irrespective of who bears them: health care costs, including those in life years gained, costs for patients and family such as travel and informal care, and costs in other sectors, each calculated as volume times price. institutional perspective of ZIN on Cream Skimming

Type institutional perspective record
concerns wiki concept Cream Skimming
has display order 3

has page URL https://www.zorginstituutnederland.nl/financiering/fondsbeheer-zvf-en-flz/zorgverzekeringsfonds/wat-is-risicoverevening
has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland explains that Dutch insurers must accept everyone for the basic insurance and may not charge higher premiums to people who are chronically ill or at higher risk, nor lower premiums to attract young, healthy people, which it calls risk selection. It carries out risk equalisation so that insurers with many members from high-risk groups, such as older people and people with chronic conditions, are compensated through the Health Insurance Fund. Payments reflect expected costs based on age, sex, region and health indicators such as medicine use and hospital visits, and insurers still bear financial risk.
has perspective title Risk Equalisation Alongside the Acceptance Obligation and Equal Premiums

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland compares a usable ICER with the reference value for the burden of disease involved: a point estimate below it is in principle favourable, while an ICER above it makes cost-effectiveness unlikely. The closer the ICER lies to the reference value, the better the methodological quality and the smaller the uncertainty must be. The reference values are a starting point for discussion rather than a cut-off, and after this test the institute, advised by its Package Advisory Committee, weighs arguments for accepting higher or lower costs per QALY alongside effectiveness, necessity and feasibility.

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland requires future costs to be discounted at a constant 3% and future effects at a constant 1.5% in the reference case whenever data are collected or modelled over more than one year. The cost rate builds on the 2.25% rate for social cost benefit analysis, adjusted upwards for current market developments. The lower rate for effects reflects the view that the value of health grows over time, and equals the cost rate minus an assumed 1.5% annual growth in the consumption value of health, set slightly below the average of an estimated Dutch range of 0.6% to 2.9%.

has perspective summary The Dutch guideline lists discrete event simulation among the commonly used model types, with the choice depending largely on the research question and the nature of the disease. has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland notes that medicines and surgical procedures can cause side effects or complications that affect quality of life, and that those with long-term and short-term consequences should be distinguished. Their effects on quality of life, usually referred to as disutilities, must be measured with the EQ-5D-5L, or the EQ-5D-Y, completed at the moment the side effects or complications occur. Where this is impossible, the disutility values and their durations should be based on scientific literature.

has perspective summary ZIN states that a fully incremental analysis should be used to report outcomes whenever more than two interventions are compared. Interventions are ranked in a table from low to high costs or QALYs, those that are strongly or weakly dominated are identified, and ICERs are calculated only for the interventions that are not dominated. The results can be presented as an efficiency frontier, and the same approach applies when several usual interventions exist or the usual intervention is not the most cost-effective option.

has perspective summary ZIN treats cost-effectiveness as one of the four criteria for the Dutch basic healthcare package, and its 2024 guideline sets a reference case with which all economic evaluations carried out for decision-making must comply. has perspective summary ZIN treats maximising health gain from premium income as a fair starting point, while recognising a competing view that resources should narrow differences in health, giving priority to patients with a high burden of disease. Citing research on solidarity, it states that society considers higher costs per QALY fair for more severe disease. Burden is measured with the proportional shortfall method, and the reference value is up to €20,000 per QALY for a burden of 0.10 to 0.40, €50,000 for 0.41 to 0.70 and €80,000 for 0.71 to 1.00.

has perspective summary ZIN requires the intervention under consideration to be one that can be applied in Dutch clinical practice within the defined patient population. An accurate description is needed of how the patient or carer will use it, and it must be clear whether the intervention replaces or supplements an existing one. It is compared with the standard or usual intervention in Dutch practice, the most cost-effective alternative is added when the standard is not, and several standard or usual interventions need separate comparisons, which can be made by fully incremental analysis.

Reports give the lower and upper ICER for each parameter in a table and show the most influential parameters in a tornado diagram.

has perspective summary ZIN requires model input parameters to be estimated from empirical data with recommended statistical methods and, where no data exist, allows expert elicitation, which must use a structured method such as SHELF, Delphi or Cooke. In deterministic analyses each parameter is varied over a range based on its standard error; without one, expert elicitation is required for parameters with a major effect, while plus or minus 20% within logical limits suffices for those with a minor effect. Distributions for probabilistic analysis must be reported and justified, use the same ranges, and preserve correlations, for example through Cholesky decomposition.

has perspective summary All economic evaluations carried out for decision-making in the Netherlands must comply with the reference case, and other choices may appear only as justified scenario analyses that cannot replace it. Value of information analysis, as EVPI and EVPPI, is obligatory for model-based evaluations.

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland expresses effects in a cost-utility analysis as QALYs by multiplying health-related quality of life, referred to as utilities, by life years. Patients describe their own health status with a validated generic questionnaire, and the resulting state is valued with a fixed tariff based on preferences in the general public. Quality of life should be measured with the EQ-5D-5L and valued with the Dutch tariff, using the EQ-5D-Y-3L for children aged 8 to 12 and proxy versions where needed; disutilities from side effects must also use the EQ-5D-5L.

has perspective summary The 2024 Dutch guideline makes value of information analysis, in the form of the expected value of perfect information (EVPI) and expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI), an obligatory element of model-based economic evaluations. Both are derived from the probabilistic analysis, scaled to the population that benefits over a time horizon of at least 5 years, and reported at least at population level in an EVP(P)I curve. EVSI and ENBS are optional further analyses, used when population EVP(P)I is high relative to the cost of more research.

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland makes value of information analysis, as the expected value of perfect information and of partial perfect information, an obligatory part of the reference case for model-based economic evaluations. All parameters in the probabilistic analysis enter the EVPI, and both measures are scaled to the population affected over a time horizon of at least 5 years. If population EVPI is below the cost of further research, decisions can rest on current information; otherwise expected value of sample information and expected net benefit of sampling can show which research is worthwhile. Results appear as EVPI curves across reference values.

has perspective summary When more than two interventions are compared, Zorginstituut Nederland's guideline requires a fully incremental analysis in which the interventions are ranked from low to high costs or QALYs and those that are strongly and weakly dominated are identified. ICERs are then calculated only for the interventions that are not dominated, and the results can be presented on an efficiency frontier. The guideline does not define weak dominance in its own text and cites Paulden (2020) for the procedure.

has perspective summary The Zorginstituut defines a reference value as, in principle, the maximum amount society wishes to spend per QALY gained, reflecting the societal value of an extra QALY. Values of €20,000, €50,000 and €80,000 per QALY apply as the proportional shortfall rises, because Dutch research on solidarity found that society accepts higher costs per QALY for more severe disease. The framework cites Dutch willingness to pay estimates of €52,000 per QALY for care for others and €83,000 for oneself or relatives, alongside opportunity cost evidence, and notes the values have not been indexed since 2015.

has perspective summary Zorginstituut Nederland requires data collected or modelled over more than one year to be discounted, with future costs at a constant 3% and future effects at a constant 1.5% in the reference case. The 3% cost rate builds on the 2.25% rate used in Dutch social cost-benefit analysis, adjusted upward for current market developments. The effects rate is the cost rate minus an assumed 1.5% annual growth in the consumption value of health. The 2024 revision adjusted the cost rate to 3%.
